prompt: Landlord Maya insures a rental house on a DP-3 and buys Coverage C for furnishings she keeps there. A supply line bursts, ruining the kitchen cabinets and soaking a sofa she owns. How does the DP-3 typically treat those two losses?

options.text: Open perils on the dwelling; named perils only on personal property
Named perils on both the dwelling and any personal property Maya schedules
Open perils on personal property and named perils only on the building shell
Fire, lightning, and internal explosion only on both dwelling and contents, regardless of cause

explanation: A DP-3 is the special dwelling form: Coverage A and B are open perils, subject to exclusions, while Coverage C personal property is named perils only. The cabinets are part of the dwelling, so water from the burst supply line is an open-peril dwelling loss unless an exclusion applies. The sofa she owns is Coverage C and is covered because accidental discharge of water from plumbing is one of those named perils. A sofa the tenant owns would not be Maya's Coverage C.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a basic/broad named-perils approach on the dwelling, not the DP-3 open-perils building coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the DP-3 split: the dwelling is open perils and personal property is named perils.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses DP-3 with the narrow DP-1 basic peril set of fire, lightning, and internal explosion.

prompt: The Nguyens want the broadest common homeowners package for their primary residence. Their agent recommends HO-5 instead of HO-3. Which difference best explains that recommendation?

options.text: HO-5 covers only the dwelling; personal property needs a separate floater
HO-5 uses open perils on both the dwelling and personal property
HO-5 is written for tenants and does not cover the building
HO-5 settles losses at actual cash value and does not offer replacement cost

explanation: HO-5 (comprehensive) is the broadest standard homeowners form because both Coverage A dwelling and Coverage C personal property are open perils, subject to exclusions. HO-3 typically keeps open perils on the dwelling but named perils on personal property, which is the gap the Nguyens want to close.

distractorExplanations.a: Incorrectly claims HO-5 omits personal property; HO-5 includes Coverage C on an open-perils basis.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses HO-5 with HO-4, the tenants form that does not insure the dwelling.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates settlement: HO-5 can provide replacement cost on the dwelling when conditions are met, not ACV-only.

prompt: Accountant Priya runs a one-room bookkeeping practice from a spare bedroom in her HO-3 residence and sees a few clients there each week. Her underwriter says the base policy's business exclusion applies. Which endorsement is designed for that limited use?

options.text: Earthquake endorsement with a separate percentage deductible
Scheduled personal property for her office laptop only
Permitted incidental occupancy for a small on-premises business
Ordinance or law endorsement raising Coverage A by a fixed percent

explanation: A permitted incidental occupancy endorsement extends homeowners coverage for a small, incidental business operated on the residence premises—such as a home office or tutoring room—where the base HO form would otherwise exclude or sharply limit business exposures. It is not a substitute for a full commercial package when the business grows beyond incidental use.

distractorExplanations.a: Addresses earth movement, not the business-use / incidental occupancy gap on the residence.
distractorExplanations.b: Schedules listed property values; it does not authorize a business occupancy on the premises.
distractorExplanations.d: Addresses building-code upgrade costs after a covered loss, not business occupancy permission.

prompt: Investor Carl buys the cheapest dwelling form for a vacant rental he plans to rehab. Wind drives a tree through the roof; the adjuster says the peril was never on the policy. Which form and settlement pattern best match that outcome?

options.text: DP-3 open perils on the dwelling with replacement cost by default
DP-2 broad named perils including falling objects without endorsement
HO-5 open perils on dwelling and contents for owner-occupants only
DP-1 basic named perils, often settling covered building loss at ACV

explanation: DP-1 covers fire, lightning, and internal explosion unless the insured adds extended coverage or vandalism. Extended coverage includes windstorm or hail. It does not add falling objects; that peril is on the DP-2 broad form. A tree driven by wind is outside the bare three-peril form, which is why the adjuster denied it. Covered building losses on DP-1 are commonly settled at actual cash value unless a replacement-cost endorsement is added.

distractorExplanations.a: A DP-3 would usually cover a wind-driven tree as an open peril. Replacement cost is not the DP-3 default; it takes an endorsement.
distractorExplanations.b: DP-2 includes windstorm and falling objects, so this tree loss would normally be covered. That is not the cheapest basic form Carl bought.
distractorExplanations.c: HO-5 is a homeowners owner-occupant form, not the bare-bones vacant rental dwelling Carl bought.

prompt: Elena's dwelling replacement cost is $400,000. Her HO-3 carries only $240,000 on Coverage A with an 80% coinsurance requirement. A covered fire causes $80,000 of dwelling damage. Ignoring the deductible, how does coinsurance affect recovery?

options.text: She recovers $60,000 because she insured only 75% of the required amount
She recovers the full $80,000 because any fire loss waives coinsurance
She recovers $32,000 by applying the 40% gap under full replacement cost to the loss
She recovers nothing because Coverage A below 80% voids the entire policy

explanation: The homeowners insurance-to-value condition works like 80% coinsurance. Required insurance is 80% of $400,000, which is $320,000. Elena carries $240,000, so the fraction is 240/320 = 0.75, and 0.75 times the $80,000 loss is $60,000 before the deductible. The form pays the greater of that proportion and actual cash value; depreciation was not given, so the coinsurance result is $60,000. Carrying less than 80% reduces the payment. It does not void the policy.

distractorExplanations.b: Fire does not waive coinsurance; the penalty still applies when Coverage A is below the required percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies the 40% gap under full replacement cost (240,000 is 60% of 400,000) to the loss and gets $32,000. The fraction uses 80% of replacement cost as the denominator: 240,000/320,000 times the loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Underinsurance reduces the payable amount; it does not void the whole homeowners policy.

prompt: College student Jamal rents an apartment and owns furniture, a TV, and a laptop. A kitchen fire started by a neighbor damages his belongings; the building belongs to the landlord. Which homeowners form fits Jamal?

options.text: HO-3, because every renter automatically gets dwelling Coverage A
HO-4, covering his belongings and liability, not the building
HO-6, written only for owners of freestanding single-family houses
HO-8, which replaces the entire apartment building after any fire

explanation: HO-4 is the tenants (contents) form: it covers the renter's personal property and Section II liability/medical payments, but not the landlord's building. Jamal needs Coverage C-style protection for his furniture and electronics, not Coverage A on walls he does not own.

distractorExplanations.a: HO-3 is an owner-occupant dwelling form with Coverage A; renters do not insure the building with HO-3.
distractorExplanations.c: HO-6 is for condominium unit owners, not apartment renters, and it is not limited to freestanding houses.
distractorExplanations.d: HO-8 is a modified owner form for older dwellings; it does not insure a landlord's apartment building for a tenant.

prompt: After a covered kitchen fire at the Ortega family's HO-3 home, the adjuster separates the claim into the house itself, the detached garage, furniture, and temporary hotel bills. Which of these is Coverage A?

options.text: The hotel and restaurant bills while the residence is uninhabitable
The detached garage and fence away from the dwelling
The dwelling and attached structures on the residence premises
The family's furniture, clothing, and other personal belongings

explanation: Coverage A insures the dwelling on the residence premises—the house and structures attached to it, plus fixtures and construction materials on site. Detached other structures are Coverage B, personal property is Coverage C, and additional living expense / fair rental value fall under Coverage D (loss of use).

distractorExplanations.a: Describes Coverage D loss of use / additional living expense, not Coverage A.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes Coverage B other structures, which are set apart from the dwelling by clear space.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes Coverage C personal property, not the dwelling building.

prompt: A moderate earthquake cracks the foundation of Dana's HO-3 house and shatters china inside. Her base policy denies the claim. What must she have added beforehand to buy back that peril?

options.text: Flood insurance through a separate NFIP or private flood policy only
A water/sewer backup endorsement for drain and sump overflow
An ordinance or law endorsement for code upgrades after a loss
An earthquake endorsement, usually with its own percent deductible

explanation: Standard homeowners and dwelling forms exclude earth movement, including earthquake. Coverage is added only by a specific earthquake endorsement (or a separate quake policy), typically with a percentage deductible of Coverage A rather than the policy's flat dollar deductible.

distractorExplanations.a: Flood is a different excluded peril; NFIP/private flood does not cover earthquake shaking damage.
distractorExplanations.b: Sewer/sump backup addresses water from drains and sumps, not seismic earth movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Ordinance or law pays code-upgrade costs after a covered loss; it does not add the earthquake peril itself.

prompt: River water rises into Luis's basement after days of rain, destroying the furnace and stored boxes. His HO-3 has no flood endorsement or separate flood policy. How should the claim be handled?

options.text: Deny it; flood and surface water are excluded on standard homeowners forms
Pay it under Coverage A because any water damage is an open peril
Pay only the furnace under Coverage B as an other structure
Pay additional living expense automatically even if the dwelling claim is denied

explanation: Flood, overflow of a body of water, and surface water are standard exclusions on HO and DP forms. Without a flood policy (NFIP or private) or a rare flood endorsement where offered, the rising river water loss is not covered—open perils on HO-3 still yield to listed exclusions.

distractorExplanations.b: Open perils still respect the flood/surface-water exclusion; not every water loss is covered.
distractorExplanations.c: A furnace serving the dwelling is not paid as Coverage B merely to dodge the flood exclusion.
distractorExplanations.d: Loss of use follows a covered property peril; an excluded flood does not trigger Coverage D.

prompt: A hailstorm destroys a 12-year-old composition roof. Replacement today costs $18,000; depreciation for age and wear is $7,000. The HO-3 pays dwelling losses at replacement cost if the insured rebuilds, otherwise at ACV. If the insured cashes out and does not replace the roof, what is payable before deductible?

options.text: $18,000, because hail always forces full replacement cost
$11,000 actual cash value after subtracting depreciation
$7,000, which is just the depreciation holdback amount
$25,000, adding replacement cost and depreciation together

explanation: Actual cash value is typically replacement cost minus depreciation for age and condition. If the insured does not repair or replace, the policy pays ACV: $18,000 − $7,000 = $11,000 (before deductible). Replacement cost is earned when the property is actually replaced under the policy's RC conditions—not when the insured simply cashes out.

distractorExplanations.a: Replacement cost usually requires repair/replacement; cashing out without replacing yields ACV.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays only the depreciation figure instead of RC minus depreciation (the ACV).
distractorExplanations.d: Incorrectly adds depreciation on top of replacement cost rather than subtracting it.

prompt: Nadia owns a condominium unit. A grease fire ruins her interior finishes, cabinets, and personal property; the association master policy covers the building shell and common elements. Which form should Nadia carry?

options.text: HO-4 tenants form, because condo owners never insure interiors
HO-8 modified form built just for historic farmhouses
HO-6 unit-owners form for interiors, contents, and liability
DP-1 dwelling basic form covering the entire high-rise structure

explanation: HO-6 is the condominium unit-owners form. It covers the unit owner's improvements, betterments, and personal property, plus Section II liability, while the association's master policy typically covers the building and common areas per the condo documents. It is the standard match for Nadia's exposure.

distractorExplanations.a: HO-4 is for renters; condo unit owners normally need HO-6 for unit interiors and betterments.
distractorExplanations.b: HO-8 is a modified form for older dwellings with valuation issues, not the condo unit-owners form.
distractorExplanations.d: A DP-1 on the whole high-rise is the association's or landlord's problem, not Nadia's unit policy.

prompt: At a backyard cookout, guest Ryan trips on a loose patio stone at the Kim family's insured residence and breaks his wrist. He sues the Kims for medical bills and lost wages. Which homeowners coverage responds to that liability claim?

options.text: Coverage A dwelling, because the patio stone is part of the house
Coverage C personal property for Ryan's damaged clothing only
Coverage D loss of use for the Kims' temporary hotel stay
Coverage E personal liability for legal liability to others

explanation: Coverage E (Section II personal liability) pays sums the insured becomes legally obligated to pay because of bodily injury or property damage to others, plus defense costs, subject to exclusions. A guest injury suit from a premises condition is a classic Coverage E claim; Coverage A/C/D are first-party property coverages.

distractorExplanations.a: Coverage A pays to repair the insured's dwelling, not third-party bodily injury lawsuits.
distractorExplanations.b: Coverage C is the insured's personal property; it does not defend premises liability suits.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage D pays the insured's extra living costs after a covered property loss, not guest injury liability.

prompt: A covered fire makes the Patel family's HO-3 house uninhabitable for six weeks. They stay in a hotel, eat more restaurant meals, and keep paying their mortgage. Which coverage pays the necessary increase in living expenses?

options.text: Coverage D loss of use for extra living costs after a covered loss
Coverage B other structures for hotels treated as temporary dwellings
Coverage F medical payments for the family's hotel stress claims
Coverage A dwelling, which automatically includes all living costs

explanation: Coverage D (loss of use) pays additional living expense—the reasonable increase in living costs when a covered peril makes the residence premises unfit to live in—and may also include fair rental value for rented portions. The mortgage continues either way; Coverage D addresses the extra hotel and meal costs caused by the covered fire.

distractorExplanations.b: Coverage B insures detached structures on the premises, not hotel bills after a loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage F is medical payments to others for guest injuries, not the insured family's living expenses.
distractorExplanations.d: Coverage A rebuilds the dwelling; it does not by itself pay additional living expense.

prompt: A city sewer main backs up through a floor drain and soaks Omar's finished basement. His HO-3 excludes water that backs up through sewers or drains. What endorsement is meant to address that gap?

options.text: Earthquake endorsement with a percentage deductible on Coverage A
Water backup / sump overflow endorsement for sewer backups
Scheduled personal property listing each piece of basement furniture
Incidental occupancy endorsement for a basement hobby workshop

explanation: Standard HO forms commonly exclude water that backs up through sewers, drains, or sumps. A water backup and sump overflow endorsement (names vary by insurer) specifically buys back limited coverage for that cause of loss, often with its own sublimit and deductible.

distractorExplanations.a: Earthquake endorsements address earth movement, not sewer or drain backup water.
distractorExplanations.c: Scheduling property raises limits/valuation for listed items; it does not add the backup peril.
distractorExplanations.d: Incidental occupancy addresses business use of the home, not sewer backup water damage.

prompt: A seasonal cottage insured on a dwelling form has been empty of people and furnishings for four months while the owner lives elsewhere. Vandals smash windows and spray-paint walls. Why might vandalism coverage be restricted or unavailable?

options.text: Because any unoccupied weekend trip immediately voids all property coverage
Because vandalism is not a covered peril on any dwelling or homeowners form
Because vacancy for a stated period often suspends vandalism coverages
Because HO-5 pays vandalism, and dwelling forms do not include that peril

explanation: Many dwelling and commercial property forms suspend or limit vandalism (and sometimes other perils) after the building has been vacant for a stated number of consecutive days. Vacancy means substantially empty of contents and occupants; mere unoccupancy (people away but furnishings remain) is treated differently. A long-empty seasonal cottage can trigger those vacancy restrictions.

distractorExplanations.a: Short unoccupancy (vacation) does not by itself void the entire property policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Vandalism is often covered when the building is not vacant; it is not universally excluded.
distractorExplanations.d: Dwelling forms can include vandalism among named or open perils; HO-5 is not the sole source.

prompt: The Rivera family buys a standard HO-3 on their owner-occupied house. A mysterious stain ruins a living-room sofa; no listed named peril applies. The roof, however, collapses from the weight of ice and snow. How does HO-3 usually treat those two losses?

options.text: Both losses are open-peril personal property claims under Coverage C
Neither loss is covered because HO-3 is named perils on the dwelling only
The sofa is covered open perils; the roof collapse needs a DP-1 upgrade
The roof loss may be open-peril; the sofa needs a named peril

explanation: On HO-3, Coverage A is open perils, but collapse is excluded except for specified causes. Collapse from the weight of ice, snow, or sleet is one of those causes, because that weight is a Coverage C named peril, so the roof loss is typically paid. Coverage C itself stays on named perils, so a mysterious stain with no matching named peril is not covered. Open perils on personal property is an HO-5, not an HO-3.

distractorExplanations.a: HO-3 does not put Coverage C on open perils; that is the HO-5 approach.
distractorExplanations.b: HO-3 is open perils on the dwelling, not named-perils-only on the building.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the HO-3 split and wrongly says a roof ice-weight loss needs a DP-1.

prompt: Lightning ignites a detached tool shed 40 feet from Marcy's HO-3 house. The shed and the tools inside are destroyed; the house is untouched. Which coverage primarily pays for the shed building?

options.text: Coverage B other structures set apart from the dwelling
Coverage A dwelling, because any building on the lot is Coverage A
Coverage E personal liability for damage to the insured's own shed
Coverage F medical payments, which rebuilds damaged outbuildings

explanation: Coverage B insures other structures on the residence premises that are separated from the dwelling by clear space (or connected only by a fence, utility line, or similar). A detached shed is the textbook Coverage B risk; tools inside are Coverage C personal property, and Section II does not rebuild the insured's own structures.

distractorExplanations.b: Coverage A is the dwelling and attached structures, not a shed separated by clear space.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage E pays liability to others; it does not insure the named insured's own shed.
distractorExplanations.d: Coverage F pays medical bills for others' injuries; it does not rebuild outbuildings.

prompt: Thieves steal Ava's $15,000 engagement ring from her HO-3 home. The unendorsed policy's special limit for theft of jewelry is far below that value. Which endorsement is designed to insure that ring for an agreed amount?

options.text: Water backup endorsement increasing basement sublimits only
Scheduled personal property (jewelry floater) listing the ring
Earthquake endorsement applying a percentage deductible to Coverage C
Vacancy permit that waives jewelry limits while the home is empty

explanation: Scheduled personal property, sometimes called a personal articles floater, lists items such as jewelry, cameras, and fine arts, often for an agreed amount and broader perils. On an unendorsed HO-3, the special limit for theft of jewelry, watches, and furs is typically $1,500, so a $15,000 ring is not fully covered without the schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Water backup addresses sewer/sump water, not jewelry theft special limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Earthquake endorsements add quake peril; they do not schedule jewelry values.
distractorExplanations.d: A vacancy permit restricts some perils while a house is empty. It does not schedule jewelry or waive the theft special limit.

prompt: A hillside slides after heavy rain and pushes the retaining wall into the Garcia family's HO-3 garage, cracking the slab. No earthquake occurred. The insurer cites an exclusion. Which exclusion most directly applies?

options.text: Intentional loss by the named insured damaging their own property
Flood exclusion for overflow of a river onto the residence premises
Earth movement exclusion, which includes landslide and mudflow
Ordinance or law exclusion for the cost of a building-permit fee only

explanation: Homeowners forms exclude earth movement, and the exclusion commonly names earthquake, landslide, mine subsidence, and mudflow. A hillside that slides into the garage is a landslide, so the exclusion applies even though there was no earthquake. Flood insurance is a separate policy for river overflow and for mudflow; it does not pay this landslide. A standard earthquake endorsement covers shaking and does not, by itself, restore landslide coverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Intentional loss requires the insured to deliberately damage property; a natural slide is not intentional.
distractorExplanations.b: Flood is a separate exclusion; this fact pattern is earth movement (landslide), not river overflow.
distractorExplanations.d: Ordinance or law limits code-upgrade payments; it is not the exclusion that bars landslide damage itself.

prompt: After a covered fire damages part of an older house, the city requires the rebuild to add sprinklers and widen hallways. The HO-3 restores like kind and quality, but not the full extra cost of those code upgrades. Which endorsement is meant for that gap?

options.text: Scheduled personal property for tools used during reconstruction
Sewer backup endorsement paying for code-required sprinklers
Incidental occupancy endorsement treating the rebuild as a business
Ordinance or law coverage for demolition and code-upgrade costs

explanation: Ordinance or law coverage pays to demolish undamaged portions when a code requires it and to rebuild to current codes after a covered loss. An unendorsed ISO homeowners form often includes only about 10% of Coverage A for that increased cost, and older forms exclude it. The endorsement raises the amount for sprinklers, wiring, or layout changes the city requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Scheduling tools does not pay municipal code-upgrade costs on the dwelling rebuild.
distractorExplanations.b: Sewer backup addresses water from drains/sumps, not building-code upgrade expenses.
distractorExplanations.c: Incidental occupancy addresses business use of the home, not ordinance or law upgrade costs.

prompt: Neighbor child Mia falls from the Brooks family's swing set and needs an ER visit. The Brooks were not negligent, but they want the policy to pay Mia's small medical bills quickly without a liability lawsuit. Which coverage fits?

options.text: Coverage F medical payments to others, without proving liability
Coverage A dwelling, which pays guest medical bills after any fall
Coverage C personal property for Mia's torn clothing only
Coverage D loss of use while the swing set is being replaced

explanation: Coverage F (medical payments to others) pays reasonable medical expenses for bodily injury to a person on the insured location with permission, or in other limited off-premises situations, without requiring the insured to be legally liable. It is goodwill/no-fault medical coverage with low limits—not a substitute for Coverage E when a large liability claim follows.

distractorExplanations.b: Coverage A repairs the dwelling; it does not pay a guest's medical bills.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage C is the insured's personal property, not medical payments for an injured guest.
distractorExplanations.d: Coverage D pays the insured's extra living costs after a covered property loss, not guest ER bills.

prompt: The declarations list Jordan Lee as named insured at 12 Maple Street. Jordan's adult daughter, who does not live there, stores a boat at a marina across town. A fire destroys the boat. Under a standard HO-3, which statement is most accurate about residence premises and insured locations?

options.text: Any property Jordan owns anywhere in the state is automatically residence premises
Residence premises is the 12 Maple dwelling listed in the declarations
The marina slip becomes residence premises because the boat is stored there
Only the daughter is the named insured for property stored off-site

explanation: Residence premises is the dwelling, other structures, and grounds at the location shown in the declarations where the named insured resides. Insured location is a broader Section II term, but a marina across town is not the residence premises. Watercraft also carry a low special limit and often need separate boat coverage. The declarations address, not every place Jordan stores property, is the residence premises.

distractorExplanations.a: Residence premises is the declared residence address, not every property Jordan owns in the state.
distractorExplanations.c: Storing a boat at a marina does not make that slip the residence premises.
distractorExplanations.d: The named insured is who the declarations name (Jordan); the daughter is not automatically the named insured.

prompt: Landlord Sam compares DP-1 and DP-2 for a duplex. He wants named-peril coverage that includes weight of ice and snow and accidental discharge of water from plumbing, which DP-1 does not provide even with basic extended coverage. Which choice matches that need?

options.text: Stay on DP-1; those perils are already in the three-peril basic form
Buy HO-8, which is the broadest landlord dwelling special form
Move to DP-2 broad form for the wider named-peril list he wants
Buy only flood insurance, which includes ice weight and plumbing discharge

explanation: DP-2 (broad form) expands the named-peril list beyond DP-1 to include perils such as weight of ice, snow, or sleet and accidental discharge or overflow of water from plumbing/appliances (subject to exclusions and conditions). DP-1 remains the narrower basic set; HO-8 is a modified homeowners form for older owner dwellings, not the landlord broad dwelling upgrade Sam needs.

distractorExplanations.a: DP-1's basic peril set does not include ice-weight and plumbing discharge the way DP-2 does.
distractorExplanations.b: HO-8 is a modified owner homeowners form, not the DP-2 broad dwelling product for landlords.
distractorExplanations.d: Flood insurance covers flood, not ice-weight roof collapse or plumbing discharge as HO/DP named perils.

prompt: Angry after an argument, named insured Travis deliberately sets fire to his own HO-3 living room curtains; the fire spreads and damages the house. How do intentional-act rules affect the claim for Travis's own property?

options.text: Pay in full because fire is always a covered peril for the named insured
Pay Coverage E liability to Travis for damaging his own dwelling
Pay just Coverage F medical payments for Travis's smoke inhalation
Deny Travis's property claim under the intentional loss exclusion

explanation: Homeowners policies exclude intentional loss, meaning a loss the insured expects or intends. Arson by the named insured is the classic first-party denial. An HO-3 otherwise covers fire damage to the dwelling, but the intentional-loss exclusion still bars Travis. Coverage E does not pay an insured for his own house, and Coverage F does not pay the insured's own medical bills.

distractorExplanations.a: Covered peril lists do not override the intentional loss exclusion when the insured starts the fire.
distractorExplanations.b: Coverage E is liability to others; it does not pay the insured for deliberately damaging their own house.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage F is medical payments to others, not first-party benefits for the insured's intentional fire.

prompt: Burglars take $2,400 cash, a $3,500 watch, and a $900 laptop from Chloe's HO-3 home. Unendorsed Coverage C special limits apply: $200 on money and $1,500 on theft of jewelry/watches; the laptop has no special sublimit beyond Coverage C. Ignoring deductible, which recovery pattern is correct?

options.text: $200 for cash, $1,500 for the watch, and $900 for the laptop
Full $2,400 cash plus full $3,500 watch because theft waives special limits
$0 on all items because burglary is excluded on every HO-3 policy
The laptop alone; money and watches are not personal property under Coverage C

explanation: Unendorsed homeowners Coverage C applies categorical special limits: money is typically capped around $200, and theft of jewelry/watches/furs around $1,500, even when the item's actual value is higher. Ordinary electronics like a laptop usually settle within the full Coverage C limit without that jewelry-style theft cap. Scheduling would be needed to raise the jewelry and money recoveries.

distractorExplanations.b: Theft does not waive special limits; money and jewelry theft caps still apply on unendorsed HO-3.
distractorExplanations.c: Theft/burglary of personal property is generally a covered named peril on HO-3 Coverage C.
distractorExplanations.d: Money and watches are personal property; they are limited, not removed from Coverage C entirely.

prompt: Helen owns a 1910 frame house whose market value is far below full replacement cost. Insurers will not write HO-3 replacement cost on Coverage A. Which homeowners form is commonly used for that older-home valuation problem?

options.text: HO-5 comprehensive, which always forces functional replacement cost
HO-8 modified form with limited perils and functional/ACV settlement
HO-4 tenants form, rewritten to insure historic owner-occupied dwellings
HO-6 unit-owners form, required for any house built before 1950

explanation: HO-8 (modified coverage) is the homeowners form for an older house when full replacement cost far exceeds market value, so insurers will not write HO-3 replacement cost. It uses a shorter named-peril list than HO-3 and settles the dwelling at functional replacement cost: repair with common construction materials and methods, not the cost to reproduce the original 1910 construction. Licensing texts often call that settlement actual cash value as well.

distractorExplanations.a: HO-5 is the broad open-perils owner form, not the modified older-home valuation product.
distractorExplanations.c: HO-4 is for tenants' contents; it is not rewritten as the historic owner dwelling form.
distractorExplanations.d: HO-6 is for condominium unit owners, not every pre-1950 freestanding house.

prompt: Owner-occupant Drew asks why his own house is written on an HO-3 while the lakeside cottage he rents to others is written on a DP-3 dwelling fire policy. Which contrast correctly explains that pairing?

options.text: The HO-3 packages his home with liability and medical payments; the DP-3 omits that package unless a supplement is added
The DP-3 is the owner-occupant package and the HO-3 is only a bare fire form for vacant rentals, so the two policies should be swapped before a guest is injured at either place
Both policies include personal liability automatically, and the HO-3 merely uses a higher deductible on the cottage
The HO-3 covers the dwelling for named perils alone, while the DP-3 covers flood and earthquake on every rental

explanation: An HO-3 is a homeowners package for a residence the named insured occupies. Section I covers the dwelling and Section II adds personal liability and medical payments to others. A DP-3 is a dwelling fire property form used for a rental the insured does not occupy. It has no homeowners liability package unless a personal liability supplement is attached. Open-peril coverage on the building can exist on both forms, so that is not the contrast that places the cottage on the DP-3.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses eligibility. The HO-3 fits the owner-occupied house, and the DP-3 is the rental property form. Swapping them would put the package on the wrong occupancy.
distractorExplanations.c: Gives the DP-3 automatic liability it does not have. A dwelling fire policy needs a liability supplement before it answers a guest's injury lawsuit.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates both peril bases. The HO-3 dwelling is not named-peril only, and a DP-3 does not pick up flood or earthquake.

prompt: Beth's HO-2 lists only named perils on the dwelling. A painter drops an open can, and paint soaks the oak floor. Spilled paint is not one of the listed perils. What does that named-peril coverage pay for the floor?

options.text: The full refinishing bill, because an HO-2 dwelling is open perils and paint is covered unless the insurer cites flood or earthquake
Nothing for the floor, because spilled paint is not a listed peril
Half the refinishing bill, because every unlisted cause on a named-peril form is shared evenly under a coinsurance split
The loss is paid unless Beth names the cause, because the insurer must disprove coverage on every HO-2 claim

explanation: A named-peril form such as the HO-2 pays only when the cause is a peril the policy lists. Spilled paint is not on that list, so the oak floor is not covered and the insurer never has to reach an exclusion. Open-peril coverage, used for the dwelling on an HO-3, starts from the other direction: the loss is covered unless an exclusion applies. Coinsurance does not create coverage for a cause that was never named.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the HO-2 with open-peril dwelling coverage. On a named-peril form an unlisted cause is outside coverage even when flood and earthquake are never cited.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an even coinsurance split for unlisted causes. Coinsurance reduces a covered loss when the limit is too low; it does not insure a peril that was never listed.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the burden of proof. On the HO-2 the insured must show a listed peril. The insurer's burden to prove an exclusion belongs to open-peril coverage.

prompt: Sasha carries $160,000 of Coverage A. Rebuilding her house would cost $300,000. Her HO-3 reduces the payment when Coverage A is below 80% of rebuild cost, and depreciation is not given. A covered fire damages $36,000 of the structure. Before the deductible, what does the proportion pay?

options.text: The full $36,000, because a partial fire waives the insurance-to-value proportion
$19,200, from dividing the $160,000 limit by the $300,000 rebuild cost and then multiplying by the $36,000 loss
$24,000 of the fire damage
Nothing, because Coverage A below 80% of rebuild cost voids the entire homeowners policy

explanation: Insurance required is 80% of $300,000, which equals $240,000. Sasha carries $160,000, so the proportion is 160,000 / 240,000 = 2/3. Two-thirds of the $36,000 loss is $24,000 before the deductible. Depreciation was not given, so this proportion is the insurance-to-value result. Using the $300,000 rebuild cost as the denominator is the wrong fraction, and carrying less than 80% reduces the payment rather than voiding the policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a partial fire as a waiver. The insurance-to-value proportion still reduces the payment when Coverage A is below 80% of rebuild cost.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses rebuild cost as the denominator: 160,000 / 300,000 times $36,000 equals $19,200. The required amount is 80% of $300,000, so the fraction is 160,000 / 240,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats underinsurance as a voided policy. The proportion reduces what is payable on the covered fire; it does not cancel the HO-3.

prompt: Rodents chew through wiring in Hector's HO-3 attic. The cable is ruined and no fire starts. The policy excludes loss caused by birds, vermin, rodents, or insects. How should the wiring claim be handled?

Paid as fire, because any electrical damage inside an attic is labeled fire even when no flame occurred
Paid at half, because rodent damage is shared evenly with the insured when the chewing does not start a fire
Denied, because rodents caused the wiring loss

The chewed cable was caused by rodents, and no fire ensued, so the wiring claim is denied. An ensuing fire that rodents set could be covered as fire, but that second cause did not happen. The exclusion applies without a schedule and without a coinsurance split.

distractorExplanations.b: Mislabels the cause as fire. No flame occurred, so the fire peril never attaches and the rodent exclusion controls the claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an even split of the rodent loss. Chewed wiring is excluded, not shared with the insured, and a coinsurance split only adjusts a loss that is otherwise covered.

prompt: Paula's declarations show Coverage A of $200,000 and Coverage B at 10% of Coverage A. Wind destroys her detached studio and does not harm the house. Rebuilding the studio costs $16,000. Before the deductible, what is payable for the studio?

options.text: $16,000 under Coverage B
$20,000, the entire Coverage B limit, even though rebuilding the studio costs only $16,000
$200,000 from Coverage A, because a detached studio shares the dwelling limit and has no separate cap
Nothing, because Coverage B pays solely when the house itself is damaged in the same storm

explanation: Coverage B equals 10% of Coverage A: 0.10 times $200,000 is $20,000. The detached studio is an other structure, and its $16,000 rebuild cost is under that $20,000 limit, so $16,000 is payable before the deductible. The limit caps the payment. It is not an automatic agreed amount, and Coverage B does not require damage to the house.

distractorExplanations.b: Pays the whole $20,000 limit instead of the $16,000 loss. Ten percent of $200,000 sets the maximum, and the unused portion of the limit is not paid.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves the studio onto Coverage A and its $200,000 limit. A detached other structure is Coverage B, here capped at 10% of Coverage A.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a requirement that the dwelling also be damaged. Coverage B can pay for the studio when the house is untouched.

prompt: Condo owner Chris receives a $4,000 assessment after a covered fire in the association lobby. His HO-6 states a $1,000 Loss Assessment limit, and he bought no higher limit. Before the deductible, how much of the assessment is paid?

options.text: The full $4,000, because an HO-6 pays every association assessment with no separate limit
$1,000, the Loss Assessment limit
Nothing, because Loss Assessment responds only to earthquake assessments and this lobby loss was a fire
$3,000, which is the $4,000 assessment minus the $1,000 limit

The coverage pays the smaller of those two amounts, so $1,000 is payable before the deductible. It does not pay the other $3,000. Fire can qualify as a covered cause for this additional coverage; the dollar limit, not the cause, is what stops the payment at $1,000.

distractorExplanations.c: Confines Loss Assessment to earthquake. A covered fire assessment can qualify, but payment still stops at the $1,000 limit.

prompt: Landlord Inez holds an unendorsed DP-1 that names only fire, lightning, and internal explosion. Gas explodes inside the rental and blows out an interior wall. She did not buy extended coverage. How does this basic form treat the wall?

options.text: The wall is excluded until extended coverage is added, because every explosion sits outside the basic named perils
The wall is paid only if the cause was wind, which an unendorsed DP-1 includes automatically along with fire
The wall is covered as internal explosion
The wall is excluded because internal explosion leaves out a gas furnace or stove the insured owns

explanation: An unendorsed DP-1 names three perils: fire, lightning, and internal explosion. A gas explosion inside the rental is an internal explosion, so the blown-out wall is covered without extended coverage. Extended coverage adds other perils, such as windstorm and hail. It is not required for this basic peril. Owning the furnace or stove does not move a gas explosion into the steam-boiler exception.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats every explosion as an extended-coverage peril. Internal explosion is already one of the basic DP-1 perils, so this wall does not wait on that endorsement.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds windstorm that the unendorsed DP-1 never lists, and this loss is an explosion rather than wind. Wind is not automatic on the basic form.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a gas furnace the insured owns like a steam boiler. Internal explosion covers gas that explodes inside the rental; the ownership exception is for steam boilers and steam pipes.

prompt: Fire damages the upstairs unit of Owen's duplex, and his DP-2 covers that fire. Coverage A is $150,000 and Fair Rental Value is 20% of Coverage A. The unit's fair rental value is $2,000 a month, no expenses discontinue, and repairs take 3 months. Before the deductible, what does Fair Rental Value pay?

options.text: It pays $30,000, the full Fair Rental Value limit, for any fire that interrupts a tenancy
It pays $2,000, because fair rental value stops after a single month of lost rent
It pays nothing, because fair rental value covers only the owner's hotel bills and Owen does not live in the upstairs unit
$6,000 of lost rental value

explanation: The Fair Rental Value limit is 20% of $150,000, which equals $30,000. Lost rental value is $2,000 times 3 months, which equals $6,000. Because $6,000 is under the $30,000 limit and no expenses discontinue, Fair Rental Value pays $6,000 before the deductible. The percentage sets a maximum, not a flat benefit, and this coverage insures the landlord's lost rent rather than the owner's hotel bills.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays the entire $30,000 limit instead of the rent actually lost. Twenty percent of $150,000 is the cap, and the loss is only $2,000 times 3 months.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops at one month, or $2,000. Repairs take 3 months, so lost rental value is $2,000 times 3, which equals $6,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Fair Rental Value with the owner's extra living costs. This DP-2 coverage pays Owen's lost rent on the unrentable upstairs unit.

prompt: Thieves enter Noah's HO-3 den in a covered theft. They take a firearm worth $2,800 and a bicycle worth $600. The policy states a $2,500 special limit for theft of firearms and no special sublimit for bicycles. Before the deductible, what is payable?

options.text: $3,100 after capping the firearm
$3,400, because the firearm special limit applies only to jewelry and both stolen items are paid in full
$2,500, because the firearm special limit also caps every other item taken in that same theft
Nothing, because an HO-3 excludes theft of firearms and bicycles from the residence

explanation: The firearm is worth $2,800, but the stated theft special limit is $2,500, so $2,500 is payable on the firearm. The bicycle has no special sublimit and is worth $600, so $600 is payable on the bicycle. Adding those amounts, 2,500 + 600 = $3,100 before the deductible. The firearm cap does not reduce the bicycle, and theft of these items from the residence is not excluded.

distractorExplanations.b: Pays both items in full and reaches $3,400. That ignores the $2,500 firearm cap; $2,800 plus $600 is not the payable sum.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies the $2,500 firearm limit to the whole theft. The bicycle is outside that sublimit and still contributes its $600.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls a covered theft an exclusion. Theft from the residence is covered, and the firearm is limited to $2,500 rather than left unpaid.

prompt: Fire destroys Grace's kitchen refrigerator. A comparable new unit costs $1,200, and age and wear account for $400 of depreciation. Her unendorsed HO-3 settles Coverage C at actual cash value. Before the deductible, what is payable?

options.text: The full $1,200, because an unendorsed HO-3 settles personal property at replacement cost whenever the insured buys a new unit
$800, replacement cost minus depreciation
$400, which is the depreciation amount standing alone
$1,600, which is replacement cost added to depreciation

explanation: Actual cash value equals replacement cost minus depreciation. A new comparable refrigerator costs $1,200 and depreciation is $400, so $1,200 minus $400 equals $800, which is payable before the deductible. The unendorsed HO-3 does not pay the full $1,200 replacement cost on Coverage C. Depreciation is subtracted from replacement cost. It is not the payment by itself, and it is not added to the $1,200.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays replacement cost of $1,200. The stem states actual cash value on Coverage C, so the $400 of depreciation comes off the $1,200.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays only the $400 of depreciation. That figure is the amount subtracted from replacement cost, not the amount of the loss payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds $400 to $1,200 and gets $1,600. Actual cash value subtracts depreciation from replacement cost.

prompt: The Ortiz family leaves their HO-3 house unoccupied through the winter, shuts the heat off, and does not drain the pipes. A freeze bursts a supply line and soaks the kitchen. The policy covers freezing only if heat was maintained or the water was shut off and the pipes were drained. How is the kitchen loss treated?

options.text: Covered in full, because any burst pipe is paid with no requirement to keep the heat on
Covered for half the repair cost, because an unoccupied-house freeze is always split evenly between the family and the insurer
Excluded, because the heat was off and the pipes were not drained
Covered, because turning the heat off is itself a named peril on the HO-3

explanation: On this HO-3, freezing of plumbing is covered only when the insured maintained heat or shut off the water and drained the pipes. The house was unoccupied, the heat was off, and the pipes were not drained, so the burst line and the soaked kitchen are excluded. Unoccupancy does not create an even split of the repair cost, and shutting the heat off is not a named peril.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops the care condition. A burst pipe from freezing is not automatic on the HO-3 when the house is unoccupied and neither heat nor draining was maintained.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents an even split of the repair. Failing both precautions takes the freeze outside coverage; the form does not pay half of an excluded freeze.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the decision to turn the heat off as a covered peril. That failure is what keeps the freezing coverage from applying.

prompt: Sam stores two machines in his HO-3 garage: a pickup registered for road use, and a riding mower used only to service the residence and not required to be registered. A covered fire destroys both. The policy covers a motor vehicle only when it is not subject to registration and is used to service the premises. Which result follows?

options.text: Both machines are covered, because any motorized item kept in the garage is Coverage C and the registration test does not apply
Only the pickup is covered, because an HO-3 automatically schedules every road-registered vehicle stored at the residence
Neither machine is covered, because homeowners property coverage excludes all motorized equipment without exception
Only the riding mower is covered

explanation: The HO-3 property section does not cover a motor vehicle that must be registered for road use, so the pickup is out. A riding mower that is not required to be registered and is used only to service the residence fits the exception stated in the policy, so the mower is covered in the garage fire. Keeping both machines in the same garage does not erase that registration test.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops the registration test and covers the pickup. Location in the garage does not bring a road-registered vehicle back under Coverage C.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the exception and covers the pickup instead of the mower. An HO-3 does not automatically schedule road vehicles stored at the residence.

prompt: Wind strips shingles from Cole's HO-3 roof. Covered roof damage is $9,000, and hauling the ruined shingles costs $1,500. Debris removal is paid inside the $180,000 Coverage A limit, and an extra 5% of that limit applies only when damage plus debris removal exceeds the limit. Before the deductible, what is paid for debris removal?

options.text: $1,500 for hauling the shingles
$9,000, the extra 5% of Coverage A, because that additional debris amount is paid on every wind loss whether or not the limit is used up
$10,500, labeling both the roof repair and the hauling as debris removal
Nothing, because debris removal is available only after a fire and this loss was wind

explanation: Roof damage of $9,000 plus debris removal of $1,500 equals $10,500. Coverage A is $180,000, and $10,500 does not exceed that limit, so the hauling cost is paid inside the limit. The debris-removal payment is $1,500. The extra 5% of $180,000 is $9,000, and that additional amount is available only when damage plus debris removal exceeds the limit, which did not happen here.

distractorExplanations.b: Pays the extra 5%, or $9,000, on a loss that never exhausted Coverage A. That additional amount is not triggered when $10,500 is still under $180,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the $9,000 repair to the $1,500 hauling and calls the $10,500 sum debris removal. The question asks only for the debris-removal payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits debris removal to fire. The stem states a covered wind loss, and debris removal follows that covered property damage.

prompt: Riley meets her HO-3 insurance-to-value test. Rebuild cost is $180,000 and Coverage A is $144,000, exactly 80%. She rebuilds after a covered fire that costs $9,000 to repair. The deductible is $500. What is payable?

options.text: $9,000, because meeting the 80% test also waives the deductible
$8,500 after the deductible
$6,700, because the test still cuts 20% from the $9,000 repair and then subtracts the $500 deductible
$144,000, the full Coverage A limit, because a fire that meets the test pays the limit

explanation: Required insurance is 80% of $180,000, which equals $144,000. Riley carries $144,000, so 144,000 / 144,000 = 1 and no reduction applies. She rebuilds, so the settlement is the $9,000 repair cost minus the $500 deductible: 9,000 minus 500 equals $8,500. Meeting the 80% test does not waive the deductible, and it does not take another 20% off a loss that is fully insured to value.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops the $500 deductible and pays the full $9,000 repair. Meeting the 80% test allows replacement cost; it does not erase the deductible.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies the $9,000 repair by 80% to get $7,200, then subtracts $500 to get $6,700. That extra haircut applies only when Coverage A is below the required $144,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the entire $144,000 Coverage A limit. The payable amount is the repair minus the deductible, not the policy limit.

prompt: A months-long shower drip rots the subfloor behind Nora's HO-3 wall. The policy excludes continuous or repeated seepage of water that goes on for weeks, months, or years. How is the rotted subfloor handled?

options.text: Paid as a sudden accidental discharge, because every plumbing leak is covered no matter how many months it has been dripping
Paid as flood, because water that reaches a floor is flood even when it came from inside the wall
Denied as continuous seepage over months
Paid in full as additional rot coverage that the base HO-3 grants for any wet wood

explanation: The HO-3 excludes continuous or repeated seepage of water that continues for weeks, months, or years. Nora's shower dripped for months, so the rotted subfloor is denied. A sudden and accidental discharge can be covered; a leak that lasts for months is the excluded pattern. Water from inside the wall is not flood, and the base form does not add a rot coverage that pays this loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls a months-long drip a sudden discharge. The exclusion is aimed at seepage that continues over weeks, months, or years, which is this shower leak.
distractorExplanations.b: Misnames an indoor plumbing seep as flood. Flood is surface water or outside overflow, and this loss is excluded as continuous seepage.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the rot as if the HO-3 granted extra rot coverage. The rot resulted from excluded continuous seepage, so the subfloor is not replaced.

prompt: A covered kitchen fire destroys the Alvarez family's eight-year-old refrigerator. A comparable new refrigerator costs $1,200, and the adjuster assigns $450 of depreciation for age and wear. Their homeowners policy settles unendorsed personal property at actual cash value. Ignoring the deductible, what is payable for the refrigerator?

options.text: $750 actual cash value
$1,200, because a fire invariably pays the full price of a new refrigerator on unendorsed contents
$450, which pays only the depreciation figure and not the value that remains
$1,650, adding the $450 of depreciation on top of the $1,200 replacement price

explanation: Actual cash value is replacement cost minus depreciation. The arithmetic is $1,200 − $450 = $750. Unendorsed personal property is settled on that basis, so the insurer does not pay the price of a new refrigerator. A personal-property replacement-cost endorsement, plus actual replacement, would be required before the $450 depreciation could be recovered.

distractorExplanations.b: Mistakes actual cash value for replacement cost. Without a contents replacement-cost endorsement, depreciation still comes off the $1,200.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats depreciation as the payment. The $450 is subtracted from replacement cost; it is not the amount the insurer owes.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds depreciation to replacement cost. Actual cash value subtracts ($1,200 − $450); it does not stack the two figures into $1,650.

prompt: First Community Bank is the mortgagee on Priya's homeowners policy under a standard mortgage clause. A fire causes $40,000 of covered dwelling damage. Priya's own claim is denied because she set the fire on purpose. The unpaid mortgage balance is $90,000. What can the bank recover for this loss?

options.text: Nothing, because denying the named insured automatically cancels the mortgagee's rights too
$40,000, the amount of the covered damage
$90,000, the full mortgage balance, even though the fire damage is only $40,000
$130,000, the mortgage balance and the fire damage added together into one bank payment

explanation: A standard mortgage clause is a separate contract with the mortgagee, so Priya's intentional act does not defeat the bank. Recovery is limited to the bank's interest and cannot exceed the loss. The loss is $40,000 and the balance is $90,000, so the smaller figure is payable: $40,000. Adding the two figures would produce $130,000, which is more than both the damage and the insurable interest. The remaining debt after this payment is $90,000 − $40,000 = $50,000.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes a denial of the named insured for a denial of the mortgagee. The standard mortgage clause keeps the bank's rights even when the insured's arson bars her claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays the mortgage balance instead of the loss. The bank cannot collect more than the $40,000 of covered damage, even though the loan is larger.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the unpaid mortgage to the fire damage. The clause does not stack those amounts into a $130,000 payment.

prompt: An HO-3 shows Coverage A of $300,000. Other structures are covered for 10 percent of Coverage A. A detached family gazebo, not used for business, is damaged by a covered fire. The adjusted loss on the gazebo, after depreciation and the deductible, is $18,000. What is payable for the gazebo, and what happens to the Coverage A limit?

options.text: $30,000, the full other-structures limit, even though the adjusted gazebo loss is $18,000
Nothing, because any structure that stands apart from the house is excluded on a homeowners form
$18,000, and Coverage A stays $300,000
$18,000 taken out of Coverage A, which leaves a $282,000 dwelling limit after this loss

explanation: Other-structures coverage on an HO-3 is 10 percent of Coverage A, and that amount is additional insurance. Ten percent of $300,000 is $30,000 (0.10 × 300,000 = 30,000). The adjusted loss is $18,000, which is under that cap, so the policy pays $18,000. Because the coverage is additional, the payment does not reduce Coverage A. Treating it as inside the dwelling limit would leave $300,000 − $18,000 = $282,000, which misstates how this form works.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays the other-structures ceiling instead of the loss. The $30,000 figure is a maximum, and an $18,000 gazebo loss does not grow to that maximum.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a detached structure as excluded. A nonbusiness gazebo set apart from the dwelling is the kind of building Coverage B is written to insure.
distractorExplanations.d: Subtracts the gazebo payment from Coverage A. On the HO-3 the other-structures amount is additional insurance, so the dwelling limit stays $300,000.

prompt: While their house is being repaired after a covered wildfire, the Chen family spends a month in a hotel costing $2,000 and pays $900 for restaurant meals. A normal month at home would have included $400 of groceries, which they do not buy while displaced. Loss-of-use coverage pays the necessary increase in living expenses. Ignoring the deductible, what is payable?

options.text: $2,900, the hotel plus the meals, with no credit for the groceries they no longer buy

$2,000 for the hotel only, leaving out the extra cost of meals over normal groceries
$2,500 of additional living expense

Meals of $900 replace groceries of $400, so the food increase is $900 − $400 = $500. The payable increase is $2,000 + $500 = $2,500. Adding the hotel and meals without the grocery credit would overstate the loss at $2,900.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds the hotel and meals with no offset for normal food costs. Loss of use pays only the increase, so the $400 of avoided groceries has to come off.
distractorExplanations.b: Pays the grocery budget they did not spend. That $400 is the normal expense being replaced, not an additional living expense.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops at the hotel and drops the extra meal cost. The $500 by which meals exceed normal groceries is part of the increase.

prompt: Wind tears open the roof on the Blake family's insured house, and the dwelling repair will cost $9,000. That evening they pay a roofer $600 to tarp the opening so rain will not ruin the rooms underneath. The dwelling limit is $250,000. Ignoring the deductible, how should the tarp expense be handled?

options.text: Pay the $600 inside the existing dwelling limit

Pay the $600 only if a debris-removal endorsement was bought before the windstorm
Pay the $600 and also raise the dwelling limit from $250,000 to $250,600 for this loss

The $600 tarp stops rain from following the wind opening, so it is part of the loss. Roof repairs plus the tarp are $9,000 + $600 = $9,600, which remains inside the $250,000 limit. The unused limit is $250,000 − $9,600 = $240,400. Adding the tarp on top of the limit would produce $250,600, which this coverage does not do.

distractorExplanations.b: Calls the tarp ordinary maintenance. Money spent right after a covered windstorm to keep rain out of the house is a reasonable repair, not routine upkeep.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a debris-removal endorsement. Covering an opening to stop further damage is already a reasonable repair in the form, not a debris-removal add-on.
distractorExplanations.d: Increases the dwelling limit by the tarp cost. Reasonable repairs are paid inside the existing limit and do not raise it from $250,000 to $250,600.

prompt: A neighbor's sedan knocks over a mature maple in the Ortiz front yard. Their homeowners policy pays up to $500 for any one tree when a vehicle not owned or operated by a resident causes the damage. Taking the tree away and planting a replacement will cost $700. Ignoring the deductible and any aggregate limit, what is payable for the maple?

$1,200, paying the $700 cost and the $500 cap as two separate benefits for the same tree

explanation: A neighbor's car is a vehicle not owned or operated by a resident, so the tree coverage applies. The policy caps any one tree at $500. The loss is $700, and $700 is greater than $500, so the payable amount is the cap of $500. The unpaid remainder is $700 − $500 = $200. The cap is a ceiling on this tree, not a reason to deny the peril and not an extra sum added to the bill.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the per-tree maximum because a car was involved. The neighbor's sedan satisfies the peril, but the stated $500 cap still limits what is paid.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats every vehicle loss as excluded. The exclusion applies to a resident's own vehicle; a neighbor's sedan is a covered cause of loss for the tree.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the cap to the repair cost. The $500 figure is the most payable for one tree, not a second benefit stacked on the $700.

prompt: Company North provides $200,000 of dwelling coverage and Company South provides $100,000 on the same house and the same insured. Each policy says it will pay only its proportion of a covered loss based on limits. A kitchen fire causes $60,000 of dwelling damage. Ignoring deductibles, what is Company North's payment?

options.text: $60,000, because the larger policy is primary and the smaller policy pays nothing on this fire
$30,000, because two property insurers always divide a shared dwelling loss into equal halves
$40,000 as North's pro rata share
$20,000, giving North the same dollar payment as the smaller South policy on this fire

explanation: Section I other insurance shares a covered property loss in proportion to the limits. Combined limits are $200,000 + $100,000 = $300,000. North's fraction is 200,000 / 300,000 = 2/3. Two-thirds of the $60,000 loss is $40,000 (60,000 × 2/3 = 40,000). South pays the other third, $20,000. Equal shares would ignore the limits the clauses actually use.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes the larger policy primary. These other-insurance clauses share the loss by limits, so North does not pay the entire $60,000 fire loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits the loss in equal shares. Pro rata property coverage uses the relative limits, and half of $60,000 is not North's fraction of the combined $300,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns North the smaller policy's dollar share. North wrote two-thirds of the limits, so its payment is $40,000, not South's $20,000.

prompt: At the closing, seller Owen signs a handwritten note giving his unexpired homeowners policy to the buyer. The insurer does not consent to that transfer. Early the next day a kitchen fire damages the dwelling, and the buyer files the claim on Owen's policy. Which outcome follows from the assignment condition?

options.text: The buyer collects the fire loss because a homeowners policy automatically follows the house at every closing
The buyer collects contents coverage only, because a sale transfers belongings coverage but never the dwelling
The insurer must rewrite the contract in the buyer's name, retroactive to the closing, with no new underwriting
The buyer gains no rights under Owen's policy

explanation: A homeowners policy is a personal contract. The assignment condition makes a transfer of the policy ineffective unless the insurer gives written consent. Owen's note at closing does not supply that consent, so the buyer does not become an insured and cannot collect for the next day's fire under that contract. Assigning a claim after a loss has already happened is a different act and is not what Owen did.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the policy as running with the land. A homeowners contract is personal and does not move to a buyer automatically when the house is sold.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits the transfer by coverage part. Without the insurer's consent the assignment fails for the whole policy, not merely for the dwelling.
distractorExplanations.c: Forces the insurer to accept the buyer's note. Consent is the insurer's choice; a handwritten transfer does not rename the contract back to the closing.

prompt: On a two-week vacation, thieves take Nora's camera from her hotel room. The camera's actual cash value is $900. Her Coverage C limit is $80,000, personal property is covered worldwide, and property usually kept at another residence is limited to 10 percent of Coverage C. No special sublimit applies to this camera. Ignoring the deductible, what is payable?

options.text: $900 for the camera
Nothing, because personal property is covered only while it remains inside the residence premises
$8,000, applying 10 percent of the Coverage C limit to this hotel-room theft
$80,000, paying the entire Coverage C limit for any theft that happens away from home

explanation: Personal property on a temporary trip is covered worldwide, and the 10 percent limit applies only to property usually kept at another residence. A two-week hotel stay is not that. Ten percent of $80,000 would be $8,000 (0.10 × 80,000 = 8,000), but that cap is the wrong one here. The loss is the camera's $900 actual cash value, and $900 is within the $80,000 Coverage C limit, so payable is $900.

distractorExplanations.b: Limits Coverage C to the residence premises. The stated worldwide coverage follows this camera on a temporary trip, so a hotel theft is not automatically excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies the other-residence percentage to a hotel stay. That 10 percent limit is for property usually kept at another residence, which this vacation camera is not.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the entire Coverage C limit for an off-premises theft. The measure of this loss is the camera's $900 value, not the $80,000 policy limit.

prompt: Ben occupies one side of his duplex and rents the other side for $1,200 a month under his homeowners policy. A covered fire leaves only the rented side unlivable for the month, and the tenant pays nothing. A $150 cleaning contract stops, while Ben's $200 water bill continues. Ignoring the deductible, what fair rental value does loss-of-use coverage pay?

options.text: $1,200, the full monthly rent, with no reduction for the cleaning contract that stopped
$1,050 of fair rental value
$850, after subtracting both the stopped cleaning contract and the water bill that still continues
$200, limited to the water bill Ben keeps paying while the rented side sits empty

explanation: Fair rental value covers the rental value of the part rented to others, minus expenses that do not continue while it is unfit to live in. Rent of $1,200 minus the $150 cleaning contract that stops equals $1,050 ($1,200 − $150 = $1,050). The $200 water bill continues, so it is not subtracted. Taking it off as well would wrongly produce $1,050 − $200 = $850.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays the full rent and skips the stopped cleaning expense. Fair rental value is reduced by expenses that do not continue, so the $150 comes off the $1,200.
distractorExplanations.c: Also subtracts the water bill that continues. Only expenses that stop are deducted; a bill Ben still pays stays out of the subtraction.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the continuing water bill instead of lost rent. Loss of use replaces rental value; it does not reimburse an expense that never stopped.

prompt: After a covered fire at the Rahman family's house, a volunteer department from a neighboring district bills them $450 under a contract. The house is outside the district that furnished the response. The policy pays fire department service charges up to $500 as additional insurance, with no deductible, and it excludes the charge when the property is inside the responding district. The Section I deductible is $1,000. What is payable for this bill?

options.text: Nothing, because the $1,000 property deductible is larger than the $450 bill and cancels it
$500, the maximum the additional coverage allows, rather than the smaller $450 invoice
$450, the amount the department billed
$1,450, the fire department invoice added to the $1,000 deductible and paid as one sum

explanation: The house is outside the district that responded, so the inside-district exclusion does not apply, and the family assumed the charge by contract. The bill is $450 and the cap is $500. Because $450 is less than $500, the coverage pays $450, leaving $500 − $450 = $50 of the cap unused. The form states that no deductible applies to this charge, so the $1,000 Section I deductible is not subtracted and is not added to the bill.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the Section I deductible to a charge the policy says is not subject to a deductible. The $1,000 deductible does not wipe out the $450 bill.
distractorExplanations.b: Pays the coverage maximum instead of the invoice. The $500 figure is a cap, and a $450 bill does not increase to that cap.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the deductible to the fire department bill. The deductible is not an extra amount the insurer pays the department on top of the invoice.

prompt: The named insured on a homeowners policy dies in March. Two weeks later, still during the policy period, smoke from a covered cooking fire damages the living room. Her husband, who lived with her in the house, and the legal representative named in her will both present claims. Who has rights under the policy for this loss?

options.text: A later purchaser of the house alone, because death ends the contract for everyone who lived there
Only the legal representative, because a resident spouse loses insured status at the moment of death
No one, because a homeowners policy terminates at death and cannot respond to a loss after that date
The resident husband and the legal representative

explanation: Death does not cancel the homeowners policy for the rest of the period. A spouse who was a member of the household at death remains an insured, and the legal representative is insured for the deceased's covered premises and property. Both may pursue this smoke loss. The contract is not handed to a future buyer, and it does not vanish on the date of death.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the policy to a later purchaser. Death does not assign the contract to a buyer, and this loss does not involve any sale of the house.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the resident spouse at death. A household member who lived with the named insured keeps insured status together with the legal representative.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats death as canceling the policy midterm. The contract continues for those people through a covered loss that occurs inside the policy period.

prompt: A fire at a dry cleaner destroys Luis's wool coat while the shop is storing it for a fee. Fire is a covered peril for personal property on his homeowners policy. Luis submits a claim for the coat, and the cleaner also demands payment under his policy for the same coat. Who may recover on that contract?

options.text: Luis may recover, and the cleaner may not
Only the cleaner may recover, because a paid bailee becomes the named insured while it holds the coat
Luis and the cleaner may each recover the coat's full value, so the policy pays the same loss twice
Neither may recover, because personal property left with a cleaner is outside the homeowners contract

explanation: Fire is a covered cause of loss for the insured's personal property, including property a bailee is holding, so Luis may present his own claim for the coat. The no-benefit-to-bailee condition blocks the cleaner from collecting on his policy, whether by assignment or by claiming the coverage directly. The shop must look to its own bailee insurance. His contract does not pay the coat once to him and again to the cleaner.

distractorExplanations.b: Makes the bailee the named insured. Holding property for a fee does not turn the cleaner into an insured on Luis's homeowners policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays the coat twice. Luis may claim his own property loss, but the cleaner takes no benefit under his contract, so the loss is not paid to each of them.
distractorExplanations.d: Excludes property that is at a cleaner. A covered fire can still reach the insured's personal property in a bailee's hands; the bar is against the bailee benefiting.

prompt: Burglars take one speaker from a matched pair in a covered homeowners theft. Before the loss the pair's actual cash value was $1,000, and the speaker left behind is worth $300 by itself. The insurer elects to pay the difference between the pair's actual cash value before the loss and the value of what remains, instead of replacing the missing speaker. Ignoring the deductible, what is payable?

options.text: $1,000, the full value of the pair, even though one speaker is still in the house
$300, which is the value of the speaker the burglars did not take
$1,300, the original pair value added to the value of the speaker that remains
$700 for the drop in value of the pair

explanation: When the insurer elects the pair-or-set difference, the loss is the drop in actual cash value of the set, not a new pair and not the leftover piece. Value before the theft was $1,000 and value remaining is $300, so the difference is $1,000 − $300 = $700. Paying another $1,000, or adding the leftover speaker to reach $1,300, would ignore the speaker the insured still has.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays for the whole pair and ignores the speaker still on hand. The elected measure is only the drop in value of the set, which is less than $1,000.
distractorExplanations.b: Pays the value of the remaining speaker. That $300 piece was not stolen; it is the amount subtracted from the pair, not the payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the leftover speaker to the original pair value. The condition subtracts what remains from the value before the loss, rather than stacking the two.

prompt: A retail tenant’s CGL is triggered when a shopper slips on a wet floor and breaks a wrist. Which loss does Coverage A typically address first?

options.text: A rival’s claim that the tenant’s ad disparaged the rival’s goods
The tenant’s cost to replace its own damaged flooring tiles
The shopper’s bodily injury claim against the insured tenant
The tenant’s fee dispute with its advertising agency

explanation: CGL Coverage A responds to third-party bodily injury and property damage for which the insured is legally liable. A customer’s slip-and-fall injury is classic Coverage A premises liability, not the insured’s own property, advertising injury, or a professional fee dispute.

distractorExplanations.a: Disparagement of a rival’s goods in an advertisement is a Coverage B offense, not Coverage A bodily injury from the fall.
distractorExplanations.b: Damage to the insured’s own property is first-party property coverage, not CGL third-party liability.
distractorExplanations.d: A fee dispute with an ad agency is a contractual/business dispute, not Coverage A liability.

prompt: A contractor carried occurrence CGL for 2021, 2022, and 2023, then a claims-made CGL only for 2024 with a retroactive date of January 1, 2024, and no extended reporting period. In 2025 a third party sues for a 2022 jobsite injury. Which policy is most likely to respond if that injury is otherwise covered?

options.text: Only the 2025 claims-made policy, because the suit was filed then
Neither policy, because the 2024 claims-made switch canceled the 2022 occurrence cover
Workers compensation, because the claimant was on a jobsite
The occurrence policy that was in force when the injury happened

explanation: An occurrence CGL responds to bodily injury that happens during its policy period, even when the lawsuit is filed later. The 2022 injury falls in the 2021–2023 occurrence policy. The 2024 claims-made policy does not respond: the claim was first made in 2025, that policy has ended, there is no extended reporting period, and the retroactive date of January 1, 2024 is after the injury.

distractorExplanations.a: The filing year triggers a claims-made policy only while that policy is in force. This suit was filed in 2025, after the 2024 claims-made term ended, so the suit year does not replace the occurrence policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Replacing an occurrence policy with a later claims-made policy does not erase bodily injury that already happened while the occurrence policy was in force.
distractorExplanations.c: Workers compensation covers an employee’s own work injury. A third-party lawsuit is a CGL question about which policy period is triggered.

prompt: An architect buys claims-made professional liability with a retroactive date of January 1, 2022. In 2025 a client sues over a design error committed in 2021. How does the retro date usually affect coverage?

options.text: No coverage, because the wrongful act predates the retroactive date
Full coverage, because any claim filed after the policy starts is covered
Coverage only for defense costs, never for indemnity payments
Automatic coverage under the architect’s CGL products-completed ops

explanation: On claims-made professional liability, the wrongful act generally must occur on or after the retroactive date, and the claim must be first made during the policy period (or an extended reporting period).
