An act in 2021 before a 2022 retro date typically falls outside coverage even if the 2025 suit is timely.

distractorExplanations.b: Claims-made still requires the act to fall on or after the retro date; filing date alone is not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: Retro date bars the claim entirely; it does not create a defense-only carve-out.
distractorExplanations.d: CGL products-completed operations does not replace professional liability for design errors.

prompt: A competitor sues a kitchen retailer, alleging the retailer’s ad falsely claimed the competitor’s product was unsafe. Which CGL coverage part is primarily designed for that allegation?

options.text: Coverage A bodily injury and property damage liability
Coverage B personal and advertising injury liability
Coverage C medical payments to others
Products-completed operations only, without Coverage B

explanation: CGL Coverage B addresses personal and advertising injury offenses such as disparagement, libel/slander in advertising, and certain copyright or slogan infringements in ads. A suit over a false safety claim in advertising is a Coverage B exposure, not Coverage A BI/PD or medical payments.

distractorExplanations.a: Coverage A is for bodily injury and tangible property damage, not advertising disparagement.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage C pays limited medical expenses without regard to fault; it does not fund advertising injury suits.
distractorExplanations.d: Products-completed ops is a Coverage A hazard; it does not substitute for Coverage B advertising injury.

prompt: A manufacturer ships a defective ladder that later collapses at a buyer’s home and injures a guest. The factory floor itself was never unsafe. Which CGL hazard best describes this claim?

options.text: Premises liability solely because manufacturing occurred at the insured’s plant building
Operations liability because assembly work was treated as unfinished ongoing operations
Products-completed operations after the product left the maker’s control
Personal injury because the guest suffered embarrassment from falling publicly

explanation: Products-completed operations covers bodily injury or property damage arising out of the insured’s products after they have been relinquished, or out of completed work away from the premises. A ladder that fails after sale is a products hazard, not a premises slip-and-fall at the factory.

distractorExplanations.a: Premises liability concerns injury on the insured’s premises; manufacture location alone does not make a post-sale injury premises liability.
distractorExplanations.b: Operations liability covers ongoing work; completed, sold products fall under products-completed ops.
distractorExplanations.d: Embarrassment is not the Coverage B personal injury offense; this is a bodily injury products claim.

prompt: A visitor twists an ankle in the insured’s office lobby. The insured wants the CGL to pay the visitor’s urgent-care bill quickly without waiting for a liability finding. Which coverage is designed for that?

options.text: Coverage A, but only after a court enters a negligence judgment
Coverage B personal injury for invasion of privacy
Umbrella liability, which typically pays first-dollar medical bills
Coverage C medical payments, typically without proving fault

explanation: CGL Coverage C medical payments pays limited medical expenses for bodily injury to others caused by an accident on the insured’s premises or from the insured’s operations, usually without requiring a determination of legal liability. It is goodwill coverage distinct from defending a Coverage A suit.

distractorExplanations.a: Coverage A responds to legal liability; it is not the no-fault medical payments grant.
distractorExplanations.b: Coverage B personal/advertising injury does not pay routine medical bills for a lobby fall.
distractorExplanations.c: Umbrella is excess liability; it is not the primary medical payments feature of the CGL.

prompt: A plumber floods a customer’s kitchen while actively repairing a pipe. Separately, a previously sold water heater later ruptures and ruins a basement. How should those two exposures be classified?

options.text: Active repair is premises/operations; the sold heater is products-completed ops
Both claims are strictly premises liability because water damage occurred indoors
Both claims are professional liability because plumbing requires a license
The active repair is products liability; the later rupture is operations liability

explanation: Injury or damage arising while work is ongoing is a premises/operations exposure. Damage arising from a product after it has been sold and relinquished, or from completed work, is products-completed operations. The live repair and the later heater failure sit in those two different CGL hazard buckets.

distractorExplanations.b: Indoor location does not convert a post-sale product failure into premises liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Licensing does not automatically move ordinary BI/PD into professional liability E&O.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the hazards: ongoing work is operations; post-sale product failure is products.

prompt: A delivery driver employed by a bakery negligently hits a cyclist while making a scheduled route drop. The injured party sues the bakery. Which liability concept most directly supports suing the employer?

options.text: Strict liability for every motor vehicle accident without regard to employment status or fault
Vicarious liability via respondeat superior for employees in the scope of employment
Absolute liability that always attaches only to product manufacturers after sale
Host liquor liability for serving alcohol at an after-hours company picnic event

explanation: Under respondeat superior, an employer can be vicariously liable for an employee’s torts committed within the scope of employment. A scheduled delivery is classic scope-of-employment conduct, so the bakery may be sued even though it did not personally drive the truck.

distractorExplanations.a: Auto negligence is fault-based; employment status matters for vicarious liability, not a blanket strict rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Absolute liability is the rule for ultrahazardous work such as blasting, not a rule aimed at product manufacturers. The bakery is sued because its employee was on a scheduled route.
distractorExplanations.d: Host liquor involves furnishing alcohol; it is unrelated to a delivery-route collision.

prompt: A consumer is injured by a toaster that left the factory with a hidden manufacturing defect. The maker used reasonable care in its process. Which liability theory still commonly allows recovery against the manufacturer?

options.text: Vicarious liability solely for the retailer’s cashier’s negligence at checkout
Absolute liability that attaches merely from owning any household appliance
Strict products liability for a defective product that injures a user
Professional liability for the appliance designer’s board ethics complaint only

explanation: Strict products liability can impose liability for injury caused by a defective product without requiring proof that the manufacturer was negligent. Reasonable care in the process does not defeat a strict products claim when the product was defective and caused harm.

distractorExplanations.a: Vicarious liability concerns another person’s tort within an employment/agency relationship, not the manufacturer’s product defect theory.
distractorExplanations.b: Owning a toaster is not an absolute-liability ultrahazardous activity.
distractorExplanations.d: Professional liability/E&O addresses professional service errors, not consumer product injury.

prompt: A blasting contractor’s carefully controlled charge still cracks a neighboring foundation. No negligence can be shown in how the blast was set. Which concept best explains liability that can still attach?

options.text: Host liquor liability for serving beer to workers after the demolition job ends
Vicarious liability that applies only if a named subcontractor lit the fuse
CGL Coverage B advertising injury for the neighbor’s cracked foundation wall
Absolute liability for ultrahazardous activities such as blasting work

explanation: Absolute liability (often discussed with ultrahazardous or abnormally dangerous activities) can impose liability for harm from activities like blasting even when the actor exercised reasonable care. Proof of negligence is not required the way it is in ordinary negligence cases.

distractorExplanations.a: Host liquor concerns alcohol furnished to guests; it does not explain blasting damage.
distractorExplanations.b: Vicarious liability may matter for agents, but the core concept here is absolute liability for the activity itself.
distractorExplanations.c: A cracked foundation is property damage, not personal/advertising injury under Coverage B.

prompt: A client sues an accountant for a tax-filing error that caused penalties. The accountant’s CGL does not cover professional service mistakes. Which coverage is the better fit for that claim?

options.text: Professional liability (E&O) for the tax-filing accounting mistake
CGL Coverage A treating the tax penalty itself as bodily injury liability
CGL Coverage C medical payments for the client’s stress-related doctor visits
Umbrella liability that automatically covers every professional service error

explanation: Professional liability / E&O is designed for financial loss arising from professional service mistakes. Standard CGL Coverage A focuses on bodily injury and tangible property damage and commonly excludes or fails to cover pure professional errors, so E&O is the appropriate product for the tax-filing claim.

distractorExplanations.b: A tax penalty is economic loss, not bodily injury under Coverage A.
distractorExplanations.c: Medical payments cover limited accident medical expenses, not professional malpractice damages.
distractorExplanations.d: A commercial umbrella does not automatically insure professional mistakes. Errors and omissions coverage is a separate policy, and umbrellas commonly exclude professional services unless that policy sits underneath.

prompt: A risk manager wants higher limits above a primary CGL and also wants the excess layer to drop down for some gaps the primary does not insure. Which structure best matches that goal?

options.text: A pure following-form excess policy that stacks limits but never broadens coverage
A commercial umbrella that can raise limits and also broaden coverage
Coverage C medical payments raised until they match the CGL aggregate limit
A claims-made endorsement alone that replaces any need for an excess liability layer

explanation: A commercial umbrella sits above primary liability, raises the available limits, and may also drop down to cover some gaps the primary does not insure, usually after a self-insured retention on those gaps. A pure following-form excess policy mainly stacks limits and follows the primary’s terms. The manager’s dual goal matches the umbrella.

distractorExplanations.a: Following-form excess mainly stacks limits; it is not the tool chosen to broaden gaps.
distractorExplanations.c: Raising medical payments does not create excess bodily injury/property damage limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Claims-made vs occurrence is a trigger choice, not a substitute for excess limits.

prompt: A licensed bar continues serving an obviously intoxicated patron who later injures a pedestrian. A statute imposes liability on the seller of alcohol. Which high-level concept describes that exposure?

options.text: Products-completed operations solely for the brand of beer that was sold
Absolute liability merely from owning a commercial kitchen grill on site
Dram shop liability from the commercial sale of alcohol
Professional liability for mistakes in the bartender’s specialty drink recipes

explanation: Dram shop laws can impose liability on commercial sellers of alcohol when they furnish drinks to intoxicated patrons who then cause injury. That is distinct from ordinary premises slip-and-fall, products liability for the beverage brand, or professional E&O.

distractorExplanations.a: Products-completed ops addresses defective products after sale, not statutory liquor seller liability.
distractorExplanations.b: Owning a grill is unrelated; absolute liability here would mislabel a liquor statute exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Bartending recipes are not a professional liability malpractice claim in this scenario.

prompt: At a private backyard party, a homeowner serves wine to adult guests. One guest drives away intoxicated and causes a crash. How does host liquor liability typically differ from dram shop exposure?

options.text: Host liquor always creates the same statutory duty that a licensed tavern faces
Host liquor applies just to employees drinking at work and not to social hosts
Dram shop does not involve alcohol service; host liquor covers beer commercials
Host liquor is social furnishing; dram shop targets commercial alcohol sellers

explanation: Dram shop liability focuses on commercial sellers of alcoholic beverages. Host liquor concerns a social host who furnishes alcohol and is not in that business. The standard CGL liquor exclusion applies to insureds in the business of selling or serving alcohol, so a social host’s exposure is treated more favorably than a tavern’s.

distractorExplanations.a: Social hosts are not automatically treated identically to licensed sellers under dram shop statutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Host liquor is about social furnishing, not limited to workplace drinking rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Both concepts involve alcohol; the commercial-sale vs social-host distinction is the key difference.

prompt: A property owner hires a roofing company as an independent contractor. The roofer’s employee drops a tool and injures a passerby. When is the owner least likely to face respondeat superior liability for that drop?

options.text: When the roofer truly controls the means and methods as an independent contractor
When the owner sets the roofer’s hours, tools, and daily supervision like an employee
When the owner directs every nail placement and supplies all crew wages
When the crew is on the owner’s payroll and must follow the owner’s work orders

explanation: Respondeat superior generally attaches to employees acting in the scope of employment, not to true independent contractors who control their own means and methods. If the roofing firm is a genuine independent contractor, the owner is less likely to be vicariously liable for the crew’s negligence (other theories like negligent hiring may still exist).

distractorExplanations.b: Heavy control of hours, tools, and supervision looks like employment, increasing vicarious exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Directing work detail and paying wages supports an employee relationship, not contractor status.
distractorExplanations.d: A crew on the owner’s payroll that must follow the owner’s work orders is employed for that job, so respondeat superior is more likely, not less.

prompt: A CGL insurer is defending a covered BI suit. The insured incurs court costs taxed against it and premiums on appeal bonds the insurer required. Where do those costs usually sit?

options.text: They always reduce the Coverage A each-occurrence limit dollar for dollar first
They are typically paid as supplementary payments outside the limit
They are paid just under Coverage C medical payments to the injured person
They are excluded because defense costs are typically the insured’s personal expense

explanation: ISO-style CGL supplementary payments cover certain defense-related costs—such as court costs taxed against the insured and premiums on bonds the insurer requires—typically in addition to the limits of insurance. They are not Coverage C medical payments and are not treated as the insured’s uninsured personal expense when the duty to defend applies.

distractorExplanations.a: Many supplementary payments are outside (in addition to) limits, not an automatic erosion of every Coverage A dollar.
distractorExplanations.c: Coverage C is limited medical expenses to injured persons, not suit costs and bond premiums.
distractorExplanations.d: When the insurer owes a duty to defend, defense-related supplementary payments are part of that obligation.

prompt: A lawsuit against a CGL insured alleges facts that, if true, would be covered—and also alleges uncovered intentional misconduct. How does the insurer’s duty to defend usually compare to the duty to indemnify?

options.text: Duty to defend arises only after a court enters a final judgment against the insured
Duty to indemnify is broader and typically pays even uncovered intentional misconduct
Duty to defend is broader and may apply if any allegation is potentially covered
Neither duty exists until the insured first pays defense counsel entirely out of pocket

explanation: The duty to defend is generally broader than the duty to indemnify: if any allegation in the complaint is potentially covered, the insurer often must defend the entire suit (subject to reservation of rights). Indemnity is owed only for covered damages actually awarded or settled within coverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Defense is triggered by a suit seeking potentially covered damages, not by waiting for a final judgment.
distractorExplanations.b: Indemnity is narrower; intentional injury exclusions commonly bar indemnity even when defense was owed.
distractorExplanations.d: The insurer typically must provide defense when the duty attaches; the insured need not fund counsel first.

prompt: An occurrence CGL was in force only during calendar year 2023. Continuous water seepage quietly damaged a neighbor’s wall throughout 2024 after the policy expired. Which statement best reflects the occurrence trigger?

options.text: The expired 2023 policy automatically covers any damage discovered in any later year
Occurrence forms ignore when damage happens and look only at when the premium was paid
Coverage attaches solely because the neighbor happened to file the claim during 2023
Coverage requires BI or property damage that occurs during the policy period

explanation: Under an occurrence form, the key trigger is that bodily injury or property damage occur during the policy period. Damage that happens only after the policy expired generally does not attach to that expired occurrence policy merely because the insured once bought it or because a claim is filed later.

distractorExplanations.a: Discovery in a later year does not by itself revive an expired occurrence period for new damage.
distractorExplanations.b: Premium payment timing is not the occurrence trigger; timing of BI/PD is.
distractorExplanations.c: Claim-filing date is the claims-made concept, not the occurrence trigger.

prompt: A furniture store’s display sofa collapses and injures a customer in the showroom. Separately, a sofa sold last month collapses in the buyer’s living room. Which statement correctly separates the exposures?

options.text: Showroom injury is premises/operations; the sold sofa is products
Both injuries are advertising injury simply because sofas appeared in store ads
Both injuries are host liquor claims merely because the store offered free coffee
Only the living-room injury counts as premises liability at the store location

explanation: Injury on the insured’s premises from ongoing retail operations is premises/operations. Injury from a product after it has been sold and left the insured’s control is products liability within products-completed operations. The same product type can create either exposure depending on where and when the injury occurs.

distractorExplanations.b: Advertising injury is a Coverage B offense, not sofa collapse bodily injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Offering coffee does not convert product injuries into host liquor claims.
distractorExplanations.d: The living-room failure after sale is products, not store premises liability.

prompt: A consultant’s claims-made E&O expires, and the consultant buys no renewal. Within the extended reporting period (ERP) purchased at expiration, a client first makes a claim for work done during the policy. What does the ERP primarily provide?

options.text: A brand-new occurrence policy that covers all future consulting work after expiration
More time to report claims for acts already within the expired claims-made policy
Automatic CGL Coverage B for every slogan used in the consultant’s advertising
Waiver of the retroactive date so wrongful acts from before that date are covered

explanation: An extended reporting period (tail) on a claims-made policy gives more time to report claims after the policy ends for wrongful acts that occurred after the retro date and before expiration. It does not create a new occurrence policy for future work or erase the retroactive date for earlier acts.

distractorExplanations.a: An ERP is not a replacement occurrence policy for new future services.
distractorExplanations.c: ERP on E&O does not grant CGL personal/advertising injury coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: A standard ERP does not waive the retro date to pick up pre-retro wrongful acts.

prompt: A warehouse supervisor clocked out, drove home in a personal car, and caused a wreck unrelated to any work errand. An injured driver sues the warehouse employer. Which analysis best fits respondeat superior?

options.text: Employer liability is automatic for any employee accident at any hour of the day
Strict products liability applies because the personal car counts as a warehouse product
Vicarious liability is unlikely because the commute was outside the scope of employment
Dram shop liability applies merely because the supervisor might have been thirsty

explanation: Respondeat superior requires that the employee’s tort occur within the scope of employment. A commute home in a personal vehicle with no work errand is typically outside that scope, so the employer is unlikely to be vicariously liable for the wreck (absent special facts like a required company vehicle or work mission).

distractorExplanations.a: Employment status alone does not make every off-duty accident the employer’s vicarious risk.
distractorExplanations.b: A personal car is not the warehouse’s product for strict products liability.
distractorExplanations.d: Speculation about thirst does not create dram shop liability.

prompt: A firm buys a following-form excess liability policy over its primary CGL. A claim is covered by the primary’s terms but exceeds the primary limit. What is the excess policy’s usual role?

options.text: Replace the primary CGL and pay the first dollar of every small liability claim
Convert the CGL claim into a professional liability E&O matter automatically
Pay Coverage C medical payments that the scheduled primary CGL never offered
Add limits that follow the primary’s coverage after that primary is exhausted

explanation: Following-form excess liability generally provides additional limits above a scheduled primary policy and follows that primary’s coverage terms. It responds after the primary is exhausted for a covered loss; it does not become first-dollar primary for every small claim or rewrite the claim as E&O.

distractorExplanations.a: Excess sits above primary; it does not replace first-dollar primary on ordinary small claims.
distractorExplanations.b: Excess does not recharacterize a CGL claim as professional liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Following-form excess tracks the underlying; it does not invent medical payments the primary never had.

prompt: A jogger proves that a motorist owed a duty of reasonable care and breached it by running a red light. The jogger's hospital bills are real. The collision happened two blocks from that light, and the red-light breach played no part in the injuries. Which negligence element fails?

options.text: Proximate cause, the link from the breach to the harm
Legal duty, because a collision two blocks from the light means the motorist owed the jogger no duty of reasonable care
Breach of duty, because running a red light is not a breach when the impact occurs two blocks from that signal
Actual damages, because hospital bills are not damages until a jury enters a verdict awarding a sum

explanation: Negligence requires a legal duty, a breach of that duty, proximate cause, and actual damages. Duty, a red-light breach, and real hospital bills can all exist and the case still fails when the breach did not produce the harm. Proximate cause is that link. A violation that played no part in a collision two blocks away is not the proximate cause of the jogger's injuries.

distractorExplanations.b: Misstates duty. The motorist still owed the jogger reasonable care. The two-block gap goes to causation, not to whether a duty existed.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates breach. Running a red light is a breach of reasonable care. What fails is the link between that breach and the injuries.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates damages. The hospital bills are actual damages now. They do not have to be reduced to a verdict before the damages element is met.

prompt: Imani is the only named insured on a CGL written for her as an individual who solely owns a flower shop. Her spouse, who is not on the payroll, is sued for a delivery injury caused while doing only that shop's work. For that claim, who is an insured?

options.text: Nobody besides Imani, because a spouse who is not on the payroll can never be an insured on an individual CGL
Imani's spouse, but only for conduct of the business she solely owns
Every relative living in Imani's household, for personal errands as well as shop deliveries and any other activity that day
Only a corporate officer listed by name, because an individual-named CGL never insures a spouse for business conduct

explanation: When the named insured is an individual, that person and their spouse are insureds, but only with respect to the conduct of a business of which the named insured is the sole owner. A delivery done for Imani's solely owned shop places the spouse inside that who-is-an-insured status. The same wording does not insure the spouse for personal activities unrelated to the shop.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes who is an insured. Payroll status is not required. The spouse is an insured for the sole owner's business conduct.
distractorExplanations.c: Overstates insured status. Household relatives are not blanket insureds, and the spouse's status stops at the solely owned business.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an individual named insured with a corporation. The individual form includes the spouse for that business without listing a corporate officer.

prompt: During a covered bodily-injury suit, the CGL insurer asks the named insured to leave the shop and testify. The policy's supplementary-payments section includes the insured's loss of earnings for that time, up to the $250 a day printed in the form. How is that payment treated?

options.text: It is subtracted from the each-occurrence limit before any judgment or settlement is paid to the injured claimant
It is part of the claimant's damages and is paid only when a judgment is entered against the insured
In addition to the limit, as a supplementary payment
It replaces Coverage C medical payments and is owed to the injured claimant rather than to the insured who left work to testify

explanation: Supplementary payments on a standard CGL are paid in addition to the limits of insurance and do not reduce those limits. They include reasonable expenses the insured incurs at the insurer's request while assisting the defense, including actual loss of earnings up to the $250 a day printed in the form. That $250 figure is the policy amount stated for this attendance, and it reimburses the insured rather than the claimant.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes a supplementary payment for a reduction of limits. Earnings paid because the insurer requested testimony sit outside the occurrence limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the insured's lost earnings with the claimant's award. This payment reimburses the insured for time away at the insurer's request, win or lose.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the payee. Loss-of-earnings supplementary payments reimburse the insured. They are not the claimant's Coverage C medical bills.

prompt: One contractor keeps two CGL policies that match except for the trigger. Policy O is occurrence. Policy M is claims-made. A visitor is hurt in April and first sues in October of that same year, while both policies are still in force. What separates the two triggers?

options.text: Nothing separates them here, because both forms respond when the injury and the suit occur in the same year while both policies remain in force
Claims-made ignores the filing date and pays solely for injuries that happened in a year before the policy began
Occurrence pays only after that policy has expired, while claims-made pays only for suits filed in some later renewal year
Occurrence uses the injury date; claims-made uses when the claim is first made

explanation: An occurrence CGL is triggered by bodily injury or property damage during its policy period, even if the lawsuit is filed later. A claims-made CGL is triggered when the claim is first made during the policy period or an extended reporting period, and the injury generally must also fall on or after the retroactive date. April harm and an October suit can satisfy both tests while both policies are in force, but each form keys off a different event.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats an overlap in dates as erasing the distinction. Each form still keys off a different event, even when both the injury and the suit fall inside the same year.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the claims-made trigger. That form depends on when the claim is first made. It does not ignore the filing date.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses both triggers. An occurrence policy does not wait until expiration, and claims-made does not require a later renewal year.

prompt: Under a pure comparative negligence rule, a jury finds a shopper 70 percent at fault and a grocer 30 percent at fault for a fall. Total damages are $10,000. How much may the shopper recover from the grocer?

options.text: $3,000, reduced for the shopper's fault
$10,000, because pure comparative negligence never reduces the verdict by the plaintiff's own share of fault
Nothing, because pure comparative negligence bars any plaintiff who is more at fault than the defendant
$7,000, because the shopper collects a sum equal to the shopper's own 70 percent share of the $10,000 damages

explanation: Pure comparative negligence reduces the plaintiff's recovery by the plaintiff's percentage of fault and still allows recovery when the plaintiff is mostly at fault. The grocer's 30 percent share of $10,000 is $3,000, so the shopper recovers $3,000. The shopper's 70 percent fault explains the reduction. The result follows the pure comparative rule stated for this case.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignores the reduction. Pure comparative negligence cuts the verdict by the plaintiff's percentage. It does not pay the full $10,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses pure comparative negligence with a modified or contributory bar. A plaintiff who is 70 percent at fault still recovers the defendant's 30 percent share.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the wrong percentage. The shopper does not collect the shopper's own 70 percent. The grocer pays 30 percent, which is $3,000.

prompt: During posted shopping hours, a customer who came to buy groceries is hurt by a loose floor mat the store never inspected. The customer was not a social guest. Which common-law premises status and duty usually fit?

options.text: Trespasser, so the store owes a duty solely to refrain from intentional harm and need not look for ordinary hazards
Invitee, owed a duty to inspect and to fix or warn
Licensee, owed a warning solely of dangers the store already knows about, with no duty to inspect the sales floor
Discovered trespasser, owed only a warning of known hazards, because open shopping hours are not an invitation onto the sales floor

explanation: A person invited onto the premises for the owner's business purpose, such as a customer shopping during open hours, is a business invitee. The common-law duty to an invitee is to inspect for unreasonable dangers and to repair them or warn of them. A loose mat the store never inspected is judged under that invitee duty. A social guest is usually a licensee, and a trespasser enters without permission.

distractorExplanations.a: Mislabels the customer as a trespasser. A shopper on the premises during open hours is invited for a business purpose, which is invitee status.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an invitee with a licensee. Licensees are owed a warning of known hidden dangers. Invitees are also owed an inspection.
distractorExplanations.d: Mislabels a shopper as a trespasser. A customer on the premises during posted hours is invited for the store's business, which is invitee status.

prompt: In a jurisdiction that still uses common-law contributory negligence, a jury finds a pedestrian 10 percent at fault and a property owner 90 percent at fault for a sidewalk injury. Damages would be $20,000 if fault shares were ignored. What is the recovery?

options.text: $18,000, because contributory negligence only subtracts the pedestrian's 10 percent from the $20,000 of damages
$20,000, because a small share of plaintiff fault is disregarded once the defendant is mostly responsible
Nothing, because any plaintiff fault is a total bar
$2,000, equal to 10 percent of the damages, because contributory negligence pays the plaintiff the plaintiff's own share

explanation: Common-law contributory negligence is a complete bar. If the pedestrian is 10 percent at fault, the pedestrian recovers none of the $20,000, even though the owner is 90 percent at fault. The rule does not reduce damages by that 10 percent the way comparative negligence does. It applies in a jurisdiction that still follows contributory negligence.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies comparative-negligence arithmetic. Contributory negligence does not subtract 10 percent from $20,000. Any plaintiff fault bars the claim.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a small fault share as harmless. Under contributory negligence, 10 percent fault bars the full $20,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the plaintiff's own percentage. Contributory negligence does not award $2,000. It awards nothing when the plaintiff is at fault.

prompt: A building owner appears only as a certificate holder on a tenant's CGL certificate of insurance. No endorsement adds the owner as an additional insured. A visitor sues the owner for a hallway fall. What does that certificate, by itself, do?

options.text: It rewrites the tenant's CGL so the owner becomes a named insured with a separate limit for the hallway claim
It transfers the tenant's duty to defend onto the owner and obligates the insurer to defend the owner without an endorsement
It creates additional-insured status for every landlord named anywhere on the certificate, including this building owner
It reports the tenant's coverage and does not make the owner an insured

explanation: A certificate of insurance is evidence that a policy was issued. It does not amend the policy, add an insured, or create a duty to defend the certificate holder. Additional-insured status for a landlord comes from an additional-insured endorsement or from policy wording that grants that status. With no such endorsement, the owner is not an insured on the tenant's CGL merely because the certificate names the owner.

distractorExplanations.a: Overreads the certificate. A certificate holder is not rewritten into a named insured, and the certificate does not create a separate limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a defense duty. The insurer's duty to defend runs to insureds. A certificate alone does not make the building owner an insured.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a certificate holder with an additional insured. Naming a landlord on the certificate does not grant additional-insured status.

prompt: A shopkeeper, angry at a complaint, deliberately punches a customer in the face and means to cause the injury. The customer sues for that battery. Which Coverage A rule on the shopkeeper's CGL is the best fit?

options.text: The expected-or-intended injury exclusion
The protective-force exception, because a punch thrown during a complaint is reasonable force used to protect the shop
No expected-or-intended exclusion applies, because that exclusion removes property damage only and a punch is bodily injury
Coverage B personal and advertising injury, because a deliberate blow is a personal-injury offense rather than bodily injury

explanation: CGL Coverage A excludes bodily injury expected or intended from the standpoint of the insured. A deliberate punch meant to injure the customer is expected or intended injury, so the exclusion applies. The exclusion has a narrow exception for bodily injury resulting from reasonable force used to protect persons or property. A punch thrown to hurt a complaining customer is outside that protective-force exception.

distractorExplanations.b: Misuses the protective-force exception. The shopkeeper punched the customer to cause injury, not as reasonable force to protect persons or property.
distractorExplanations.c: Misreads the exclusion's scope. Expected or intended injury removes bodily injury as well as property damage when the insured meant to cause it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Coverage B with a bodily-injury claim. A punch is not a listed personal or advertising offense. The fitting rule is the expected-or-intended exclusion.

prompt: A signed commercial lease requires the tenant to assume the landlord's tort liability for bodily injury arising out of the leased shop. The tenant's CGL has the contractual-liability exclusion and the insured-contract exception. The injury occurs after the lease is signed. How does that assumption usually sit?

options.text: It is excluded in every case, because every assumption of another person's liability in a lease falls outside the insured-contract exception
It qualifies as an insured contract, so the exclusion gives it back
It remains excluded, because the insured-contract exception gives back only liability the tenant would have had without the lease
It voids the tenant's CGL from the start, because naming a landlord's tort liability in a lease cancels Coverage A entirely

explanation: The contractual-liability exclusion removes bodily injury or property damage the insured must pay only because it assumed that liability in a contract. A lease of premises is an insured contract, and the exclusion gives back liability for damages assumed in an insured contract when the injury occurs after the contract is executed. Assuming the landlord's tort liability for injury arising out of the leased shop is the assumption that exception addresses.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the insured-contract exception. A lease of premises is an insured contract, so this tort assumption is not automatically excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the wrong exception. Liability the tenant already had does not need the lease. The insured-contract exception gives back this assumption of the landlord's tort liability.
distractorExplanations.d: Overstates the lease. An indemnity clause does not cancel Coverage A. The insured-contract exception is how the CGL treats this assumption.

prompt: A landscaping employee is cut by the firm's mower while mowing a client's lawn and sues the landscaping employer under the firm's CGL. The injury arose in the course of employment. No third party sued. Which Coverage A result is standard?

options.text: Covered under Coverage A, because the employer's-liability exclusion stops at the insured's own premises and this cut happened on a client's lawn
Covered under Coverage A, because only the workers compensation obligation is excluded and the employee's own negligence suit stays covered
Excluded as injury to an employee in the course of employment
Paid under Coverage C with no exclusion, because medical payments is designed to replace workers compensation for employees on the payroll

explanation: The CGL employer's-liability exclusion applies to bodily injury to an employee of the insured arising out of and in the course of employment. A mower cut while the employee is mowing for the firm is that injury. The employee's remedy runs through workers compensation and, where the employer carries it, employers liability coverage. Coverage A of the CGL is written to leave that employer-employee exposure out.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a premises limit the exclusion does not have. An employee cut while mowing for the firm is injured in the course of employment, including on a client's lawn.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the workers compensation exclusion with the employer's-liability exclusion. The employee's own suit for an on-the-job injury is excluded from Coverage A.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses Coverage C. Medical payments does not replace workers compensation for an employee hurt in the course of employment.

prompt: A caterer's contaminated main dish makes a guest ill and is itself ruined. The guest sues for hospital bills and for the price of that dish. The dish is the caterer's product. How does Coverage A usually split the two demands?

options.text: Both demands are excluded, because any illness caused by food is treated as damage to the insured's own product and nothing else
Both demands are covered in full, because a food claim does not fall under the exclusion for damage to the insured's own product
Only the price of the dish is covered, and the guest's illness is excluded as an expected result of serving any meal
The illness can be bodily injury; the dish itself is excluded

explanation: Coverage A can apply to a guest's bodily injury caused by a contaminated product. A separate exclusion applies to property damage to the insured's own product arising out of that product. The ruined dish, and a demand for its price, is damage to your product and stays excluded. The guest's illness is bodily injury to another person, so the your-product exclusion does not take that part of the suit.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the your-product exclusion erase the bodily-injury claim. That exclusion targets the dish itself, not the guest's illness.
distractorExplanations.b: Ignores the your-product exclusion. The price of the ruined dish is property damage to the caterer's product and is excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the split. The illness is the bodily-injury claim that can be covered. The dish is the excluded product.

prompt: A general contractor turns over a finished house. A roof installed entirely by a subcontractor then leaks and damages the completed interior. The CGL your-work exclusion applies to completed operations and contains the usual subcontractor exception. Which result fits that exception?

options.text: The subcontractor's leak can remain covered
The your-work exclusion bars every completed-operations loss, including work a subcontractor performed, so this leak is out
The exception applies solely when the general contractor performed the roofing, so a subcontractor's leak stays outside Coverage A
The exception pays only to replace the subcontractor's roof, and water damage to the finished interior remains excluded

explanation: The your-work exclusion removes property damage to the insured's completed work arising out of that work and included in the products-completed operations hazard. The exclusion does not apply when the damaged work, or the work out of which the damage arises, was performed on the insured's behalf by a subcontractor. A leak from roofing that a subcontractor performed is the situation that exception covers, so the loss can remain inside Coverage A.

distractorExplanations.b: Skips the subcontractor exception. The your-work exclusion is not absolute when a subcontractor performed the work out of which the damage arises.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the exception. The your-work exclusion drops out when a subcontractor performed the work out of which the damage arises, which is this roof.
distractorExplanations.d: Cuts the exception down to repair of the roof alone. Interior damage arising out of the subcontractor's roofing is part of the loss the exception can leave covered.

prompt: A tenant's employee negligently starts a fire that damages only the landlord's building, which the tenant rents. The CGL excludes property damage to premises the insured rents, with a give-back for fire damage to those premises. Which loss can that give-back address?

options.text: Fire damage to the tenant's own inventory, because the give-back insures the tenant's business personal property against fire
Fire damage to the rented premises
Every peril that harms the building, including flood and earthquake, because the give-back deletes the whole property-damage exclusion
Fire damage to a building next door that the tenant does not rent, because the give-back follows the fire beyond the leased premises

explanation: The CGL excludes property damage to premises the insured owns, rents, or occupies. That exclusion gives back damage by fire to premises while rented to the named insured or temporarily occupied with the owner's permission. Negligent fire damage to the landlord's rented building is the loss that give-back covers. Payment is subject to the Damage to Premises Rented to You limit printed on that policy's declarations.

distractorExplanations.a: Points at the tenant's own property. The give-back covers the tenant's liability for fire damage to the landlord's rented building, not the tenant's inventory.
distractorExplanations.c: Widens the give-back. The exception is for fire damage to the rented premises. It does not restore flood, earthquake, or every other peril.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the give-back off the rented premises. Damage by fire to a building the tenant does not rent is not what this rented-premises give-back addresses.

prompt: During a business argument, one partner of an insured partnership intentionally injures a vendor. The other partner did not take part and did not expect the injury, but is named in the same suit. The CGL has a separation-of-insureds condition. What must the insurer do?

options.text: Deny both partners automatically, because any intentional act by one partner is imputed to every insured on the policy
Cover both partners, because separation of insureds waives the expected-or-intended exclusion for every partner on the policy
Judge the innocent partner separately from the other partner's intent
Deny the innocent partner as well, because separation of insureds divides only the limits and applies each exclusion once to all insureds

explanation: Separation of insureds applies the coverage separately to each insured against whom a claim is made, except for the limits and duties reserved to the first named insured. The expected-or-intended injury exclusion is applied from the standpoint of the insured seeking coverage. The insurer therefore judges the partner who did not expect or intend the injury on that partner's own conduct, rather than automatically imputing the other partner's intent.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores separation of insureds. One partner's intent is not automatically imputed to the other insured when the condition requires a separate application.
distractorExplanations.b: Overreads the condition. Separation of insureds does not waive the expected-or-intended exclusion for the partner who meant to injure the vendor.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses what is separated. The limits stay shared. Coverage, including the intent exclusion, is applied separately to the partner who did not expect the injury.

prompt: Several diners are injured by a packaged food the insured sold after the food had left the insured's premises. The payments are products-completed operations claims. Which CGL aggregate do those payments reduce?

options.text: Only the general aggregate, because every food injury is reclassified as a premises claim once someone eats the product
Both the general aggregate and the products-completed operations aggregate, dollar for dollar, for the same payment
Neither aggregate, because products claims are paid entirely outside the limits shown on the declarations
The products-completed operations aggregate

explanation: A standard CGL has a general aggregate and a separate products-completed operations aggregate. Damages for bodily injury included in the products-completed operations hazard are paid under the products-completed operations aggregate. Those payments do not also reduce the general aggregate, which applies to other Coverage A damages, personal and advertising injury, and medical payments. Food injury after the product left the premises is a products-completed operations claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Reclassifies a products claim as premises. Injury from a product that has left the premises reduces the products-completed operations aggregate.
distractorExplanations.b: Double-counts one payment. A products payment reduces the products-completed operations aggregate, not both aggregates for the same dollars.
distractorExplanations.c: Places the claim outside the limits. Products-completed operations claims are subject to that aggregate and to the each-occurrence limit.

prompt: One falling shelf injures a browsing customer and an employee who was stocking that aisle. Both ask Coverage C medical payments to pay urgent-care bills. No lawsuit is filed. The employee was hurt in the course of employment. Whom is Coverage C designed to pay?

options.text: The customer, not the employee
The employee alone, because a customer must file a Coverage A lawsuit before any medical bill can be considered
Both of them, because medical payments is no-fault coverage for every person on the premises, including employees on the payroll
Neither person, because Coverage C pays only after a court enters a liability judgment against the named insured

explanation: Coverage C pays reasonable medical expenses for bodily injury caused by an accident, without regard to fault, and it does not require a lawsuit. It is aimed at others, such as a customer injured on the premises. It excludes a person hired to do work for an insured and injury for which workers compensation benefits are payable. An employee hurt while stocking the aisle is outside Coverage C.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the payees and invents a lawsuit requirement. The customer is the Coverage C claimant. Medical payments does not wait for a Coverage A suit.
distractorExplanations.c: Includes the employee. Medical payments is no-fault for others. It does not cover an employee injured in the course of employment.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds a judgment requirement. Coverage C is written to pay medical expenses without a finding that the insured is liable.

prompt: Forty days after a claims-made CGL expires, with no renewal and no purchased supplemental tail, a claimant first makes a claim. The injury occurred during the policy period and after the retroactive date. The form's basic extended reporting period lasts 60 days. What can respond?

options.text: No reporting period of any kind, because a claims-made policy that has expired cannot receive a claim first made on day 40
The automatic basic extended reporting period
Only a purchased supplemental tail, because the basic period never covers a claim made after the expiration date on the declarations
A later occurrence policy the insured might buy, because a claims-made tail cannot apply to an injury that already happened

explanation: A basic extended reporting period on a claims-made CGL is provided automatically, without an extra premium, when the policy ends and is not renewed. For a claim that was not already reported, that basic period lasts 60 days after expiration. A claim first made 40 days after expiration falls inside those 60 days. The supplemental tail is the optional longer period, and the insured did not need to buy it for a claim that arrives within the basic 60 days.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the basic tail. Expiration does not by itself bar a claim first made on day 40 when the basic extended reporting period runs 60 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the two tails. The supplemental tail is the purchased extension. The basic period is what covers a claim made within 60 days.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the claim onto a future occurrence form. An occurrence policy responds to injury during its own period. This claim is a claims-made reporting question.

prompt: An apartment LLC's CGL names only the LLC. An outside firm, which is not the LLC's employee or volunteer, manages the building and is sued for a tenant injury caused by that management. Under standard who-is-an-insured wording, what is the firm?

options.text: A certificate holder alone, so it has no insured status unless a separate certificate is issued after the tenant files suit
An insured for any personal activity of its staff, including conduct that has nothing to do with managing the apartment building
An insured while acting as real estate manager
Uninsured in every case, because only the named LLC and its executive officers can ever qualify as insureds

explanation: Standard CGL who-is-an-insured wording includes a person or organization, other than an employee or volunteer worker, while acting as the named insured's real estate manager. An outside firm managing the LLC's building is an insured for liability arising out of that management role. The status is limited to acting as real estate manager. It does not insure the firm for unrelated conduct of its staff.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a real estate manager with a certificate holder. Manager status comes from the who-is-an-insured wording, not from a certificate issued after suit.
distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the status. The firm is an insured while acting as real estate manager, not for personal activity unrelated to the building.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads who-is-an-insured too narrowly. The named LLC and its officers are not the only insureds. A real estate manager is an insured for that role.

prompt: A runner is knocked down by a dog after the walker lets the leash go slack. The runner sues the walker for negligence and must prove the full case. Which list is the complete negligence formula?

options.text: Intent to cause the harm, a voluntary act, and damages, which is the formula for a battery rather than for negligence
Duty and damages only, because breach and causation are presumed once any dog is on a public sidewalk
Strict liability alone, because the person walking the dog is liable for the knockdown without proof of duty, breach, or fault
Duty, breach, proximate cause, and damages

explanation: A negligence claim requires the plaintiff to prove a legal duty owed to the plaintiff, a breach of that duty, proximate cause connecting the breach to the harm, and actual damages. A slack leash that lets a dog knock a runner down is analyzed under those four elements. Intent to injure belongs to an intentional tort. Strict liability is a different theory and does not replace this formula.

distractorExplanations.a: States the intentional-tort elements. A negligence case does not require intent to harm. The runner must still prove duty, breach, proximate cause, and damages.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops two required elements. Duty and damages are not enough. The runner must also prove breach and proximate cause.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes strict liability. The question asks for the negligence formula the runner must prove, and strict liability is a different theory.

prompt: Before starting down a trail marked icy, a skier reads the posted ice warning, understands it, and chooses to ski that trail. The skier falls on the ice and sues the resort in negligence. Which defense best matches those facts?

options.text: Assumption of the risk
Contributory negligence, because skiing after reading the warning is carelessness that completely bars the skier
Comparative negligence, because the posted warning assigns the skier a share of fault and reduces the recovery by that share
An express waiver, because the posted ice warning is a written release of the resort that the skier accepts by starting down

explanation: Assumption of the risk applies when the plaintiff voluntarily encounters a danger the plaintiff knows and appreciates. Reading an ice warning, understanding it, and choosing to ski that trail is that choice. The defense goes to the skier's acceptance of the known ice. It answers the negligence suit on these facts. It is a tort defense, separate from how a liability policy would be triggered.

distractorExplanations.b: Names contributory negligence. These facts are knowledge of the ice and a voluntary choice to ski it, which is assumption of the risk, not a carelessness bar.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the warning into a fault percentage. The matching defense is the skier's knowing choice to meet the ice, and the stem states no share of fault to subtract.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a warning sign as a signed release. A posted ice warning is notice of the danger. It is not a written waiver of the resort's liability.

prompt: Where joint and several liability applies to an indivisible injury, two negligent drivers cause one crash that injures a pedestrian. The pedestrian holds a judgment for the entire loss. From whom may the pedestrian collect that judgment?

options.text: Only from both drivers together, and only after each driver has first paid an equal half of the judgment into court
The full amount from either driver
From neither driver, because joint and several liability cancels the judgment whenever more than one person was negligent
From the pedestrian's own uninsured-motorist insurer alone, because drivers who are jointly liable are immune from collection

explanation: Where joint and several liability applies, each defendant who caused an indivisible injury is liable for the full judgment. The pedestrian may collect the entire amount from either driver. The driver who pays may then seek contribution from the other driver so the two of them share the loss. The pedestrian does not have to collect half from each driver before either one is liable for the whole.

distractorExplanations.a: Requires a simultaneous split payment. Joint and several liability lets the plaintiff collect the whole judgment from either defendant.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the doctrine. Joint and several liability keeps the judgment alive against each negligent driver. It does not cancel collection.
distractorExplanations.d: Points at the wrong payor. Uninsured-motorist coverage is a separate auto contract. It does not replace collection from jointly liable drivers.

prompt: Lawyers for a CGL insurer have billed more to defend a covered suit than the each-occurrence limit on the declarations. No settlement or judgment has been paid. How do those defense bills usually relate to that limit?

options.text: They wipe out the limit, so the insurer may stop defending once legal bills merely equal the each-occurrence limit
They are reimbursed by the insured as a deductible before the insurer owes any defense of a covered suit
They are outside the limit and do not reduce it
They increase the each-occurrence limit by the amount of the bills, so a later judgment can use a higher limit than the declarations show

explanation: On a standard CGL, the cost of defending a covered suit is a supplementary payment in addition to the limits of insurance. Those defense bills do not reduce the each-occurrence limit. The duty to defend ends when the applicable limit has been used up by payment of judgments or settlements. Legal bills that exceed the printed limit, with no settlement or judgment yet paid, leave the limit available for damages.

distractorExplanations.a: Ends the defense too soon. Defense costs do not exhaust the occurrence limit. Exhaustion comes from paying judgments or settlements.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a defense deductible. The insured does not reimburse ordinary defense bills before the insurer defends a covered suit.
distractorExplanations.d: Misreads payments made in addition to the limits. Defense costs do not raise the each-occurrence limit available for a later judgment or settlement.

prompt: Dana's Personal Auto Policy shows Part A liability limits of 100/300/50. While driving her listed sedan, she negligently hits a pedestrian and also damages a parked delivery van. Which of these losses does Part A cover?

options.text: Bodily injury to the pedestrian and property damage to the van, for which Dana is legally liable.
Dana's own medical bills from soft-tissue injuries she suffered when her airbag deployed in the crash.
Collision repair to Dana's sedan after the impact, subject only to her Part D deductible.
Rental-car charges while Dana waits for her sedan to be repaired at a body shop after the crash.

explanation: PAP Part A is liability coverage. It pays damages for bodily injury and property damage for which an insured becomes legally responsible because of an auto accident, up to the policy limits. Dana's own medical bills, her car's collision repair, and rental costs are handled under other parts, not Part A.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Part A liability with Part B Medical Payments. Med pay can cover Dana's own medical expenses without regard to fault; Part A pays third-party BI/PD liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Part A with Part D Collision. Repair of the insured's own auto is physical damage, not liability.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Part A with a rental or transportation benefit. Those charges are not a Part A liability payment.

prompt: Marcus is the named insured on a Personal Auto Policy. His 19-year-old daughter lives in his household, has a learner's permit, and borrows his listed car with permission. She causes a covered BI accident. Who is an insured for Part A liability on that loss?

options.text: Only Marcus, because Part A never covers a household resident who is not listed by name on the declarations.
Marcus and his resident daughter using the covered auto with permission.
The daughter, because Marcus was not in the car when the accident happened.
Neither person, until the insurer first endorses the daughter as a named driver for an extra premium.

explanation: Under the PAP, insureds for Part A include the named insured and family members, and any person using a covered auto with permission. A resident daughter using the listed auto with permission is an insured even if she is not separately named on the declarations. Marcus remains an insured as the named insured.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates who is an insured. Family members who reside in the household are insureds for Part A; they need not be named on the declarations to qualify.
distractorExplanations.c: Incorrectly requires the named insured to be in the vehicle. Liability status does not depend on Marcus occupying the auto at the time of the crash.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a named-driver endorsement as a condition of coverage. Permissioned use by a resident family member is already within the PAP definition of insured.

prompt: While riding as a passenger in a friend's car, Lena is hurt when another driver runs a red light. Lena has her own Personal Auto Policy with Part B Medical Payments. How does Part B typically respond to her medical expenses from this accident?

options.text: It pays only after Lena proves the at-fault driver was negligent and recovers a judgment against that driver.
It pays when Lena was driving her own covered auto at the moment of the collision, and not as a passenger.
It can pay Lena's reasonable medical expenses for covered injuries, without requiring a finding of fault.
It pays the friend's auto repair bill first, then applies any leftover limit to Lena's medical bills.

explanation: PAP Part B Medical Payments covers reasonable expenses for necessary medical and funeral services because of bodily injury caused by an auto accident. The named insured and resident family members are covered while occupying a motor vehicle, including as a passenger in someone else's car, and Part B does not require proof of fault. It does not pay to repair another person's vehicle.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses med pay with liability recovery. Part B is not conditioned on proving another party's negligence or obtaining a judgment.
distractorExplanations.b: Narrows Part B too far. Med pay can apply when the insured is a passenger in another auto, not only when driving their own covered auto.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Part B with physical damage. Med pay addresses medical/funeral expenses, not the friend's collision repair costs.

prompt: Omar carries Part C Uninsured Motorists coverage on his PAP. An unidentified hit-and-run driver strikes his car and flees. Omar is injured and has no other BI recovery from that driver. Which statement best describes Part C's role?

options.text: Part C pays Omar's collision deductible only and never addresses bodily injury from a hit-and-run.
Part C replaces Omar's liability limits so he can pay passengers he injured in the same crash.
Part C is available after Omar first exhausts the Part D physical damage limits on his auto.
Part C can respond to Omar's covered BI damages caused by an uninsured or hit-and-run motorist.

explanation: PAP Part C Uninsured Motorists coverage pays compensatory damages an insured is legally entitled to recover from the owner or operator of an uninsured motor vehicle because of bodily injury. Hit-and-run vehicles that strike the insured auto are treated as uninsured motor vehicles under the typical PAP wording, so Part C can address Omar's covered BI claim when the at-fault driver cannot be identified or has no liability insurance.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates Part C. UM is primarily a bodily injury coverage for the insured's damages from an uninsured/hit-and-run motorist, not a collision-deductible reimbursement.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses UM with Part A liability. Part C protects the insured for BI caused by an uninsured motorist; it does not replace Omar's liability coverage for injuries he causes.
distractorExplanations.c: Creates a false sequencing rule. Part C UM is not conditioned on first exhausting Part D physical damage limits.

prompt: Priya's PAP includes Collision and Other Than Collision (comprehensive). A deer runs into the side of her parked covered auto overnight, crushing a door panel. No other vehicle is involved. Which Part D coverage applies to the door damage?

options.text: Other Than Collision (comprehensive), because animal contact is an OTC peril.
Collision, because any impact that dents metal is always paid only as Collision.
Neither Collision nor OTC, because the auto was parked and not being driven.
Part A liability, because striking an animal creates third-party property damage.

explanation: Under PAP Part D, contact with a bird or animal is listed as an Other Than Collision (comprehensive) loss, not Collision. Collision covers upset of the covered auto or its impact with another vehicle or object, subject to the policy's Collision definition and exceptions. Because a deer caused the damage with no other vehicle involved, OTC applies, typically subject to the OTC deductible.

distractorExplanations.b: Misclassifies animal contact as Collision. The PAP specifically treats contact with a bird or animal as an OTC peril, even though metal is damaged.
distractorExplanations.c: Incorrectly requires the auto to be in motion. Part D physical damage can apply whether the covered auto is driven or parked when a covered peril occurs.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses first-party physical damage with liability. Damage to Priya's own auto is Part D; Part A responds to liability to others, not to her own vehicle.

prompt: Tanya owns one private passenger auto already listed on her PAP. She buys a second private passenger auto and wants the new car covered. Under the standard newly acquired auto rules, what must she generally do for continued coverage after the automatic period?

options.text: Nothing; every newly purchased auto stays covered forever without notice to the insurer.
Ask the insurer to insure the new auto within the policy's required notice period.
Cancel the PAP and buy a Business Auto policy before driving the second car.
Wait until the next renewal date; midterm additions of autos are never allowed.

explanation: An additional private passenger auto gets temporary PAP coverage, but the named insured must ask the insurer to insure it within the policy's notice period or that coverage ends. Liability, medical payments, and uninsured motorists commonly require the request within 14 days. Physical damage can have a shorter request window when the policy does not already provide collision or other-than-collision on any auto. Reporting the new auto is what keeps coverage in force.

distractorExplanations.a: Overstates automatic coverage. Newly acquired auto protection is time-limited; the insured must request coverage within the policy's notice period.
distractorExplanations.c: Incorrectly forces a BA policy. A second private passenger auto for personal use can be added to a PAP; commercial auto is not required solely because a household owns two cars.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates midterm rules. Newly acquired autos can be added during the policy period when the insured complies with the PAP notice requirements.

prompt: After a total theft of Jamal's listed auto, Part D transportation expenses apply because the PAP provides Other Than Collision on that auto. Which expense is that coverage designed to help pay while the auto is withdrawn from use?

options.text: Jamal's speeding ticket from an earlier stop, together with the court costs on that citation.
The unpaid balance of Jamal's car loan above the vehicle's actual cash value after the total loss.
Temporary rental or substitute transportation costs, subject to daily and aggregate limits.
Medical payments for a passenger hurt in a different crash, paid under Part B.

explanation: Part D transportation expenses pay temporary transportation costs, such as a rental or other substitute transportation, while a covered auto is out of use after a total theft. Other Than Collision must apply to that auto. Payment is subject to the policy's daily limit, maximum, and waiting period. The benefit does not pay traffic fines, a loan balance above actual cash value, or medical payments.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses transportation expense with fines. Traffic tickets and penalties are not covered transportation expenses under Part D.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses transportation expense with gap/loan coverage. Paying the loan balance above ACV requires separate coverage, not rental reimbursement.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses transportation expense with Part B Medical Payments. Passenger medical bills are not paid as transportation expenses.

prompt: In a parking-lot argument, the named insured deliberately drives his covered auto into another person's car to damage it. He later files a Part A claim for the other owner's repair bill. How does the PAP typically treat this claim?

options.text: Part A pays in full because any accident involving a covered auto is automatically covered.
Part A pays, but only up to the property damage limit shown for hit-and-run losses.
Part D Collision pays the other owner's car, and Part A stays silent on intentional harm.
Coverage is excluded because intentionally caused injury or damage is not covered.

explanation: The PAP excludes liability coverage for an insured who intentionally causes bodily injury or property damage. Deliberately ramming another vehicle is intentional damage, so Part A does not respond. Calling the event an accident, or shifting the claim to Part D, does not create coverage for harm the insured meant to cause.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the intentional-act exclusion. Not every incident involving a covered auto is covered; injury or damage the insured causes on purpose is excluded.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a hit-and-run property-damage sublimit for intentional ramming. Hit-and-run rules do not override the exclusion for harm the insured causes on purpose.
distractorExplanations.c: Misapplies Part D. Collision pays for damage to the insured's covered auto, not for intentionally damaging another person's vehicle under liability.

prompt: Chris carries only a Personal Auto Policy. He regularly uses his listed private passenger auto to deliver restaurant meals for pay during evening shifts. During a paid delivery run he hits a parked car. Which coverage problem is most likely?

options.text: A public-or-livery exclusion for carrying property for a fee may bar liability on this delivery run.
Part A always covers any business delivery because the auto is listed on the declarations page as a covered auto.
Part D is affected; Part A liability still pays the business delivery claim in full without exclusion.
Coverage is automatic if Chris notifies the insurer after the accident, even for paid food delivery work.

explanation: Part A excludes liability while a vehicle is used as a public or livery conveyance. Carrying persons or property for a fee is the exposure that exclusion targets, along with many delivery endorsements. A share-the-expense car pool is the usual exception. Regular paid meal delivery often falls outside the PAP for that reason. A separate business exclusion does not, by itself, drop liability for an owned private passenger auto used in an occupation. Listing the auto on the declarations does not erase the livery exclusion.

distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the declarations. Listing the auto as a covered auto does not override a public or livery exclusion for carrying property for a fee.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrong about Part A. A livery exclusion for carrying property for a fee can bar the delivery claim; Part A does not stay fully in force merely because physical damage may also be affected.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats post-loss notice as a cure. Reporting after an accident does not create coverage that an exclusion already removes.

prompt: During a weekend track day, the named insured enters his covered sports car in an organized timed race on a closed course. He crashes into a barrier and injures a spectator. His PAP has Part A and Part D. Which outcome is most accurate under typical PAP racing exclusions?

options.text: Part A and Part D both apply fully because organized racing is treated like ordinary commuting on public roads.
Liability and physical damage are excluded while the auto is used in organized racing.
Only Part B Medical Payments is excluded; Parts A and D still cover racing crashes at the track.
Coverage applies if the named insured signs a track waiver before the first practice lap of the day.

explanation: The PAP excludes coverage when a covered auto is located inside a facility designed for racing and is being used to practice for, prepare for, or participate in any prearranged or organized racing, speed contest, or stunting activity. Both liability and physical damage are typically barred for that use. A track waiver does not restore PAP coverage that the racing exclusion removes.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats organized racing like normal road use. The PAP specifically excludes racing and similar competitive use, so Parts A and D do not apply as in ordinary commuting.
distractorExplanations.c: Understates the exclusion. Racing exclusions are not limited to Part B; they commonly eliminate liability and physical damage for the racing use.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a track waiver with insurance. A liability waiver may affect the track's claims against the driver but does not override the PAP racing exclusion.

prompt: After a multi-car crash, Nora's PAP Part E Duties After an Accident or Loss applies. Besides promptly notifying the insurer, which duty is she most clearly expected to fulfill for a covered claim?

options.text: Admit liability in writing to every other driver before speaking with her insurer about the claim.
Destroy damaged parts immediately so the insurer cannot inspect salvageable pieces from the crash.
Cooperate with the insurer and allow reasonable inspection of the damaged property.
Wait thirty days before reporting the accident so witnesses can leave the scene without statements.

explanation: PAP Part E requires the insured to give prompt notice, cooperate in the investigation and settlement of claims, send the insurer copies of notices or legal papers, submit to examination under oath when required, and protect and allow inspection of damaged property. Admitting liability, destroying evidence, or delaying notice violates those duties and can jeopardize coverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Conflicts with cooperation duties. The insured should not assume or admit liability; that can prejudice the insurer's defense.
distractorExplanations.b: Violates the duty to protect and permit inspection of damaged property. Destroying parts can void or reduce coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Conflicts with prompt notice. Part E requires timely reporting; waiting to let witnesses disappear is the opposite of the required duty.

prompt: A plumbing contractor owns three vans used only for job sites and carries tools and crew between commercial locations. The owner asks whether a Personal Auto Policy alone is the right form. Which comparison is most accurate?

options.text: A PAP is preferred because commercial vans are always scheduled as private passenger autos on a household policy.
A PAP automatically covers unlimited fleet vehicles used solely for business deliveries between job sites.
Business Auto and PAP forms are interchangeable for any vehicle the insured happens to own or lease.
A Business Auto policy better fits vehicles used primarily in the business.

explanation: The PAP is designed for private passenger autos and limited personal exposures. Vehicles used primarily in a trade or business—especially a small commercial fleet of vans—are generally written on a Business Auto (BA) or other commercial auto form that uses covered auto symbols and business-use underwriting. A PAP alone is not the appropriate primary form for that commercial fleet.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies commercial vans as private passenger autos for PAP purposes. Job-site vans used in the trade belong on commercial auto, not a household PAP.
distractorExplanations.b: Overstates PAP capacity. A PAP does not automatically insure an unlimited business fleet used for commercial deliveries.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats BA and PAP as interchangeable. The forms serve different exposures; commercial use belongs on BA/commercial auto.

prompt: On a Business Auto declarations page, Symbol 7 is shown for liability. The insured buys a new truck midterm and wants liability on it. What does Symbol 7 generally require compared with a broader "any auto" symbol?

options.text: Only specifically described autos are covered, so the new truck must be scheduled as required.
