Symbol 7 covers every auto the insured owns, hires, or borrows worldwide with no scheduling of vehicles.
Symbol 7 applies only to private passenger cars and never to trucks used in the plumbing business.
Symbol 7 automatically converts to Symbol 1 the day any new vehicle is purchased by the insured.

explanation: Business Auto covered auto symbols define which vehicles have which coverages. Symbol 1 is "any auto," while Symbol 7 is "specifically described autos" listed on the declarations. Newly acquired autos may receive limited automatic coverage, but under Symbol 7 the insured must generally report/schedule the vehicle within the policy's required period for liability to continue. Broader symbols do not require that same specific description for owned autos.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a broad symbol such as Symbol 1 (any auto), not Symbol 7. Symbol 7 is limited to specifically described autos.
distractorExplanations.c: Falsely restricts Symbol 7 to private passenger cars. Symbol 7 can schedule trucks and other commercial vehicles that are described.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents an automatic symbol conversion. Buying a vehicle does not rewrite Symbol 7 into Symbol 1 without an endorsement or an underwriting change.

prompt: Someone steals Reese's covered auto from a shopping-center lot. The thief is never found, and the car is a total loss. Reese has Other Than Collision on the PAP. How should the theft loss be classified under Part D?

options.text: As Collision, because theft always requires impact with another vehicle before payment.
As Other Than Collision (comprehensive), which includes theft of the covered auto.
As Part A liability, because the thief created a third-party property damage claim.
As uninsured motorists property damage, not as Part D physical damage.

explanation: Theft is an Other Than Collision peril under PAP Part D. OTC (comprehensive) covers loss to the covered auto caused by theft, fire, vandalism, glass breakage, and similar perils listed in the policy, typically subject to the OTC deductible. Collision is not required, and Part A or UM do not replace OTC for the insured's own stolen auto.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies theft as Collision. Theft is an OTC peril; Collision addresses upset or impact with another vehicle/object under the Collision definition.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses first-party theft with liability. Part A responds to the insured's legal liability to others, not to theft of the insured's own auto.
distractorExplanations.d: Misplaces the claim under UM. Uninsured motorists addresses BI (and sometimes PD, where offered) from an uninsured motorist—not standard theft of the insured's parked auto under Part D OTC.

prompt: In a no-fault state, Ava is injured in an auto accident and her policy includes Personal Injury Protection (PIP). At a high level, how does PIP typically differ from traditional at-fault liability claims for her own medical expenses?

options.text: PIP always replaces every state's tort system and permanently bans all lawsuits for any injury, without exception.
PIP pays after Ava wins a negligence lawsuit against the other driver in civil court and collects a judgment.
PIP can pay certain first-party benefits, such as medical expenses, without proving fault.
PIP is identical to Part A liability and exists to pay for damage to the other driver's car after a crash.

explanation: Personal Injury Protection is a first-party no-fault benefit found in states that use a no-fault system. PIP generally pays defined benefits—commonly medical expenses and sometimes lost wages or other benefits set by state law—to the insured without requiring proof that another driver was negligent. Exact benefit types and lawsuit thresholds vary by state and should not be invented as universal percentages.

distractorExplanations.a: Overstates no-fault. States differ; many preserve tort suits above thresholds or for certain harms rather than banning all lawsuits forever.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses no-fault logic. PIP is designed to pay first-party benefits without first winning a negligence lawsuit.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses PIP with Part A liability. PIP is first-party protection for the insured's benefits, not coverage that pays the other driver's vehicle damage.

prompt: A state financial responsibility law requires drivers to show ability to pay for injuries or damage they cause. After a reportable accident, which item most clearly serves as common proof of that ability for a typical private passenger driver?

options.text: A cancelled check stub from the driver's last oil change at a local shop near the accident scene.
An expired learner's permit that no longer authorizes operation of any vehicle on public roads.
A vehicle title showing the lienholder's name but no liability insurance information for the driver.
A valid auto liability insurance ID card evidencing required liability coverage.

explanation: Financial responsibility laws require motorists to demonstrate the ability to respond in damages for liability arising from auto accidents—most often by maintaining auto liability insurance that meets state minimums. An insurance ID card or similar evidence of current liability coverage is the usual proof. Maintenance receipts, expired permits, and titles alone do not prove financial responsibility.

distractorExplanations.a: An oil-change receipt shows maintenance, not liability insurance or other financial responsibility compliance.
distractorExplanations.b: An expired learner's permit does not prove current liability coverage or ability to pay accident damages.
distractorExplanations.c: A title identifies ownership/lien status; it is not proof of the liability insurance financial responsibility laws require.

prompt: Kai borrows a neighbor's private passenger auto with permission and causes a covered BI accident while running a personal errand. Kai has his own PAP; the neighbor also has a PAP on that auto. Which liability coverage generally responds as primary for the borrowed auto?

options.text: The neighbor's PAP on the borrowed auto is typically primary; Kai's PAP may be excess.
Only Kai's PAP pays, because the borrower's policy always replaces the owner's coverage.
Neither PAP responds until both insurers first deny coverage in writing to each other.
Part D on Kai's policy pays the injured person's bodily injury claim as primary.

explanation: For liability, the PAP on the vehicle involved is generally primary, and a permissive driver's own PAP may provide excess liability if needed. Kai is using a non-owned auto with permission, so the neighbor's policy on that auto typically pays first, subject to its terms, with Kai's PAP potentially excess. Part D physical damage does not pay third-party bodily injury.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses primary/excess. The owner's policy on the auto being driven is ordinarily primary; the borrower's PAP does not automatically replace it.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a mutual-denial prerequisite. Primary and excess coordination does not require both insurers to deny the claim before either one responds.
distractorExplanations.d: Misapplies Part D. Physical damage covers the insured auto's damage, not third-party bodily injury liability claims.

prompt: Underinsured Motorists (UIM) coverage is part of Part C on many PAPs. The at-fault driver carries liability insurance, but those limits are too low to pay all of Sam's covered BI damages. How does UIM typically help compared with basic UM for a driver with no insurance at all?

options.text: UIM pays Sam's Collision deductible only and never addresses a shortfall in the at-fault driver's BI liability limits after a crash.
UIM can cover Sam's remaining covered BI damages after the at-fault driver's inadequate limits are used.
UIM replaces Part A so Sam can pay passengers even when Sam was the negligent driver in the crash.
UIM applies when the other vehicle has zero liability insurance and carries no bond.

explanation: Uninsured Motorists coverage addresses BI caused by a motorist with no liability insurance (or certain hit-and-run situations). Underinsured Motorists coverage addresses the shortfall when the at-fault driver has liability insurance that is insufficient relative to the insured's damages and UIM limits. UIM therefore responds after the other driver's inadequate liability limits are applied, subject to state stacking and limit rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates UIM as deductible reimbursement. UIM is for the insured's remaining covered BI damages, not merely a Collision deductible refund.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses UIM with Part A liability. UIM protects the insured for damages caused by an underinsured motorist; it does not replace Sam's liability coverage for injuries Sam causes.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes UM (no insurance), not UIM. UIM exists precisely when the other driver has some liability insurance that is inadequate.

prompt: Hail dents every body panel of Luis's listed sedan while it sits empty in his driveway. No other vehicle is involved, and nobody is injured. His Personal Auto Policy includes liability, collision, and other-than-collision. Which coverage applies to those hail dents?

options.text: Other-than-collision, because hail damage to his covered auto is a comprehensive peril.
Collision, because any dent in the metal of a covered auto is paid only as collision no matter what caused it, including weather that strikes a parked car.
Liability, because Part A property damage pays to repair the named insured's own sedan when hail is the cause and no other driver can be named.
No coverage applies, because other-than-collision is written for a car that is being driven, and hail that dents a parked sedan is treated as wear rather than a covered peril.

explanation: Other-than-collision, often called comprehensive, applies to direct loss to the covered auto from hail. Hail is not collision, which is upset or impact with a vehicle or object. It is not a liability loss either, because nobody else was injured and no other vehicle was damaged. The parked sedan's hail dents stay on the comprehensive coverage.

distractorExplanations.b: Misclassifies hail as collision. Collision is upset or impact with a vehicle or object. Hail striking a parked sedan is an other-than-collision peril even though the metal is dented.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats hail damage to Luis's own sedan as Part A property damage. Liability pays others when the insured is legally responsible. It does not repair his hail-damaged car.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats parked hail damage as wear that other-than-collision will not pay, and limits that coverage to a car that is being driven. Hail to a covered auto is a comprehensive peril even while the sedan is parked.

prompt: Elena is the named insured on a Personal Auto Policy. Her unrelated roommate, who lives in the same apartment, borrows Elena's listed car with Elena's permission and negligently injures a cyclist. Who is an insured for liability on that loss?

options.text: Elena alone, because an unrelated household resident cannot qualify as an insured even with permission to drive the listed car.
Elena and the roommate, because permissive use of the covered auto makes that driver an insured.
Only the roommate, because the named insured loses insured status whenever she is not sitting in the car at the moment of impact.
Neither person, until the insurer first adds the roommate by name and charges an extra premium for the trip that already happened.

explanation: The named insured is an insured for the listed auto, and any person using that covered auto is also an insured. The roommate had Elena's permission, so the exclusion for use without a reasonable belief of entitlement does not apply. The roommate does not have to be a relative, and does not have to be listed on the declarations, to be an insured for this permissive use.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses family-member status with permissive use. An unrelated roommate is not a family member, but permission to use the covered auto still makes that driver an insured for liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Incorrectly requires the named insured to occupy the car. Elena remains an insured for the listed auto whether or not she is in it when the roommate injures the cyclist.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a named-operator endorsement as a condition of coverage. Permissive use of the covered auto already fits the liability definition of an insured.

prompt: A caterer's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 8 for liability, with a $100,000 limit and no broader symbol. For one wedding the caterer rents a cargo van from a rental company. The employee driver hits a parked luxury sedan and causes $120,000 of covered property damage to that sedan. What does Symbol 8 pay?

options.text: Nothing, because Symbol 8 reaches only autos the caterer already owns and describes on the declarations, never a short-term rental from a rental company.
The full $120,000, because Symbol 8 means any auto, including employees' personal cars on days off, and the printed limit is ignored.
The $100,000 limit on this hired van.
It pays $20,000, the part of the damage above the $100,000 limit, because Symbol 8 responds to the overflow on a hired van.

explanation: Symbol 8 means hired autos only: autos the insured leases, hires, rents, or borrows, other than from employees or members of their households. A cargo van rented from a rental company fits. The covered damage is $120,000 and the liability limit is $100,000. Symbol 8 pays $100,000. The unpaid amount is 120000 minus 100000, which equals 20000.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates Symbol 8 as specifically described owned autos. That scheduling rule belongs to a different symbol. Symbol 8 is the hired-auto symbol and can cover this rental van.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Symbol 8 with any-auto coverage and ignores the limit. Employee cars used off duty are not this symbol, and $120,000 is not payable when the limit is $100,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the amount above the limit instead of the limit. Symbol 8 covers this hired van, and the most it pays for the $120,000 loss is the $100,000 liability limit, not the $20,000 overflow.

prompt: Wesley's covered sedan runs a red light and hits a parked truck. He is legally liable for the truck's $3,000 repair. Repair of his own car is $2,000. His Part A property-damage limit is $25,000, and his collision deductible is $500. Which payment pattern is correct?

options.text: Liability pays both the truck and Wesley's own car in full, because every vehicle touched in the crash is third-party property up to the property-damage limit.
Collision pays the truck's full repair and Wesley's full repair, because the deductible is waived when the other vehicle was parked and unoccupied.
Neither coverage pays, because running a red light is an intentional act that removes both liability and collision until a court assigns fault.
Liability pays the truck's $3,000, and collision pays $1,500 of his own repair.

explanation: Part A liability pays the parked truck because Wesley is legally liable for that property damage. The truck repair of $3,000 is within the $25,000 property-damage limit, so liability pays $3,000. Unused property-damage limit is 25000 minus 3000, which equals 22000. Collision pays his own repair minus the deductible: 2000 minus 500 equals 1500. The collision deductible is not subtracted from the truck payment, and liability does not repair his own car.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses liability with first-party physical damage. Part A pays the other party's truck. It does not pay to repair the named insured's own sedan.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the truck to collision and waives the deductible without a policy basis. Collision applies to Wesley's car, and the $500 deductible still comes off that repair.
distractorExplanations.c: Misreads negligence as an intentional-act exclusion. Running a red light is careless driving, not harm he set out to cause, so liability and collision can both respond to their own parts of the loss.

prompt: A bakery's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 9, and only Symbol 9, for liability, with a $100,000 limit. An employee uses her own sedan, which the bakery does not own, to deliver a wedding cake. The bakery is legally liable for $40,000 of covered bodily injury from that delivery. What does Symbol 9 do?

options.text: It covers the bakery's liability and pays the $40,000.
It pays nothing, because Symbol 9 reaches solely autos the bakery owns and lists, and an employee-owned sedan is outside that symbol by definition.
It pays to repair the employee's sedan as collision, because Symbol 9 is a physical-damage symbol and does not respond to bodily injury in any respect.
It pays the injury only if the bakery had already scheduled that sedan as a specifically described auto before the cake delivery began.

explanation: Symbol 9 means non-owned autos only: autos the named insured does not own, lease, hire, rent, or borrow that are used in the business, including an employee's own auto while used that way. The bakery is legally liable for this delivery. The bodily-injury amount is $40,000 and the limit is $100,000, so Symbol 9 pays $40,000. Remaining limit is 100000 minus 40000, which equals 60000. The symbol does not become collision coverage for the employee's car.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses Symbol 9. Owned and scheduled autos belong to a different symbol. Symbol 9 is the non-owned symbol and includes an employee's own car used for the bakery's delivery.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a liability symbol with physical damage. Symbol 9 is shown for liability here. It does not pay collision repairs to the employee's sedan.
distractorExplanations.d: Imports a specifically described scheduling rule into Symbol 9. An employee-owned auto used in the business does not have to be listed for this non-owned symbol to apply.

prompt: While Maya's listed sedan is in the shop for repairs, she drives a short-term dealer loaner on a personal errand. The dealer gave permission, and the loaner is not available for her regular use. She causes a liability crash. How does her Personal Auto Policy treat that loaner for her liability coverage?

options.text: As an uninsured non-owned auto that liability does not cover, because solely the autos printed on the declarations can create any liability coverage whatsoever.
As a temporary substitute, so Maya is an insured while using it.
As a newly acquired auto she must already own, because a loaner is covered only after the title transfers into her name and she pays sales tax.
As a commercial hired auto that her Personal Auto Policy cannot cover until she first buys a Business Auto policy in the dealer's name.

explanation: A temporary substitute is an auto the named insured does not own, used because her covered auto is out of normal use for breakdown, repair, servicing, loss, or destruction. This short-term dealer loaner fits, and it is not furnished for her regular use. Maya is an insured for that liability use. She does not have to take title, and she does not need a Business Auto policy for this personal substitute.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a temporary substitute with an unlisted auto that has no coverage. Liability can extend to a qualifying temporary substitute even though that loaner is not printed on the declarations.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a loaner with a newly acquired auto. A temporary substitute is used while her own car is being repaired. Coverage does not wait until Maya buys the loaner.
distractorExplanations.d: Forces a commercial form onto a personal loaner. A dealer loaner used while her private passenger car is repaired can be a temporary substitute on her Personal Auto Policy.

prompt: River water floods the garage stall where Ingrid's covered auto is parked. The cabin and electronics are soaked. The car was not driven, and it struck nothing. She carries both collision and other-than-collision. Which physical-damage coverage applies to the soaked auto?

options.text: Collision, because contact with standing water is defined as an upset of the covered auto and is paid only under the collision agreement.
Liability, because Part A property damage pays for flood loss to the named insured's own auto when the car was parked and no other driver is involved.
Other-than-collision, because flood and water are comprehensive perils.
No physical-damage coverage, because flood belongs on a homeowners policy, and water that soaks a covered auto inside a garage falls outside the Personal Auto Policy.

explanation: Other-than-collision includes water and flood damage to the covered auto. Ingrid's car was parked and struck nothing, so this is not collision and not an upset from impact with an object. Liability does not repair her own flooded auto. This soaked sedan is not pushed onto a homeowners policy. The cabin and electronics stay on comprehensive coverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies flood as collision. Collision is upset or impact with a vehicle or object. Water and flood damage to a parked car are other-than-collision perils.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses first-party flood damage with liability. Liability pays others when the insured is legally responsible. It does not pay Ingrid for flood damage to her own auto.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves an auto flood loss to a homeowners policy. Water and flood damage to a covered auto are other-than-collision perils on the Personal Auto Policy.

prompt: A landscaper's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 1 for liability with a $300,000 limit. With the owner's permission, a crew member borrows a customer's pickup for a single job and backs into a bystander's parked car, causing $6,000 of covered property damage. How does Symbol 1 respond?

options.text: It does not respond, because Symbol 1 applies solely to autos the landscaper owns, so the customer's pickup must be scheduled before any gate or vehicle claim is considered.
It pays the $6,000 as comprehensive damage to the customer's pickup, because Symbol 1 converts this liability loss into physical damage on the borrowed truck.
It declines the claim, because Symbol 1 never includes a pickup or truck and is limited to private passenger autos used by the owner.
It can cover this borrowed pickup and pays the $6,000.

explanation: Symbol 1 means any auto, so a customer's pickup that the business borrows can be a covered auto for liability. The bystander's car is someone else's property. The damage is $6,000 and the limit is $300,000, so the policy pays $6,000. Unused limit is 300000 minus 6000, which equals 294000. Symbol 1 does not have to be rewritten when this borrowed pickup is used.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes owned autos or specifically described autos, not Symbol 1. Symbol 1 means any auto and can include a borrowed pickup without scheduling it on the declarations.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the $6,000 as comprehensive damage to the borrowed pickup. That sum is liability damage to the bystander's car. Symbol 1 does not convert it into physical damage on the customer's truck.
distractorExplanations.c: Restricts Symbol 1 to private passenger autos. Symbol 1 means any auto and can include a pickup used with permission on a job.

prompt: Jordan is the only person named on the Personal Auto Policy declarations. Jordan's spouse lives in the same household, is not listed by name, and causes a liability crash while driving the listed car. Is that resident spouse an insured for the crash?

options.text: Yes. A spouse who lives in the household is an insured.
No. Liability insureds are limited to the single name printed on the declarations, so an unlisted spouse has no insured status while driving the listed car.
No. A resident spouse is an insured solely while riding in a non-owned auto and is excluded while driving the car described on the policy.
Yes, but only after the insurer issues a named-driver endorsement and the spouse pays a separate premium for the trip that already occurred.

explanation: On the Personal Auto Policy, the word you includes the named insured shown in the declarations and the spouse if a resident of the same household. Jordan's spouse lives there and does not have to be listed separately to be an insured. Driving the listed car is a covered use for that resident spouse. A named-driver endorsement is not required before that status exists.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the declarations listing with who is an insured. A resident spouse is an insured for liability even when only one name is printed on the declarations.
distractorExplanations.c: Inverts where the resident spouse is covered. That spouse is an insured for use of the listed car, not merely for a non-owned auto.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats an endorsement and an extra premium as conditions that must be met after the crash. Resident-spouse status already exists under the policy without that endorsement.

prompt: An accounting firm's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 2 for liability and no other liability symbol. A staff accountant drives her personally owned car, not a firm car, while taking a client to court and causes $20,000 of bodily-injury damages. How much of that $20,000 does Symbol 2 pay?

options.text: All $20,000, because any personal car used to transport a client is treated as owned by the firm for the day of the courthouse trip.
None of the $20,000, because this is not an owned auto.
It pays the $20,000, because Symbol 2 means non-owned autos and an employee's own car used to transport a client is the auto that symbol covers.
All $20,000, because Symbol 2 automatically broadens to any auto for that one courthouse errand without a change to the policy.

explanation: Symbol 2 means owned autos only. The sedan belongs to the accountant, not to the firm, so it is not a covered auto under Symbol 2. The bodily-injury damages are $20,000. Symbol 2 pays $0 of that amount. The unpaid amount is 20000 minus 0, which equals 20000. Liability for an employee-owned car used in the business would need a non-owned or any-auto symbol.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a client trip as a transfer of ownership. Using a personal car for work does not make that car an owned auto under Symbol 2, so the $20,000 is not paid by this symbol.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls Symbol 2 a non-owned symbol. Symbol 2 means owned autos only. The accountant's sedan is not owned by the firm, so Symbol 2 does not pay the $20,000 bodily-injury loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents an automatic rewrite from Symbol 2 to any-auto coverage. A courthouse errand does not change the symbol printed for liability.

prompt: Someone keys the doors of Andre's covered auto in a restaurant lot and does not steal the car. No other vehicle struck it. He carries collision and other-than-collision. Which coverage applies to the keyed paint on his own auto?

options.text: Collision, because damage a person causes on purpose is paid under the collision agreement and is never classified as comprehensive.
Liability, because Part A property damage pays to repaint the named insured's own auto when a stranger keys the doors and no other vehicle struck it.
Other-than-collision, because vandalism is a comprehensive peril.
Uninsured motorists property damage, because the person who keyed the doors left and cannot be identified, so the keyed paint is paid as a hit-and-run loss.

explanation: Vandalism and malicious mischief are other-than-collision perils. Keying the paint is deliberate damage by someone else, but it is not collision, because Andre's car did not upset or strike a vehicle or object. Liability does not repair his own paint. An unidentified person with a key is not a hit-and-run motorist. The loss stays on comprehensive coverage.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies vandalism as collision. A keyed door is malicious mischief, which the physical-damage definitions treat as other-than-collision rather than as an impact loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses first-party vandalism with liability. Liability pays others when the insured is legally responsible. It does not pay Andre to repaint his own keyed doors.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats an unidentified vandal as a hit-and-run motorist. Uninsured motorists property damage does not pay malicious mischief to the named insured's own paint.

prompt: One covered crash on a Business Auto policy produces a $320,000 bodily-injury settlement and a $240,000 property-damage settlement. The policy has a $500,000 combined single liability limit and no separate split limits. How much does that single limit pay for the two settlements together?

options.text: It pays $560,000, because a combined single limit adds the two settlements and then ignores the dollar cap printed on the declarations.
It pays $320,000 and no more, because a combined single limit covers bodily injury and drops property damage arising from the same crash.
It pays $240,000 only, because a combined single limit pays the smaller settlement and excludes the larger bodily-injury amount.
It pays the $500,000 limit.

explanation: A combined single limit is one amount available for bodily injury and property damage together. Add the settlements: 320000 plus 240000 equals 560000. That total is above the $500,000 limit, so the policy pays $500,000. The unpaid amount is 560000 minus 500000, which equals 60000. The limit does not pick only one of the two settlements.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the stated cap. Adding the settlements produces $560,000 of damages, but payment stops at the $500,000 combined single limit rather than paying the whole sum.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits a combined limit back into bodily injury only. The single limit applies to both settlements together, not to the $320,000 bodily-injury figure alone.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays only the smaller settlement. A combined single limit does not choose the lesser loss. It pays up to $500,000 of the combined damages.

prompt: A Personal Auto Policy declarations page shows Part A split limits of $50,000 per person, $100,000 per accident for bodily injury, and $25,000 for property damage. Those figures are this policy's limits. One pedestrian has $80,000 of covered bodily-injury damages, and no other person is hurt. What is the most Part A pays for that pedestrian?

options.text: It pays $50,000, the per-person bodily-injury limit.
It pays $80,000, because Part A must match the full bodily-injury demand whenever only one person is injured and no second claimant exists.
It pays $100,000, because the per-accident bodily-injury figure replaces the per-person figure when the injured person is a pedestrian rather than an occupant.
It pays $25,000, because the property-damage limit is the cap that applies to a pedestrian's bodily-injury claim under split limits.

explanation: The split limits give $50,000 of bodily injury for each person, $100,000 of bodily injury for the accident, and $25,000 of property damage. This pedestrian's damages are $80,000. The per-person cap is $50,000, so Part A pays $50,000. The unpaid amount is 80000 minus 50000, which equals 30000. The $100,000 per-accident limit does not raise the per-person cap. The $25,000 limit is property damage and does not apply to this injury.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignores the per-person cap. Covered damages of $80,000 do not raise the $50,000 bodily-injury limit that applies to this one pedestrian.
distractorExplanations.c: Misuses the per-accident figure. The $100,000 limit is the most for all bodily injury in the accident. It does not replace the $50,000 cap for this one person.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the property-damage limit to a bodily-injury claim. The $25,000 figure is for property damage, not for the pedestrian's injuries.

prompt: A hauler's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 4 for liability with a $50,000 limit. The hauler owns both a dump truck and a sales manager's private passenger car. The dump truck strikes a parked sedan the hauler does not own and causes $9,000 of covered property damage. The manager's car is not in the crash. What is the Symbol 4 result?

options.text: Symbol 4 would also have covered the manager's private passenger car, because the symbol means every auto the hauler owns, of any body type, and the payment rule is identical.
Symbol 4 covers this dump truck and pays the $9,000.
Symbol 4 covers solely the manager's private passenger car, so this dump-truck crash is outside the symbol and no part of the $9,000 is paid.
Symbol 4 applies only to vehicles rented for a few days, so an owned dump truck never qualifies and the parked-sedan damage is declined.

explanation: Symbol 4 means owned autos other than private passenger autos. The owned dump truck qualifies, and the owned private passenger car would not. This loss is $9,000 and the limit is $50,000, so Symbol 4 pays $9,000. Unused limit is 50000 minus 9000, which equals 41000. The manager's car was not involved and is not the kind of owned auto Symbol 4 describes.

distractorExplanations.a: Broadens Symbol 4 to every owned auto, including a private passenger car. Symbol 4 leaves owned private passenger autos off the coverage, even though this truck loss is covered.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the symbol. Symbol 4 covers the owned dump truck that struck the parked sedan, not the manager's private passenger car.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Symbol 4 with hired autos. Symbol 4 is an owned-auto symbol for vehicles other than private passenger autos, not a short-term rental symbol.

prompt: A contractor rents a cargo van from a rental company. The Business Auto policy shows Symbol 8 for liability with a $250,000 limit. The contractor's employee, driving with permission, causes $7,500 of covered property damage to a parked motorcycle. Which statement about who is an insured is correct?

options.text: The rental company is an insured for its own liability as owner of the van, and the contractor's policy is written to pay that ownership exposure first.
Only the rental company's garage staff are insureds, and the contractor's employee is excluded because a permissive driver of a hired van is never an insured.
The contractor and the permissive employee can be insureds; the rental company is not.
Nobody is an insured on this rental unless the rental company is rewritten as the named insured before the employee starts the trip.

explanation: Symbol 8 makes the rented van a hired auto. The named insured is an insured for a covered auto, and a person using a hired auto with permission can be an insured. The rental company, as the owner from whom the van is hired, is not an insured for that auto. The motorcycle damage is $7,500 and the limit is $250,000, so the covered liability payment is $7,500. Unused limit is 250000 minus 7500, which equals 242500. That sum is available to insureds under the contractor's policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives insured status to the rental company. The owner from whom a covered auto is hired is not an insured for that hired auto under the business auto who-is-an-insured provisions.
distractorExplanations.b: Excludes the permissive employee and invents coverage for the rental company's garage staff. A permissive user of the hired van can be an insured; the owner is the usual exception.
distractorExplanations.d: Requires the rental company to become the named insured. The contractor is already the named insured, and Symbol 8 can cover the hired van without that rewrite.

prompt: During a heavy rain, Paige's covered car hydroplanes and strikes a guardrail. The impact creases one fender. The car was moving and was not sitting in floodwater. She carries collision and other-than-collision. Which coverage applies to that fender?

options.text: Other-than-collision, because every loss that happens while rain is falling is classified as flood, even when the moving car hits a guardrail.
Liability, because the guardrail belongs to someone else, so Part A pays to repair Paige's fender as property damage from this crash.
Other-than-collision pays the hydroplaning portion of the fender and collision pays the guardrail portion, because those two causes divide a single crease into separate claims.
Collision, because this is impact with an object.

explanation: Collision includes the upset of the covered auto or its impact with another vehicle or object. Hitting the guardrail is that kind of impact. Rain on the roadway does not reclassify the loss as flood, and it does not split the fender between two coverages. Flood and water damage apply when water itself damages the auto, such as a car sitting in floodwater. Liability may address damage to the guardrail, but it does not pay Paige's fender.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats rain as flood. Other-than-collision would apply to flood or water damage. This loss is the impact with the guardrail, so it is collision rather than a flood peril.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses liability with first-party physical damage. Liability may respond to damage to the guardrail. It does not pay to repair Paige's own fender.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits one guardrail impact into a hydroplaning payment and a collision payment. The crease came from striking the guardrail, so the fender is collision rather than a flood loss.

prompt: Nina borrows a neighbor's private passenger car. The neighbor is not a family member, and the car is not furnished for Nina's regular use. Her Personal Auto Policy says the $250 collision deductible applies to this non-owned auto. She hits a post. The covered repair cost is $1,000, and the neighbor has no collision insurance. What does Nina's collision coverage pay?

options.text: It pays $750.
It pays $1,000, because a collision deductible is waived whenever the damaged auto is borrowed rather than owned by the named insured.
It pays $250, because the deductible is the most collision will pay on a non-owned auto no matter how large the repair bill is.
It pays nothing, because collision on a Personal Auto Policy never applies to a non-owned auto and only the car owner's policy can pay physical damage.

explanation: Collision can apply to a non-owned private passenger auto that is not owned by, or furnished for the regular use of, the named insured or a family member, while she is operating it. The neighbor has no collision insurance. The covered repair is $1,000 and the stated deductible is $250. Payment is 1000 minus 250, which equals 750. Nina bears the deductible; it is not the insurer's maximum payment.

distractorExplanations.b: Waives the deductible because the car is borrowed. The policy states that the $250 collision deductible applies to this non-owned auto, so the full $1,000 repair is not payable.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the deductible as a maximum payment. The deductible is the part Nina bears. Collision pays the repair above that $250, not a $250 cap.
distractorExplanations.d: Denies non-owned collision entirely. Collision can cover a qualifying non-owned auto when the policy provides it and no other collision insurance applies to that car.

prompt: A realtor's Business Auto policy shows Symbol 3 for liability with a $100,000 limit. The realtor owns a private passenger car for client showings and a box truck for hauling open-house signs. The car knocks down a fence the realtor does not own and causes $4,500 of covered property damage. The box truck stays parked. What does Symbol 3 do with the fence loss?

options.text: It would pay the same way if the box truck had knocked down the fence, because Symbol 3 means every owned vehicle regardless of body type.
It covers this private passenger car and pays the $4,500.
It covers the box truck alone, so this showing-car loss is outside Symbol 3 and no part of the fence damage is paid.
It applies only to autos leased for a month or less, so the realtor's owned showing car is not a Symbol 3 auto and the fence claim is declined.

explanation: Symbol 3 means owned private passenger autos only. The realtor's showing car qualifies, and the owned box truck would not. The fence loss is $4,500 and the limit is $100,000, so Symbol 3 pays $4,500. Unused limit is 100000 minus 4500, which equals 95500. The parked box truck is outside this symbol even though the realtor owns it.

distractorExplanations.a: Extends Symbol 3 to the box truck. Symbol 3 is limited to owned private passenger autos and would not pick up the owned box truck if that truck had caused the loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the symbol. Symbol 3 covers the owned private passenger car that knocked down the fence, not the box truck used for signs.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses Symbol 3 with hired autos. Symbol 3 is an owned private passenger symbol, so the realtor's owned showing car can qualify without being a short-term rental.

prompt: A stranger steals the named insured's car from the driveway and, while fleeing, injures a pedestrian. The stranger had no permission and no reason to believe that use of the car was allowed. Does the Personal Auto Policy cover the stranger's liability to that pedestrian?

options.text: Yes. Anyone occupying a covered auto is covered for liability, and a thief is treated the same as a driver who was handed the keys.
Yes. Liability follows the car itself, so every driver is covered until the insurer cancels the policy, including a driver who stole the car from the driveway.
No. Use without a reasonable belief of permission is excluded.
No, but only because a theft is paid as other-than-collision, and that physical-damage coverage replaces liability for the pedestrian's bodily injury.

explanation: The Personal Auto Policy excludes liability coverage for a person who uses a vehicle without a reasonable belief of being entitled to do so. A stranger who steals the car has neither permission nor that belief. Other-than-collision may address theft damage to the named insured's own car, but it does not pay the stranger's bodily-injury liability to the pedestrian.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a thief as a permissive user. Sitting in the car is not enough when the driver has no reasonable belief of permission. That use is excluded from liability coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: Claims the policy follows every driver until cancellation. Cancellation is not the issue. Use without a reasonable belief of entitlement is excluded while the policy is still in force.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses other-than-collision on the stolen car with liability to a pedestrian. Comprehensive theft coverage does not pay the thief's bodily-injury liability.

prompt: Cole's covered sedan is recovered after thieves crash it into a fence and flee. He carries collision and other-than-collision. The damage to his sedan resulted from the theft, and nobody claims a bodily injury. Which Part D coverage applies to his sedan?

options.text: Collision only, because the sedan hit a fence and impact with an object can never be paid as other-than-collision once the metal is bent.
Part A liability for the fence, because that property belongs to someone else, and Part D pays nothing for Cole's sedan when the same crash also harms another person's property.
Transportation expenses, because a theft is handled as the cost of a substitute car, and the crash damage to the sedan itself is left unpaid under Part D.
Other-than-collision, because the cause is theft.

explanation: Collision does not include loss caused by theft or larceny. The fence impact happened while thieves had the sedan, and the damage to Cole's car resulted from the theft, so Part D treats it as other-than-collision. That comprehensive coverage pays to repair his sedan. Damage to someone else's fence does not cancel that payment, and the repair is not replaced by the cost of a substitute car.

distractorExplanations.a: Classifies the thief's impact as collision. Once the cause is theft, the physical-damage definitions keep the damage to Cole's sedan in other-than-collision rather than moving it to collision.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the fence owner's property to wipe out Part D on Cole's sedan. Other-than-collision still pays the theft damage to his auto. Any liability for the fence is a separate coverage question.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops at transportation expenses and leaves the sedan unpaid. A theft can include a substitute-car benefit, but other-than-collision still pays the theft damage to Cole's car.

prompt: Maya wants to insure a lake cabin her uncle owns and still lives in. Maya has no ownership interest, mortgage, or lease on the cabin, and she will not suffer a financial loss if it burns. On a national P&C licensing exam, what must be true for Maya’s fire policy on that cabin to be enforceable at the time of a loss?

options.text: Maya only needs the uncle’s verbal permission to buy the policy, because family consent creates an insurable interest even without any financial stake.
Maya can insure any property she chooses as long as she pays the premium in full before the loss date and names the uncle as an additional insured.
Maya must have an insurable interest—a financial stake that would suffer if the cabin is damaged—at the time of loss.
Maya needs an insurable interest when she applies for coverage; after the policy is issued, a later lack of financial stake does not affect recovery.

explanation: Property insurance requires an insurable interest: a lawful financial stake that would be harmed by loss of the property. For property coverage, that interest must exist at the time of loss. Mere family relationship or premium payment without a financial stake does not create it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses family consent with insurable interest. Verbal permission from a relative does not create a financial stake that supports a property policy.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats premium payment and naming another party as enough. Paying premium and listing an additional insured does not invent an insurable interest for Maya.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates the timing rule. For property insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time of loss, not only at application.

prompt: A warehouse fire destroys inventory that cost the insured $80,000 to acquire and that would cost $80,000 to replace with identical stock. After depreciation and policy terms, the insurer’s ACV payment would be $80,000 before the deductible. The insured demands $120,000 because that is what a competitor recently paid for a similar lot. Which principle limits the recovery?

options.text: Contribution, which forces every insurer that ever quoted the risk to share the claim equally even if only one policy is in force.
Utmost good faith, which lets the insured name any settlement figure so long as the application was filled out honestly.
Adhesion, which automatically awards the higher of ACV or a competitor’s purchase price whenever the forms are standard.
Indemnity, which restores the insured to approximately the same financial position as before the loss, not a profit.

explanation: Indemnity means insurance restores the insured to roughly the pre-loss financial position and is not meant to create a windfall. Paying $120,000 when the insured’s ACV loss is $80,000 would leave the insured better off than before the fire.

distractorExplanations.a: Misapplies contribution. Contribution addresses sharing among multiple insurers covering the same interest, not inflating one insurer’s payment above loss value.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses utmost good faith with claim valuation. Honest application does not entitle the insured to invent a higher settlement figure.
distractorExplanations.c: Misuses adhesion. Standard-form adhesion does not rewrite valuation into the higher of ACV or a competitor’s price.

prompt: A delivery truck owned by another company backs into an insured’s storefront. The property insurer pays the covered repair cost under the store’s commercial property policy. The insured has not yet sued the trucking company. What right does the paying insurer typically obtain?

options.text: Subrogation: the insurer steps into the insured’s shoes to recover from the legally responsible third party.
Assignment of the entire property policy to the trucking company, which then becomes the named insured for future losses.
Abandonment: the insurer must take title to the damaged storefront and the land under it before it can seek recovery.
Salvage only against the insured’s remaining inventory, with no right to pursue the at-fault trucking company at all.

explanation: After paying a covered loss caused by a third party, the insurer typically gains subrogation rights: it stands in the insured’s place to recover from the party legally responsible. That recovery right is separate from abandoning property or assigning the whole policy.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses subrogation with policy assignment. Paying a claim does not transfer the entire policy to the at-fault party as the new named insured.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses subrogation with abandonment. The insurer need not take title to the building and land before pursuing the responsible third party.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits recovery to salvage of inventory. Salvage concerns remaining property after a loss; subrogation is the path against the at-fault trucking company.

prompt: Jordan sells a commercial building mid-term and wants the buyer to take over Jordan’s existing property policy without contacting the insurer. The policy is a standard commercial property form with the usual assignment language. Before a loss occurs, which statement best describes assignment of that policy?

options.text: Jordan may freely assign the entire policy to any buyer because property policies travel with title like a deed covenant.
Jordan generally cannot assign the policy to the buyer without the insurer’s written consent before a loss occurs.
Assignment is automatic once the deed records, and the insurer must accept the buyer even if underwriting would decline the risk.
Only the mortgagee can assign the policy; the named insured never needs consent because the contract is personal to lenders only.

explanation: A property insurance contract is personal to the insured. Before a loss, the named insured generally cannot assign the policy to a buyer without the insurer’s consent. After a loss, the claim (right to payment) is often assignable even when the policy itself is not freely transferable.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the policy like a deed covenant that rides with title. Insurance is a personal contract and does not automatically follow a sale without consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Assumes recording the deed forces the insurer to accept the buyer. Underwriting consent still matters; assignment is not automatic on recording.
distractorExplanations.d: Incorrectly limits assignment rules to mortgagees. The named insured’s assignment of the policy before loss still typically needs insurer consent.

prompt: Lightning strikes a bakery’s roof and starts a fire that guts the kitchen equipment. While the bakery is closed for repairs, the owner also loses three weeks of normal sales. On a standard property policy that covers direct physical loss but needs a separate time-element form for business income, how are these losses classified?

options.text: Both the kitchen damage and the lost sales are direct losses because they share the same lightning event as the original cause.
Both are indirect losses only; direct loss exists solely when an earthquake or flood is the first peril listed on the form.
Kitchen damage is a direct physical loss; the lost sales are an indirect (consequential) loss from the interruption.
Lost sales are a direct loss, and kitchen damage is consequential because equipment value is harder to prove than revenue.

explanation: Direct loss is physical damage to covered property from a covered peril—here, the fire-damaged kitchen. Lost sales while the bakery cannot operate are an indirect or consequential (time-element) loss. Many property forms cover direct physical loss but require business income or similar coverage for the interruption.

distractorExplanations.a: Mislabels the revenue interruption as a direct loss merely because lightning started the chain. Lost sales are consequential, not physical damage to property.
distractorExplanations.b: Falsely ties the direct/indirect distinction to earthquake or flood wording. The distinction is physical damage versus resulting economic interruption, not those perils alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the labels. Physical damage to the kitchen is direct; lost sales during downtime are the consequential/indirect piece.

prompt: An agent compares two commercial property forms for a metal shop. Form A lists fire, lightning, explosion, and a short list of other causes, and pays only if the loss is from a listed cause. Form B covers risk of direct physical loss unless an exclusion applies. How should the agent describe those approaches?

options.text: Form A is open perils because any short list of causes is treated as all-risk once the declarations are signed.
Form B is named perils because exclusions convert an open form into a closed list of covered causes of loss.
Both forms are named perils; open-perils wording appears just on inland marine floaters, not on building forms.
Form A is named perils; Form B is open (special) perils that cover losses unless a listed exclusion applies.

explanation: Named-perils coverage pays only for causes of loss specifically listed on the form. Open or special perils coverage pays for direct physical loss unless an exclusion or limitation applies. Form A matches named perils; Form B matches open/special perils.

distractorExplanations.a: Misreads a listed-cause form as open perils. A short enumerated list is classic named-perils wording, not all-risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the open-perils idea. Exclusions refine an open form; they do not turn it into a named-perils list of covered causes.
distractorExplanations.c: Incorrectly claims building forms never use open perils. Commercial property special causes of loss are open-perils style for buildings and business personal property.

prompt: A five-year-old commercial roof that would cost $40,000 to replace new has depreciated 25% from wear. A covered windstorm destroys the roof. The policy settles building losses at actual cash value with no replacement-cost endorsement. Ignoring the deductible, what settlement concept applies?

options.text: Actual cash value: typically replacement cost of the roof minus depreciation for age and condition.
Replacement cost: pay the full $40,000 to rebuild without subtracting wear, then bill depreciation later as a surcharge.
Valued policy: pay a pre-agreed face amount for the roof alone even if repair cost and depreciation differ.
Market value of the entire building only, because ACV never looks at the damaged component’s replacement cost.

explanation: Actual cash value for property is commonly described as replacement cost minus depreciation for age, wear, and condition. With no replacement-cost endorsement, the worn roof is settled at ACV, not the full undepreciated rebuild price.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes replacement cost, which this policy does not use for the building loss. ACV subtracts depreciation rather than paying full new cost up front.
distractorExplanations.c: Invokes a valued-policy agreed amount. Ordinary ACV settlement is based on depreciated value of the damaged property, not a separate agreed roof face amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Claims ACV ignores component replacement cost. ACV calculations routinely start from the cost to replace the damaged item, then subtract depreciation.

prompt: A boutique’s business personal property is written with a replacement-cost endorsement. Covered smoke damage ruins display fixtures that would cost $12,000 to replace with new like-kind fixtures and that had $4,000 of depreciation. The insured replaces the fixtures. Ignoring deductible and coinsurance, what does replacement-cost settlement generally pay for?

options.text: Only the $8,000 ACV figure, because replacement-cost endorsements never remove depreciation on business personal property at all.
The cost to replace with new like-kind fixtures, without subtracting the $4,000 of depreciation.
Twice the ACV as a statutory penalty whenever smoke rather than fire causes the damage to indoor fixtures.
The original purchase invoices from five years ago, even if like-kind replacement today costs substantially more.

explanation: Replacement-cost coverage pays the cost to replace damaged property with new property of like kind and quality, without a depreciation deduction, subject to limits and any rebuild/replace conditions. Here that points to the $12,000 like-kind cost, not the depreciated ACV.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the RC endorsement as still forcing ACV. The point of replacement cost is to avoid subtracting depreciation when the insured actually replaces.
distractorExplanations.c: Invented a smoke-versus-fire penalty multiplier. Settlement method does not double ACV simply because the peril was smoke.
distractorExplanations.d: Locks payment to old invoices. Replacement cost looks to current like-kind replacement cost, not the historic purchase price alone.

prompt: An antique steam engine is scheduled on a valued inland marine floater for an agreed amount of $75,000. A covered collision totals the engine. At the time of loss, a qualified appraisal shows the engine’s market/ACV figure is $60,000. Assuming a true valued-policy/agreed-value schedule and a covered total loss, what amount does the valued approach generally contemplate before deductible?

options.text: $60,000, because valued forms always reopen the schedule after a total loss and pay only the current market appraisal.
$135,000, combining the agreed scheduled amount and the later appraisal as a stacked recovery for one engine.
$75,000, the agreed scheduled amount for a covered total loss of the engine.
$15,000, the difference between schedule and appraisal, paid as a penalty to the insured after the collision.

explanation: A valued (agreed-value) approach sets the amount payable for a total loss of the scheduled item in advance. The insurer generally pays the agreed amount—here $75,000—rather than re-litigating ACV down to the later $60,000 appraisal, subject to the policy’s terms and deductible.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a valued schedule as if it always collapses to current market. The purpose of agreed value is to avoid that post-loss ACV fight on a total loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Stacks agreed value on top of the appraisal. The insured does not collect both figures for one total loss of the same item.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays only the gap as a ‘penalty.’ Valued settlement contemplates the agreed amount, not a difference-only payment to the insured.

prompt: Wind from a covered storm tears open a warehouse roof. Rain then soaks inventory that would have stayed dry if the roof had held. Separately, adjusters sometimes face claims where a covered peril and an excluded peril (such as flood) combine in the same event. At a high level, which pair of ideas best matches how property coverage analysis often starts?

options.text: Proximate cause always means the last peril in time is the only one considered, so rain alone decides coverage and the earlier wind opening the roof is ignored entirely.
Concurrent causation typically voids the entire policy for the rest of the policy term whenever two perils are named anywhere in the claim file notes.
Indirect loss rules replace proximate cause, so chains of events after physical damage to stock are analyzed under business-income forms.
Proximate cause seeks the efficient dominant cause in the chain; concurrent causation concerns covered and excluded perils acting together.

explanation: Proximate cause analysis asks which peril is the efficient dominant cause in an unbroken chain—for example, covered wind opening the roof so that rain damages stock. Concurrent causation, at a high level, deals with situations where covered and excluded perils combine; policy wording and jurisdiction matter, but the concepts are distinct.

distractorExplanations.a: Overstates a ‘last peril in time’ shortcut. Proximate cause focuses on the efficient dominant cause in the chain, not automatically the final peril clocked.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats concurrent causation as an automatic policy-wide void. It is a coverage-analysis issue for combined perils, not a cancellation of the whole contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Claims only time-element forms care about causal chains. Proximate cause is central to property physical-damage coverage questions as well.

prompt: A commercial property declarations page shows a $2,500 deductible on building coverage. After a covered fire, the adjuster finds $22,500 of covered building damage before applying the deductible. Which statement correctly describes how that flat deductible usually works?

options.text: The insured bears the first $2,500; the insurer’s payment starts on the covered loss above that amount.
The insurer pays the first $2,500 and the insured pays everything above that figure as a reverse deductible.
A flat deductible multiplies the loss by 2.5% instead of subtracting a fixed dollar amount from the claim.
Flat deductibles apply only to liability claims; property claims always use a percentage of the building limit.

explanation: A flat (fixed-dollar) deductible is the amount of each covered loss the insured retains. On a $22,500 covered building loss with a $2,500 deductible, the insured bears $2,500 and the insurer pays the covered remainder, subject to limits and other conditions.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses who pays the deductible layer. The insured retains the deductible; the insurer does not pay that first slice.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a flat dollar deductible with a percentage deductible. $2,500 is subtracted as a fixed amount, not converted into a 2.5% multiplier.
distractorExplanations.d: Falsely limits flat deductibles to liability. Property forms commonly use fixed-dollar deductibles on building and personal property claims.

prompt: A building’s replacement cost is $500,000. The policy has an 80% coinsurance clause and the insured carries $300,000 of coverage. A covered fire causes $100,000 of damage. Ignoring the deductible, how much does the coinsurance formula say the insurer pays?

options.text: $100,000, because coinsurance never reduces a partial loss when the damage is under 25% of replacement cost.
$75,000, from (insurance carried ÷ insurance required) × loss, with required coverage equal to 80% of $500,000.
$80,000, by multiplying the $100,000 loss by the 80% coinsurance percentage alone and skipping the limit carried.
$60,000, by dividing $300,000 by $500,000 and multiplying that ratio by the loss without using the 80% requirement.

explanation: Insurance required = 80% × $500,000 = $400,000. Did/should = $300,000 ÷ $400,000 = 0.75. Payment = 0.75 × $100,000 = $75,000 before the deductible. Carrying less than the required amount produces a coinsurance penalty on the partial loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Invented a 25% partial-loss safe harbor that waives coinsurance. Underinsurance still reduces recovery under the standard did/should formula.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies loss by 80% and ignores carried limit versus required limit. Coinsurance compares amount carried to amount required, then applies that ratio to the loss.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses face amount over full replacement cost and drops the 80% requirement. Required insurance is 80% of value, not 100% of value, in this clause.

prompt: After a severe fire, an insured tells the property adjuster to ‘take the burned building—it’s yours—and just pay the full policy limit.’ The structure still has some remaining value, and the policy contains a standard abandonment clause. What does that clause generally prevent?

options.text: It forces the insurer to accept title to any damaged property whenever the insured prefers a total-loss check instead of repairs.
It lets the insured abandon the property only if the mortgagee agrees in writing within 48 hours of the fire department leaving.
It stops the insured from abandoning damaged property to the insurer and demanding that the insurer take ownership.
It voids coverage entirely if the insured asks about salvage, even when the insured keeps title and mitigates further damage promptly.

explanation: Standard property policies include an abandonment clause: the insured cannot dump damaged property on the insurer and insist the insurer take ownership in exchange for a full payment. The insurer may choose to take salvage in some total-loss situations, but the insured does not control that by abandonment.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the clause into a forced takeover. Abandonment language protects the insurer from being compelled to accept title at the insured’s demand.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds a mortgagee-48-hour rule that is not the standard abandonment concept. Consent timing of that sort is not what the clause is about.
distractorExplanations.d: Punishes the insured for asking about salvage. Discussing salvage or mitigation does not void coverage under an abandonment clause.

prompt: An insurer pays a covered total loss on a commercial truck’s cargo under an inland marine form and then sells the recoverable undamaged portion of the shipment to a salvage buyer. Which concept best describes the insurer’s right in the recovered property after paying the loss?

options.text: Subrogation against the insured’s employees, which is treated as the only lawful way an insurer may ever handle leftover recovered goods.
Assignment of the entire inland marine policy to the salvage buyer, who then becomes responsible for future premiums on that form.
Bailee coverage for the salvage yard, automatically extending the shipper’s policy to every downstream buyer of scrap materials.
Salvage: after paying, the insurer may take rights in recovered property and apply sale proceeds against the loss.

explanation: Salvage is the insurer’s interest in damaged or recovered property after it pays a loss. Selling recoverable goods and applying the proceeds against the paid loss is classic salvage handling, distinct from subrogation against a wrongdoer or assigning the insurance contract.

distractorExplanations.a: Mislabels salvage as subrogation against employees. Subrogation pursues a legally responsible third party; salvage deals with leftover property value.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses salvage sale with assigning the insurance policy. Selling recovered goods does not make the salvage buyer the new named insured on the form.
distractorExplanations.c: Invented automatic bailee coverage for scrap buyers. Salvage disposition does not extend the shipper’s policy to every downstream buyer.

prompt: An insured and a property insurer agree that a fire loss is covered, but they sharply disagree on the dollar amount of the building damage. The policy’s appraisal clause is invoked. At a high level, what does appraisal decide, and what does it not replace?

options.text: Appraisal sets the amount of loss through appraisers and often an umpire; it does not decide whether coverage exists.
Appraisal is a full coverage trial that can rewrite exclusions and bind the insurer to pay uncovered flood damage.
Appraisal only elects a public adjuster for the insured and never produces a dollar figure for the loss.
Appraisal transfers the claim to arbitration about who was at fault for the fire, leaving the building's dollar valuation to the mortgagee.

explanation: The appraisal clause is a valuation tool used when the parties dispute the amount of a covered loss. Each side typically names an appraiser, and an umpire may break a deadlock. Appraisal determines the amount of loss; it is not a substitute for deciding coverage questions such as whether an exclusion applies.

distractorExplanations.b: Overstates appraisal as a coverage court that can erase exclusions. Appraisal addresses amount of loss, not rewriting the policy’s coverage grant.
distractorExplanations.c: Reduces appraisal to hiring a public adjuster. The process produces a binding valuation pathway for the amount of loss, not merely an adjuster referral.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses appraisal with liability arbitration and mortgagee-only valuation. Property appraisal is about loss amount between insured and insurer.

prompt: A dry cleaner takes in customers’ garments for cleaning and temporary storage on the shop premises. A nighttime fire destroys those garments while they are in the cleaner’s custody. From a P&C risk perspective, what exposure does the cleaner primarily face regarding the customers’ property?

options.text: No property exposure at all, because garments always remain covered only under each customer’s homeowners policy without bailee issues.
Bailee exposure: care, custody, or control of others’ property that the cleaner may be responsible for if it is damaged.
Workers compensation exposure, because customer property losses are reclassified as employee injury claims.
Automobile physical damage exposure, because garments in a shop are treated as mobile equipment under PAP rules.

explanation: A bailee holds property of others under a bailment—care, custody, or control. The dry cleaner’s fire loss to customers’ garments is a classic bailee exposure. Ordinary commercial property forms often limit coverage for property of others, so bailee or similar coverage is a common solution.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes customers’ homeowners policies erase the cleaner’s risk. The bailee still faces responsibility and often needs coverage for property of others in its care.
distractorExplanations.c: Misclassifies garment damage as workers compensation. WC addresses employee injury, not destruction of customers’ clothing in custody.
distractorExplanations.d: Forces the loss into auto physical damage. Shop-stored garments are not handled as PAP mobile-equipment auto losses.

prompt: A coastal dwelling policy uses a percentage deductible stated as 2% of the dwelling Coverage A limit for windstorm losses. Coverage A is $400,000. A covered windstorm causes $50,000 of dwelling damage. Ignoring other adjustments, how does that percentage deductible generally apply?

options.text: The deductible is a flat $2,000 on windstorm claims, because a 2% deductible is treated as two thousand dollars no matter the Coverage A limit.
The insured pays 2% of the $50,000 loss ($1,000), and percentage deductibles do not use the dwelling Coverage A limit as the base.
The deductible is 2% of the $400,000 Coverage A limit ($8,000), retained by the insured on that wind claim.
Percentage deductibles apply just after the insurer pays in full, as a surcharge billed later with the next renewal premium notice.

explanation: A percentage deductible for windstorm is commonly a percentage of the dwelling limit (Coverage A), not a percentage of the loss amount. Here 2% of $400,000 equals an $8,000 deductible retained by the insured on the wind claim before the insurer pays the covered remainder.

distractorExplanations.a: Converts the 2% limit-based deductible into an invented flat $2,000 rule. The percentage is of Coverage A, producing $8,000 here.
distractorExplanations.b: Bases 2% on the loss amount instead of the dwelling limit. Wind percentage deductibles are typically limit-based, not loss-based.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the deductible as a renewal surcharge after full payment. Deductibles reduce the claim payment at loss time; they are not billed later as a premium add-on for that purpose.

prompt: Northbridge Bank's unpaid mortgage on Ellis Storage's warehouse is $90,000. Rebuilding the warehouse would cost $240,000. A covered fire destroys the building, and the bank is the mortgagee. How far does the bank's insurable interest in that property extend?

options.text: Only the $90,000 unpaid balance, which is the bank's financial stake.
The full $240,000 rebuild cost plus Ellis's future rents, because the mortgagee's interest is the entire property securing the loan, not merely the unpaid balance.
Nothing, because naming Ellis as owner cancels a lender's stake as soon as the policy is issued.
The original construction price from a decade ago, even though the note balance is $90,000.

explanation: A mortgagee's insurable interest is the debt the property secures, measured at the time of loss. That unpaid balance is $90,000, so the bank's stake stops at $90,000. The $240,000 figure is the cost to rebuild the warehouse, not the lender's financial stake, and the bank does not collect Ellis's future rents.

distractorExplanations.b: Measures the lender's interest by the full rebuild cost and the lost rents. A mortgagee's insurable interest is the $90,000 secured debt, not the warehouse's replacement cost or the owner's income.
distractorExplanations.c: Claims that issuance in the owner's name erases the lender's interest. A mortgagee keeps an insurable interest up to the unpaid balance while the debt remains.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes an old construction price for the present debt. This lender's insurable interest is the $90,000 unpaid balance, not a historic build cost.

prompt: Rental income stops after a covered fire makes Lena's insured duplex unlivable for a month. The same fire chars the kitchen cabinets. Her property form covers direct physical loss and has no fair-rental-value coverage. Which description of the two results is right?

options.text: Both the charred cabinets and the missing rent are indirect losses, because every fire result is consequential.
Charred cabinets are a direct loss; the missing rent is an indirect loss.
Missing rent is the direct loss because the duplex is held out for tenants, and the cabinet damage is only indirect once those tenants have moved out for the month.
Both the charred cabinets and the missing month of rent are direct losses, because a direct-physical-loss grant pays every financial result of a covered fire.

explanation: A direct loss is physical damage to covered property from a covered peril. The charred kitchen cabinets are that direct loss. Rent the duplex does not earn during the month it cannot be lived in is an indirect, or consequential, loss. With no fair-rental-value coverage, the direct-loss grant does not pay that month of missing rent.

distractorExplanations.a: Labels the physical cabinet damage as indirect merely because fire caused it. Cabinet charring is the direct loss; the missing rent is the consequential result.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses which result is direct because the property is a rental. Lost rent is indirect, and the charred cabinets are the direct physical loss even after the tenants leave.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the direct-physical-loss grant as paying every financial result of the fire, including lost rent. The grant pays the charred cabinets; the missing rent is indirect and needs fair-rental-value coverage.

prompt: Firefighters soak a dining room while putting out a covered grease fire that started in a fryer. Their water warps the wood floor. The policy covers fire and does not exclude water used to extinguish a covered fire. Which analysis supports paying for the warped floor?

options.text: Only a flood peril applies, because any water on a floor is flood even when hoses fought a fire.
The last event in clock time controls, so the water is a new cause and the grease fire drops out.
Proximate cause: the fire is the efficient cause, so extinguishing water stays in that loss.
Concurrent causation treats the hose water as an independent flood cause, so the warped floor is denied even though the grease fire was covered and extinguishing water is not excluded.

explanation: Proximate cause is the efficient, dominant cause that starts an unbroken chain. The covered grease fire is that cause. Water firefighters use to put the fire out follows in the same chain, so the warped floor is part of the fire loss rather than a separate flood. The stem states that water used to extinguish a covered fire is not excluded.

distractorExplanations.a: Misnames hose water as flood. Flood is rising or surface water, not water applied to stop a covered fire already in progress.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses a last-in-time shortcut and drops the fire. Proximate cause follows the efficient cause through the chain, not merely the final splash of water.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses concurrent causation to deny the floor as a separate flood. Extinguishing water that the policy does not exclude stays with the covered fire as one proximate cause.

prompt: Hail cracks shingles on a retail building, and the covered repair cost is $18,400. The declarations show a $1,000 flat building deductible, and the limit can pay the remainder. How much does the insurer pay on this loss?

options.text: The insurer pays the full $18,400 and waives the deductible, because a hail repair is paid in full whenever the building limit is high enough to cover that repair.
The insurer pays $19,400 by adding the $1,000 deductible to the $18,400 repair cost.
The insurer pays only the $1,000 deductible, and the insured pays the other $17,400.
The insurer pays $17,400, the $18,400 loss minus the $1,000 deductible.

explanation: A flat deductible is subtracted from the covered loss before the insurer pays. $18,400 minus $1,000 equals $17,400. The insured retains the first $1,000, and the insurer pays the remaining $17,400 because the building limit is high enough to cover that remainder.

distractorExplanations.a: Waives the deductible because the limit can pay the hail repair. The $1,000 flat deductible is still subtracted, so the payment is $17,400 rather than the full $18,400.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds the deductible on top of the loss. $18,400 plus $1,000 is $19,400, which is the wrong direction; the deductible is subtracted.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps who retains the deductible. The insured keeps the $1,000 layer; the insurer does not pay only that amount and leave the insured with $17,400.

prompt: Once the deed transfers at closing, Camille keeps no mortgage, lease, or other stake in the warehouse she just sold. Her property policy is still inside its printed term. A fire the next morning destroys the building. What is true of Camille's insurable interest?

options.text: It ended when the deed transferred, so she cannot collect for that fire.
It lasts through the printed expiration, so she collects the full rebuild cost as if she still owned the warehouse.
It follows the deed to every later buyer automatically, and Camille may still claim without a financial stake at the time of the fire because the printed term has not ended.
It is tested only on the application date, so a sale the day before the fire does not matter.

explanation: Property coverage requires an insurable interest at the time of the loss. Camille conveyed the warehouse and kept no mortgage, lease, or other financial stake, so the next morning she would not suffer a financial loss if the building burned. A policy that is still inside its printed term does not keep a seller's interest alive after that stake is gone.
