distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a false application fact with agency authority. Apparent authority is about binding power, not lying about sprinklers.

prompt: A producer tells a satisfied auto insured that the current carrier "never pays claims" and that switching will "double the limits for half the premium," knowing both statements are false, solely to earn a new commission. What practice is this?

options.text: Twisting — inducing replacement through misrepresentation of an existing policy.
Liberalization — automatically broadening the old policy without a new application.
Facultative reinsurance — ceding one auto risk to another carrier.
Law of large numbers — improving loss predictability by moving one insured.

explanation: Twisting is inducing a policyholder to replace existing coverage through misrepresentation or incomplete comparison, often to generate commission. False claims that the current insurer never pays and that the new policy doubles limits at half price are textbook twisting. Liberalization, facultative reinsurance, and the law of large numbers are unrelated concepts.

distractorExplanations.b: Misstates liberalization. That clause extends improved coverage on an in-force policy without charging more; it is not a sales inducement.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses producer misconduct with reinsurance. Facultative reinsurance is insurer-to-insurer placement of a single risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Misapplies the law of large numbers. Moving one insured does not create predictability for a book of business.

prompt: A covered kitchen fire ruins a five-year-old refrigerator in Nora's insured home. She asks the adjuster to pay the price of a brand-new model so the loss leaves her better off than before the fire. Which principle limits what this property policy is designed to do?

options.text: Indemnity — put Nora back where she stood before the fire, without a gain.
Replacement cost, which is meant to leave Nora richer than the position she held before the fire.
Subrogation — she must sue the appliance maker and collect from it before the insurer may pay anything.
Adhesion — any unclear sentence is read so the payment exceeds the position she held before the fire.

explanation: Indemnity means a property policy should return the insured to about the same financial position as before a covered loss, not a better one. Paying Nora a profit beyond the damaged refrigerator would break that rule. Replacement cost, when the form provides it, pays the cost to replace the item. It measures the loss. It is not a principle that the fire should leave her richer. Subrogation recovers from a responsible third party after payment, and adhesion is a rule for reading ambiguous wording.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a valuation method with a right to profit. Replacement cost, when the form allows it, pays to replace the refrigerator. It does not mean a covered fire should leave Nora richer than she was.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses indemnity with subrogation. Subrogation is the insurer's recovery from a responsible party after it pays; Nora need not sue the maker before a covered loss is adjusted.
distractorExplanations.d: Misapplies adhesion. Ambiguous wording is read against the drafter. That rule does not raise the payment above the pre-loss position indemnity allows.

prompt: Luis asks an agent to place property coverage on a vacation cabin he does not own, does not rent, and has no mortgage, lien, or other financial stake in. His cousin owns the cabin and never asked Luis to insure it. What is missing?

options.text: A family relationship with the owner, which by itself gives a cousin an insurable interest in a cabin he does not stand to lose.
An insurable interest in that cabin, meaning a real financial stake in it.
A surplus lines license, because cabin risks may be written only through nonadmitted carriers.
Apparent authority, which Luis can create on his own by asking an agent to insure the cousin's cabin.

explanation: Insurable interest means the person would suffer a financial loss if the property were damaged. Luis has no ownership, lease, lien, or other lawful stake, so a fire at his cousin's cabin would not hurt him financially. A family tie alone does not create that stake in property. Without that interest the contract would be a wager, which property insurance will not enforce. A surplus lines license and apparent authority do not create a stake in someone else's cabin.

distractorExplanations.a: Imports a life-insurance family rule into property. Being the owner's cousin does not give Luis a financial loss if the cabin is damaged, so it is not an insurable interest.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates the surplus lines market. Nonadmitted placement is for risks the admitted market declines. It does not replace the need for Luis to have an insurable interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a missing stake with agency law. Asking for coverage does not create apparent authority, and authority would not give Luis an interest in the cabin.

prompt: Grease-soaked rags sit in an open bin beside a bakery oven. Overnight the rags ignite, and the flames destroy the prep table. In property insurance terms, how should the rags and the flames be classified?

options.text: Both are perils, because any condition stored near heat is itself the cause of the loss that followed.
Both are morale hazards, because the bakery must have grown careless once a property policy was in force.
The rags are a physical hazard; the fire is the peril.
The rags are a moral hazard, and the fire is a physical hazard of the prep table.

explanation: A hazard is a condition that increases the chance or severity of a loss. Grease-soaked rags next to an oven are a physical hazard. A peril is the cause of the loss itself. The fire that destroyed the prep table is the peril. The facts do not say anyone grew careless because a policy existed, so this is not morale hazard. The rags are not a moral hazard of dishonesty, and the fire is not a hazard of the table.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses a hazard into a peril. The rags raised the chance of fire; they are a condition. The flames are the cause that destroyed the prep table.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds a morale hazard the facts do not support. Morale hazard is indifference because insurance exists. Nothing here says the bakery bought coverage and then stopped taking care.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the labels. Grease-soaked rags are a physical condition that raises the chance of fire, not a moral hazard of dishonesty, and the fire that destroyed the table is the peril.

prompt: Dana's auto insurer pays her repair bill after a covered collision caused by another driver's negligence. Dana then demands that same driver pay her the repair bill a second time. Which insurer right usually stops that second collection?

options.text: Liberalization, which broadens Dana's in-force auto policy so she may collect the same repair cost from the driver and from her insurer.
Salvage, which uses the insurer's right in the damaged car to make the negligent driver pay Dana the same repair bill again.
The law of large numbers, which spreads one repair bill across every auto policy written in the state.
Subrogation, limited to the amount the insurer paid.

explanation: Subrogation moves the insured's rights against the responsible party to the insurer, up to the amount the insurer paid, and it stops the insured from collecting that amount twice. Dana has already been indemnified for the repair bill, so she cannot collect that same bill again from the negligent driver. Liberalization can broaden her form when the insurer improves it, but it does not authorize a second collection. Salvage concerns rights in the damaged car, not another payment of the repair bill. The law of large numbers predicts losses in a large group and does not decide this claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Misuses liberalization. That clause broadens an in-force policy when the insurer improves the form. It does not let Dana collect the same repair bill from the driver again.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses salvage with subrogation. Salvage is the insurer's interest in damaged property it pays for. It does not make the negligent driver pay the repair bill a second time.
distractorExplanations.c: Misapplies a pricing idea. The law of large numbers helps predict average losses for a large group of similar risks. It does not decide whether Dana may bill the driver twice.

prompt: Camille's new food truck might earn a profit or lose money on sales. A windstorm might also wreck the truck, and that wreck cannot make her richer. Which statement correctly sorts the two uncertainties?

options.text: Sales results are speculative risk; wind damage to the truck is pure risk.
Both uncertainties are pure risks, so a property policy is built to insure her sales profit as well as physical damage to the truck.
Both are speculative risks, because a storm might raise the prices she can charge for meals from the truck.
Both are hazards rather than risks: wind damage is a physical hazard, and uncertain sales are a morale hazard.

explanation: Speculative risk can end in either gain or loss, which is the food truck's sales result. Insurance is not designed to protect that chance of profit. Pure risk offers only loss or no loss, which is a windstorm that might wreck the truck. Property insurance addresses that pure risk. Those two uncertainties are risks, not hazards. A physical hazard is a tangible condition, and morale hazard is carelessness because coverage exists.

distractorExplanations.b: Erases the difference and overstates the policy. Profit or loss on sales is speculative. A property policy can address damage to the truck, not the upside of the business.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels the windstorm. Damage that can only hurt Camille is pure risk. A possible change in meal prices does not turn the wreck itself into a chance of gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses risks with hazards. Wind damage is pure risk from a peril, not a physical hazard, and a chance of profit or loss on sales is speculative risk, not morale hazard.

prompt: A landlord buys a property policy so a large fire is transferred to the insurer, and the declarations require the landlord to absorb the first part of any covered loss. In risk-management terms, what is that first part?

options.text: Avoidance, because agreeing to it means a fire can no longer occur at the insured building.
Retention — the landlord keeps that layer of the loss.
Loss control, because keeping the first part of a fire is a safety step that lowers the chance the insured building will burn.
Estoppel, because accepting the policy bars the insurer from holding the landlord to the first part the declarations say to keep.

explanation: Retention means the person keeps part of the financial consequence of a loss. The first part the landlord must absorb is a retained layer, commonly shown as a deductible, while the policy transfers the covered amount above it. Avoidance would remove the exposure, for example by selling the building. Keeping that first part does not lower the chance of a fire. Accepting the policy does not erase that layer, and the insurer still pays a valid claim above it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses retention with avoidance. The building can still burn. The landlord kept the first part of a covered loss instead of eliminating the chance of fire.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses retention with loss control. The landlord kept the first part of the loss. That financing layer does not lower the chance that the building will burn.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses estoppel. The first part is the layer the landlord agreed to keep. Accepting the policy does not cancel that layer or stop the insurer from paying above it.

prompt: An insured can pay for a property policy for years and never report a loss, or one covered fire can obligate the insurer for far more than the insured has paid. Which contract feature does that uneven result illustrate?

options.text: A commutative contract, because each side must exchange roughly equal value on every policy.
A bilateral promise that forces the insured to keep paying long after the insurer has paid a total loss.
An aleatory contract, because the outcome depends on chance.
A contract of adhesion, because an unequal result is corrected by reading the printed form in the insured's favor.

explanation: An insurance contract is aleatory: whether the insurer must pay, and how much, depends on a chance event, so the values exchanged can be very unequal. Many insureds pay and have no loss, while one covered fire can cost the insurer far more than it has received from that insured. A commutative contract looks toward a roughly equal swap. These facts are not a bilateral promise to keep paying, and reading the printed form against the drafter does not equalize a chance outcome.

distractorExplanations.a: Names the opposite feature. Commutative contracts aim at a relatively equal exchange. A covered fire can obligate the insurer for much more than that insured has paid.
distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the insured's position. The insurer must pay covered losses, but these facts are about an unequal chance outcome, not a duty to keep paying forever.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses aleatory with adhesion. Reading an ambiguous form against the drafter resolves unclear wording. It does not make the size of the outcome depend on chance.

prompt: A homeowners policy is printed entirely by the insurer. The applicant cannot bargain over the sentences and must accept those terms or decline the policy. One sentence is genuinely ambiguous. How do courts usually read it?

options.text: Against the insured, because the party who printed the form is favored whenever a sentence is unclear.
As canceling every exclusion, so unclear wording means the policy covers losses that clear exclusion language removes.
As the reading the insured prefers, after the insured proves the private intent the insurer held when it printed the form.
Against the insurer that drafted the ambiguous sentence.

explanation: A property policy is a contract of adhesion: the insurer drafts the form and the applicant adheres to it. When a sentence is truly ambiguous, courts construe it against the drafter, the insurer, and in favor of the insured. Clear exclusions are still enforced as written. The insured does not have to prove the insurer's private intent before that rule applies.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the construction rule. The insured had no real chance to draft the sentence, so genuine ambiguity is resolved against the insurer that wrote it.
distractorExplanations.b: Overreads a narrow rule. Construing one ambiguous sentence against the drafter does not erase exclusions that are written in clear language.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a burden the ambiguity rule does not impose. A genuinely ambiguous sentence is read against the insurer that drafted it, without proof of the insurer's private intent.

prompt: After a property insurer issues the policy, the insurer alone is legally bound to pay covered losses. The insured may stop and let the policy end rather than continue it. Which contract trait do those facts illustrate?

options.text: Unilateral — only the insurer made a promise the law will enforce.
Bilateral — both parties made enforceable promises, so the insured must keep the policy in force after it is issued.
Commutative — each side's performance must match in value, or the policy never took effect at all.
Conditional — the insurer's promise becomes enforceable when the insured agrees to keep the policy until a loss occurs.

explanation: Property and casualty policies are unilateral. Once the policy is issued, only the insurer has made a promise the law will enforce: to pay covered losses if the conditions are met. The insured is not obligated to keep the policy in force. A bilateral contract would bind the insured to continue. Matching values is a commutative idea, and these facts are not a condition that the insured agree to stay until a loss occurs.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a bilateral contract. The insured made no enforceable promise to continue, so the policy is not bilateral and the insured may let it end.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses unilateral with commutative. Commutative contracts contemplate a relatively equal exchange. These facts show that only the insurer's promise is enforceable.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses unilateral with conditional. These facts show that the insured made no promise to continue. A condition on payment is not an agreement to keep the policy until a loss.

prompt: At renewal, an underwriter learns the insured installed an unapproved wood stove, a breach that would support nonrenewal. The underwriter notes the stove and still accepts the renewal with no exclusion. After a later stove fire, the company denies the claim for that known breach. What did the insurer do?

options.text: Preserved a denial defense, because noting the stove at renewal keeps that known breach available if a stove fire occurs later.
Waived its known right to deny the claim for that breach.
Estopped the insured from a stove-fire claim, because the insured relied on the prior policy and lost the right to be paid.
Rescinded the renewal for misrepresentation, because a file note of the stove cancels the policy without a separate notice.

explanation: Waiver is the voluntary, intentional giving up of a known right. The underwriter knew about the unapproved stove, knew it would support nonrenewal, and accepted the renewal without adding a restriction. The insurer cannot later deny a stove fire on the same known breach it chose to overlook. A file note of that known fact does not preserve the defense. The renewal does not estop the insured from claiming, and accepting the risk is not a rescission.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the effect of the renewal. Noting a known breach and renewing without an exclusion gives that defense up. It does not save the breach for a later denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Points estoppel at the insured. Knowledge plus renewal binds the insurer that chose to continue. It does not take away the insured's right to be paid for the later fire.
distractorExplanations.d: Misnames the remedy. The underwriter accepted the renewal with the stove on file. That act did not rescind the policy, and the facts state no misrepresentation.

prompt: A commercial application asks whether the building suffered a fire in recent years. The owner remembers a serious fire and deliberately leaves the answer blank so the underwriter will not see it. The policy is issued. What is that omission?

options.text: A misrepresentation, because a blank answer is a false statement that the building had no serious fire.
Twisting, because a blank answer is what a producer uses to push replacement of an existing policy.
Concealment of a material fact the owner knew.
A waiver of the insurer's question, because the owner gives up the company's right to a material fact by leaving the answer blank.

explanation: Concealment is intentionally withholding a material fact the other party needs in order to accept or price the risk. A prior serious fire is material to that decision. Deliberately leaving the answer blank so the underwriter will miss it is concealment and can give the insurer grounds to void the policy. A blank is not a false statement that no fire occurred. It is not twisting, and the owner does not waive the insurer's question by hiding the answer.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses concealment with misrepresentation. Misrepresentation is a false statement. Deliberately leaving a known fire off the form is concealment, not a statement that no fire occurred.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses concealment with twisting. Twisting is a producer's misleading push to replace coverage. This owner hid a fire history on an application.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates who can waive. The applicant does not waive the insurer's rights by hiding a fire. Intentional silence about a material fact is concealment.

prompt: Lightning, a covered cause of loss, hits a barn and ignites a fire. Firefighters soak stored grain while putting the fire out, and that water, not the flames, ruins the grain. Which causation analysis is correct?

options.text: The water is a new independent cause, so the covered lightning never reaches the loss to the grain.
Firefighter water is flood, so a flood exclusion removes the grain loss even though the water was used to put out the fire.
Flame damage is the whole fire peril, so water firefighters used to put the fire out is a separate cause the policy leaves uncovered.
The fire is the proximate cause, so the extinguishing water follows it.

explanation: Proximate cause is the dominant cause that sets a loss in motion without an efficient break in the chain. Covered lightning started the fire, and water used to extinguish that fire is a consequence of the fire, not a separate flood and not a break in the chain. The ruined grain is treated as fire damage. The fire peril is not limited to scorching by flames, and hose water used to fight that fire is not flood.

distractorExplanations.a: Breaks the chain too early. Water from fighting a covered fire stays with that fire. It is not a new independent cause that erases the lightning.
distractorExplanations.b: Mislabels extinguishing water as flood. Flood means defined natural inundation. Hose water used on a covered fire follows that fire, and a flood exclusion does not remove it.
distractorExplanations.c: Cuts the fire peril down to flames. Water used to extinguish a covered fire is a result of that fire, not a separate uncovered cause.

prompt: A covered fire burns the inventory on a retailer's shelves. The shop then stays closed for weeks and loses the net income those weeks would have produced. Which statement separates the two results?

options.text: Burned inventory is a direct loss; the lost net income is indirect.
Both results are direct losses, because every financial effect of a fire is physical damage to tangible goods on the shelves.
Lost net income is the direct loss, and the burned inventory is an indirect result of the shop staying closed.
Both results are speculative risk, so neither the stock nor the lost income can be the subject of insurance.

explanation: A direct loss is physical damage to covered property from a covered peril, here the inventory the fire burned. An indirect, or consequential, loss is the financial result that follows, such as net income the closed shop does not earn. Calling the lost income direct and the burned stock indirect reverses those results. Business-income coverage, when the retailer has bought it, is what responds to that second result. This fire loss is not a speculative bet.

distractorExplanations.b: Merges two different results. Destruction of the inventory is direct physical loss. Income lost while the shop is closed is consequential, even though the same fire set it off.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the two results. Burned inventory is the direct physical loss. Net income the closed shop does not earn is the indirect loss, not the other way around.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses speculative risk. Ordinary profit or loss with no fire is speculative. Fire damage, and the income lost because of that fire, are pure-risk results that insurance can address.

prompt: Helen insured her house while she still owned it. She then deeded the house to a buyer and kept no mortgage, lien, or other stake. The house burns the next day. Why is Helen's own claim generally barred?

options.text: Property interest is required solely on the application date, so a later sale cannot affect a claim she files.
She had no insurable interest when the loss happened.
A deed assigns the property policy to the buyer automatically, even when the insurer never consented to the transfer.
Estoppel bars the insurer from using the missing interest, because the policy was issued while Helen still owned the house.

explanation: For property insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss, not only when the policy was purchased. After the deed, with no mortgage or other stake, Helen would suffer no financial loss from the fire, so there is nothing for indemnity to repay. The policy is personal to her and does not follow the house to the buyer merely because a deed was signed. Issuing the policy while she owned the house does not estop the insurer from requiring that interest on the day of the fire.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the timing rule used for property. Interest on the application date is not enough. Helen still needed a stake when the house burned, and the sale ended that stake.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates assignment. A property policy generally cannot be handed to a new owner without the insurer's consent. The deed alone does not move Helen's contract to the buyer.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses estoppel. Issuing the policy while Helen owned the house does not lock her interest to that date. Property insurance still requires a stake when the loss happens.

prompt: Two property policies, both in force for the same insured and the same building, cover the same fire. Each policy says it will share with other insurance in proportion to its limit. Which sharing method is that?

options.text: Primary and excess, so the second policy pays the entire loss and the first policy pays nothing at all.
Contribution by equal shares, so each policy pays matching dollars until a limit is used up, no matter how the two limits compare.
Pro rata sharing by each policy's limit.
Subrogation against the other insurer, so the company that pays collects the entire fire loss from the second policy.

explanation: Pro rata other-insurance wording pays each policy's fraction of the loss, that policy's limit compared with the total limits covering the same loss. When the limits differ, the shares differ. Excess wording would make one policy pay only after the other is used up. Equal shares would split the dollars evenly rather than by limits. Subrogation pursues a responsible outsider. It is not a demand that one of these policies collect the entire fire from the other.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes an excess result, not pro rata sharing. When policies share in proportion to limits, both contribute. One does not pay the whole loss while the other pays nothing.
distractorExplanations.b: Names a different other-insurance clause. Equal shares split the loss in matching dollars. Pro rata splits it by each policy's limit, so unequal limits mean unequal shares.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses pro rata sharing with subrogation. The two policies divide one fire by their limits. One insurer does not collect the entire loss from the other.

prompt: Right after a loss, and before notifying the insurer, the insured accepts payment from a negligent roofer and signs a full release of every claim. The release leaves the insurer nothing to pursue. Which duty did the insured breach?

options.text: The duty to notify the negligent roofer before the insurer, so the release fails because the roofer was not given the carrier's name.
The duty to submit a proof of loss before accepting repair money, which turns the roofer's release into the insurer's consent.
The duty to protect the remaining property from further damage, which is breached by accepting the roofer's payment.
The duty not to impair the insurer's subrogation rights.

explanation: After a loss, the insured must cooperate and must not prejudice the insurer's subrogation. A full release of the negligent roofer wipes out the claim the insurer would have taken over once it paid the insured. The insurer may deny or reduce payment to the extent that release harmed its recovery. Notice of the loss runs to the insurer, a proof of loss does not authorize the release, and protecting the property does not mean refusing the roofer's payment.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates who must be notified. The insured owes the insurer notice of the loss. Giving the roofer the carrier's name is not the duty a full release violates.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses proof of loss with subrogation. A proof of loss documents the claim for the insurer. It does not authorize a full release of the person who caused the roof damage.
distractorExplanations.c: Misnames the duty. Protecting property means limiting further physical damage. It does not forbid a payment from the roofer, and it is not the duty a full release violates.

prompt: A theft policy agrees to pay only when the insured gives prompt notice, protects the remaining property from further damage, and cooperates in the investigation. The insured refuses all three steps. Why can the insurer deny the claim?

options.text: Because the contract is commutative, so a promise to pay exists only when the form contains no conditions.
Because refusing notice and cooperation shows the insured had no insurable interest when the theft occurred.
Because the contract is aleatory, and a chance outcome excuses notice, protection of the property, and cooperation.
Because the contract is conditional, and those duties were not met.

explanation: Insurance contracts are conditional. The insurer's duty to pay a covered theft arises only if the insured meets the policy conditions, including prompt notice, protecting property from further damage, and cooperation. Refusing all three is a failure of those conditions and can defeat the claim even though theft itself is a covered cause of loss. The refusal does not show that insurable interest was missing, and an aleatory chance outcome does not excuse the duties.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates commutative contracts and conditions. Conditions are part of the agreement. Listing them does not erase the promise to pay when the insured actually performs them.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses conditions with insurable interest. Interest is a financial stake in the stolen property. Refusing notice and cooperation does not show that this stake was missing.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a conditional contract with an aleatory one. Aleatory means the amount paid depends on chance. It does not excuse the duties the insured must meet before the insurer pays.

prompt: A commercial insured opens a new policy and wants the page that lists the named insured, policy period, covered locations, and coverage limits. Which policy part holds those personalized facts?

options.text: The exclusions, which list only what the policy never covers under any circumstance.
The declarations, which personalize who, what, when, and limits.
The insuring agreement, which just lists duties after a loss.
The conditions, which just name the perils the insurer will pay.

explanation: Declarations personalize the contract: named insured, addresses, policy period, limits, deductibles, and schedules. The insuring agreement states the insurer's broad promise. Conditions set rules and duties. Exclusions carve out what is not covered. Duties after loss and covered perils are not what the declarations primarily do.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses declarations with exclusions. Exclusions remove coverage; they do not list named insured, period, and limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates the insuring agreement. That section states the coverage promise; duties after loss usually appear in conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates conditions. Conditions set policy rules and duties; covered perils appear in the insuring agreement or cause-of-loss forms.

prompt: After a windstorm, an adjuster points first to the section that promises to pay for covered causes of loss, then to language that removes flood, then to rules requiring prompt notice. Which order matches standard policy structure?

options.text: Exclusions promise payment; declarations remove flood; endorsements alone set every notice duty after loss.
Conditions promise payment; insuring agreement removes flood; declarations set notice.
Insuring agreement promises coverage; exclusions remove flood; conditions set notice.
Liberalization promises coverage; McCarran-Ferguson removes flood; FCRA sets notice.

explanation: The insuring agreement contains the insurer's promise of coverage. Exclusions take coverage away for specified perils or situations such as flood. Conditions impose duties and procedural rules, including notice of loss. Declarations personalize the risk; statutes like McCarran-Ferguson and FCRA are not policy parts.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses roles. Exclusions do not promise payment; declarations do not remove flood; notice duties are conditions, not endorsements by default.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps sections. Conditions do not make the coverage promise; the insuring agreement does not remove flood; declarations do not set notice duties.
distractorExplanations.d: Names statutes and a clause that are not the standard four-part structure for promising, excluding, and conditioning coverage.

prompt: A study group debates whether Congress or the states primarily regulate the business of insurance after federal antitrust concerns arose decades ago. Which high-level rule does McCarran-Ferguson establish?

options.text: Only the federal government may license every P&C producer in every state and set all local rates.
Insurance is entirely exempt from every federal law of any kind forever.
States may not regulate rates, forms, or insurer solvency.
States regulate insurance; federal antitrust yields to the extent state law regulates it.

explanation: The McCarran-Ferguson Act leaves regulation of the business of insurance with the states. Federal antitrust law applies to that business to the extent state law does not regulate it. Boycott, coercion, and intimidation remain subject to the Sherman Act. A federal statute overrides state insurance law when it specifically relates to the business of insurance. The Act does not create exclusive federal producer licensing, erase unrelated federal laws, or forbid state rate and solvency regulation.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses McCarran-Ferguson. Producer licensing is primarily a state function, not an exclusive federal license regime.
distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the exemption. Antitrust can still apply where state law does not regulate the business of insurance, and a federal statute that specifically relates to insurance can still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Contradicts the Act's purpose. McCarran-Ferguson supports state regulation of rates, forms, and solvency.

prompt: An insurer ends a homeowners policy during the policy term after discovering a material underwriting issue, while another file simply is not offered a new term when the current term expires. How do these actions differ conceptually?

options.text: Cancellation ends coverage mid-term; nonrenewal declines a new term at expiration.
Cancellation only happens at expiration; nonrenewal ends coverage mid-term without exception.
Cancellation and nonrenewal are identical and do not require any notice.
Nonrenewal typically requires a court order; cancellation does not need notice.

explanation: Cancellation terminates coverage before the natural end of the policy period. Nonrenewal means the insurer will not continue the relationship for a new term after expiration. Both typically require advance notice under state law, but exact day counts vary by state and should not be memorized as a single national number. They are not identical, and a court order is not the normal nonrenewal path.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the definitions. Cancellation is mid-term termination; nonrenewal occurs at or for the next term after expiration.
distractorExplanations.c: False. The concepts differ, and notice requirements generally apply under state insurance law.
distractorExplanations.d: Invented procedure. Nonrenewal is an insurer underwriting decision with notice rules, not a routine court-order process.

prompt: An underwriter orders a consumer credit report while evaluating a personal lines applicant and then declines the application based partly on that report. Which Fair Credit Reporting Act duty most clearly applies?

options.text: Ignore FCRA because insurance underwriting is never a permitted report purpose.
Provide an adverse action notice identifying the reporting agency used.
Publish the full credit file on the declarations page of every declined quote.
Cancel other household policies mid-term without sending any notice.

explanation: FCRA permits consumer reports for insurance underwriting when the user follows the Act. If an insurer takes adverse action based in whole or in part on a consumer report, it must give an adverse action notice that identifies the consumer reporting agency, states that the agency did not make the decision, and tells the applicant how to obtain and dispute the report. FCRA does not ban insurance use, require printing the file on a declarations page, or authorize silent mid-term cancellation of other policies.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates FCRA. Insurance underwriting is a recognized permissible purpose for consumer reports when rules are followed.
distractorExplanations.c: Invented disclosure. Adverse action notices point the consumer to the agency; they do not put the full file on a declarations page.
distractorExplanations.d: Unrelated and unlawful as stated. FCRA adverse-action rules do not authorize silent mid-term cancellation of other policies.

prompt: A hailstorm damages a roof. The insured waits weeks to tell the insurer, then refuses to submit the signed proof-of-loss form the policy requires. Which policy duties are at issue?

options.text: Only the insurer's duty to liberalize flood coverage automatically for every form.
The producer's fiduciary duty to invest premium float.
The insured's duties of prompt notice and required proof of loss.
McCarran-Ferguson duties that replace policy conditions nationwide.

explanation: Property policies typically require the insured to give prompt notice of loss and to submit a sworn proof of loss within the time and form the conditions require. Failure can prejudice the insurer's investigation and may jeopardize coverage. Liberalization, producer premium handling, and McCarran-Ferguson do not replace these claim duties.

distractorExplanations.a: Misapplies liberalization. That clause broadens coverage when the insurer improves forms without charge; it is not a hail-notice duty.
distractorExplanations.b: Names a producer money-handling issue, not the insured's notice and proof-of-loss obligations after hail damage.
distractorExplanations.d: Overstates McCarran-Ferguson. That Act addresses state vs federal regulation; it does not rewrite every insured's claim conditions.

prompt: During a policy period, an insurer revises its homeowners form to add a small extra coverage at no additional premium for new business. An existing policyholder with the older form asks whether the improvement applies automatically. What does a typical liberalization clause provide?

options.text: The insured must buy a new policy before any free broadened wording can ever apply mid-term.
Broader wording applies only if the insured pays a mid-term surcharge.
Liberalization cancels the policy mid-term so the insured must reapply.
If the insurer broadens coverage without charge, the insured gets the benefit.

explanation: A liberalization clause provides that if the insurer broadens coverage without an additional premium during the policy period, the existing policy receives that broadening. The insured does not have to buy a new policy or pay extra for the free improvement. A program revision that both broadens and restricts coverage is often outside the clause. Liberalization does not cancel the policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Contradicts liberalization. The point of the clause is automatic benefit without requiring a new policy for the free broadening.
distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the clause. Liberalization applies when the insurer broadens coverage without additional premium.
distractorExplanations.c: Invented effect. Liberalization extends benefits; it does not cancel the policy mid-term.

prompt: A grease fire is out, but it opened a hole in the kitchen roof, and heavy rain is forecast tonight. The named insured plans to leave the hole uncovered until an adjuster arrives next week and to haul the burned cabinets to the dump before anyone lists them. Which loss condition applies?

options.text: Protect the property from further damage and keep the damaged property for an inventory.
Leave the roof open until the adjuster arrives, because covering the hole admits the insured caused the fire and forfeits the claim.
Abandon the damaged kitchen to the insurer, because reporting the claim transfers the property and ends the duty to protect it.
Haul the burned cabinets to the dump now, because the inventory can be prepared from memory after the debris is gone.

explanation: After a loss, property conditions require the insured to protect covered property from further damage, keep a record of reasonable emergency repairs, and prepare an inventory while showing the damaged property. Covering the roof opening and holding the burned cabinets meet those duties. Leaving the hole open ahead of rain, dumping the debris, or abandoning the loss does the opposite of what the condition requires.

distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the duty to protect property. A temporary cover limits added rain damage and is not an admission that the insured caused the fire.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats reporting the claim as an abandonment. The insured must still protect the kitchen and cooperate; a claim report does not transfer the property to the insurer.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes a list from memory can replace the cabinets. The insured must keep the damaged property so the insurer can inspect it, and that duty starts at the loss.

prompt: A homeowners policy expires on June 1, and the premium is paid through that date. On May 20 the insurer mails a notice that it will not offer a new term and that coverage will stop on June 1. The policy's nonrenewal condition requires at least 30 days' written notice before the expiration date. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: This is a mid-term cancellation for nonpayment, so the insurer may drop coverage on June 1 without the notice the nonrenewal condition describes.
This is a nonrenewal, and the May 20 notice does not meet the 30 days the condition requires before June 1.
Cancellation and nonrenewal are the same act, so the May 20 mailing ends coverage that night.
Because the term expires on June 1, the insurer may nonrenew with no notice despite the 30-day condition.

explanation: Nonrenewal means the insurer will not continue coverage for a new term after the current term expires. Cancellation ends coverage during the term. This policy expires on June 1 and the premium is paid, so a notice that coverage stops on June 1 and that no new term will be offered is a nonrenewal, not a cancellation for nonpayment. The condition requires at least 30 days' written notice before June 1. A notice mailed on May 20 does not provide those 30 days.

distractorExplanations.a: Misreads a paid policy that runs to June 1. Refusing the next term is nonrenewal, not a cancellation for nonpayment, and the notice condition still applies.
distractorExplanations.c: Collapses two different acts. Cancellation cuts the current term short; nonrenewal declines the next term and must still meet the 30-day notice before June 1.
distractorExplanations.d: Ignores the condition in the policy. An expiration date on June 1 does not excuse the 30-day nonrenewal notice.

prompt: A dwelling applicant writes that the house is owner-occupied and has a central alarm. The house is a vacant rental with no alarm. The insurer issues the policy at the owner-occupied rate. After a theft, the carrier learns both answers were false and that either truth would have led it to decline the risk or to price it differently. What is the carrier's strongest contract position?

options.text: The answers are only opinions about future use, so the carrier must keep the owner-occupied rate and pay the theft in full.
A property claim is unaffected unless a criminal court first convicts the applicant of fraud.
The answers are material misrepresentations and can support rescission of the policy.
The dwelling policy became incontestable when it was issued, so the carrier must pay the theft and cannot rescind.

explanation: A misrepresentation is a false statement of fact on the application. It is material when the truth would have changed the insurer's decision to accept the risk or the premium it charged. Owner-occupancy and alarm protection are present facts the carrier relied on, not opinions about later use. A material misrepresentation gives the insurer grounds to rescind. That contract remedy does not wait for a criminal conviction, and issuing a dwelling policy does not make the application incontestable.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats underwriting facts as opinions. Occupancy and alarm protection are present facts, and a material falsehood does not lock in the owner-occupied rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a contract remedy with a criminal case. Rescission for a material misrepresentation does not require a fraud conviction.
distractorExplanations.d: Imports life-insurance incontestability into a dwelling policy. Issuance does not lock in a material misrepresentation, and the carrier can still seek rescission.

prompt: A shop owner needs a commercial package in force before a Saturday delivery. An appointed agent holds an agency agreement that grants express binding authority for this class of risk. A broker is shopping several markets and holds no binder from any insurer. A clerk at the agency was instructed in writing not to bind, and the owner was told the clerk cannot bind. Who has express authority to bind the insurer today?

options.text: Only the broker, because a broker that is shopping several markets can bind an insurer before that insurer grants authority.
The clerk, because preparing the owner's application at that agency gives the clerk express authority to bind this class of risk.
No one, because express authority to bind arises only after a home-office underwriter countersigns the policy.
The appointed agent, and only within the binding authority the agreement grants.

explanation: Express authority is the power an insurer actually gives an agent in the agency agreement. The appointed agent may bind this class of risk because the agreement says so, and only within that grant. A broker who represents the shop owner and holds no binder has no express authority to bind an insurer. A clerk forbidden to bind does not have express authority either. That power does not wait for a home-office underwriter to countersign the policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the broker's role. Shopping markets for the shop owner does not confer express authority to bind an insurer that has granted no binder.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents express authority from preparing the application. The clerk was instructed in writing not to bind, so the clerk has no express power to put the package in force.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves express authority from the agency agreement to a later countersignature. The appointed agent already has express power to bind this class today, within the agreement.

prompt: After a theft, the policy's loss conditions let the insurer require each insured to answer questions under oath, out of the presence of any other insured, and to sign the transcript. The named insured refuses and says an examination under oath is available only after a prosecutor files a criminal charge. What does the condition require?

options.text: The named insured must submit to the examination and sign the transcript as a claim duty.
The insured may refuse, because an examination under oath is a criminal proceeding and cannot appear in a property policy.
The insurer must drop the request unless a court has already ordered a deposition in a filed lawsuit.
The named insured may answer the questions but may refuse to sign the transcript, because a signature admits the theft.

explanation: Examination under oath is a loss condition, not a criminal case. When the policy requires it, the insured must answer questions under oath, separately from other insureds, and sign the transcript. Signing is not an admission that the insured committed the theft. Refusal can jeopardize the claim because the examination is one of the insured's duties after a loss. The insurer does not need a prosecutor's charge or a court-ordered deposition before it can require the examination the policy already describes.

distractorExplanations.b: Miscasts the examination as a criminal proceeding. The condition is a contractual claim duty and can be required without a criminal charge.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the policy examination with a lawsuit deposition. The loss condition stands on its own and does not wait for a court order.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the signature as a confession of theft. The loss condition requires the insured to sign the transcript, and that signature is a claim duty rather than an admission of the crime.

prompt: A neighbor's tree crew drops a limb on the insured's fence. Before the property insurer pays the repair, the named insured signs the crew's full release and accepts a small cash sum. The loss conditions bar the insured from doing anything that harms the insurer's recovery rights. Which condition did the release impair?

options.text: The cooperation duty only, because a release signed before payment leaves subrogation intact once the insurer pays the fence repair.
Subrogation, because the release can wipe out the insurer's right to recover from the crew.
Appraisal, because the cash sum the insured took from the crew becomes the agreed fence value and ends the dispute over the amount of loss.
Other insurance, because the crew's cash payment is treated as other coverage and must be exhausted before this property policy pays.

explanation: Subrogation lets the insurer, after it pays a covered loss, recover from the party that caused the loss. The insured must not prejudice that right. A full release signed before the insurer pays can destroy the claim the insurer would have taken over. Calling the problem cooperation alone misses that point, because payment does not revive a right the release already gave up. Appraisal only resolves the amount of loss with the insurer, and the crew's payment is not other insurance.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at cooperation and assumes later payment restores the recovery. A full release before payment can extinguish the right that subrogation would have transferred to the insurer.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the crew's payment with appraisal. Appraisal settles a value dispute between the insured and the insurer; cash from the crew does not set that amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Mislabels a tort payment as other insurance. Other insurance is another policy covering the same interest, not cash paid by the party that dropped the limb.

prompt: A dwelling policy includes a standard mortgage clause naming the lender. Investigators conclude the named insured intentionally set the fire. The lender did not know of the arson, still has a valid insurable interest, and is prepared to submit its own proof of loss. How does the clause treat the lender?

options.text: The insured's arson automatically voids the lender's recovery, with no separate right under the clause.
The lender must obtain a judgment against the named insured before the insurer has any obligation to pay the lender.
The lender may still recover its interest even though the insured's own claim is barred.
The clause cancels every interest in the policy, including the lender's, as soon as arson is suspected.

explanation: A standard mortgage clause is a separate agreement between the insurer and the mortgagee. An innocent lender can recover its insurable interest even when the named insured's claim fails because of the insured's own act, such as arson, if the lender meets its own duties, including proof of loss. A simple loss-payable wording would pay the lender only if the insured had a valid claim. Suspicion of arson does not cancel the lender's interest, and the lender need not first sue the named insured.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a simple loss-payable result, not the standard mortgage clause. The insured's arson does not automatically void an innocent lender's recovery under the standard clause.
distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the clause. It is a direct agreement with the insurer, so the lender does not have to sue the named insured before presenting its claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a cancellation. Suspicion of arson does not, by itself, terminate the mortgagee's protection under the standard clause.

prompt: A landlord asks to be an additional insured on a tenant's liability policy. The tenant's agent issues a certificate of insurance that lists the landlord as an additional insured, but no additional-insured endorsement is added to the policy. A visitor is injured in the rented space. Which document controls the landlord's status?

options.text: The certificate replaces the policy and creates additional-insured coverage even though the policy was never endorsed.
The landlord becomes the named insured, because the person listed on the certificate is the named insured on the policy.
The agent had authority to issue the certificate, and that authority makes the landlord an additional insured without an endorsement.
The policy controls. The certificate alone does not make the landlord an additional insured.

explanation: A certificate of insurance is evidence that a policy exists. It does not amend, extend, or alter the coverage. An agent's authority to issue a certificate is not authority to amend the policy. Additional-insured status is created by the policy or an endorsement, not by a certificate line the policy does not match. If the certificate and the policy disagree, the policy controls, so the landlord does not become an additional insured, and does not become the named insured, merely because the certificate says so.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the certificate the force of an endorsement. A certificate reports coverage; it does not replace the policy or create an additional insured the policy never added.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a certificate listing with the declarations. Being listed on the certificate does not make the landlord the named insured on the policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats authority to issue a certificate as authority to amend the policy. Issuing the certificate does not add an additional insured the policy never endorsed.

prompt: Two fire policies cover the same building, and each other-insurance condition says the policy pays only its pro rata share of a covered loss based on limits. Policy One's limit is twice Policy Two's limit. A covered fire causes a loss smaller than either limit. How is the loss divided?

options.text: Policy One pays the entire loss because it was issued earlier, and Policy Two pays nothing until a later claim exhausts Policy One.
The insurers share the loss in proportion to their limits, so Policy One pays twice Policy Two's share.
Each insurer pays the full amount of the fire loss, so the insured collects that damage once under each policy.
Policy Two pays the entire loss, because the larger policy is excess and a loss below the smaller limit never reaches Policy One.

explanation: A pro rata other-insurance condition divides a covered loss by each policy's share of the total limits. Policy One's limit is twice Policy Two's limit, so Policy One pays two shares and Policy Two pays one share of the same loss. The insured is not paid twice the damage. The larger policy is not excess over the smaller one, and an earlier issue date does not make Policy One primary when both conditions require a pro rata share.

distractorExplanations.a: Imposes a primary-and-excess order the conditions do not use. Both policies owe a pro rata share, so the earlier issue date does not place the whole loss on Policy One.
distractorExplanations.c: Double-pays the loss. Pro rata sharing limits the insured to the covered damage, split between the two policies by their limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the pro rata conditions into an excess ladder. Both policies share the loss by limits, so the larger policy does not wait behind the smaller one.

prompt: A claims rep knows the insured's notice of loss was late. The rep writes that the company intentionally gives up any defense based on late notice and will adjust the loss on the merits. The insured then repairs the damage. The carrier later denies the claim solely for late notice. What is that letter?

options.text: A reservation of rights, because agreeing to adjust the loss on the merits keeps the late-notice defense available.
Estoppel alone, because a written statement that the company gives up a known defense is not a waiver.
An implied waiver only, because the letter never uses the word waiver and an express waiver has to use that word.
An express waiver: the insurer intentionally gave up a known late-notice defense.

explanation: Waiver is the intentional relinquishment of a known right. The letter states that the company knows of the late notice and intentionally gives up that defense, which is an express waiver even though the letter does not use the word waiver. A reservation of rights would do the opposite and keep the defense while the loss is adjusted. Estoppel is different: it bars a party when someone else reasonably relied on misleading conduct. Reliance may also support estoppel here, but the letter itself is the waiver.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the letter with a reservation of rights. A reservation would keep the late-notice defense while the loss is adjusted; this letter intentionally gives that defense up.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps waiver and estoppel. Estoppel turns on reliance; an intentional written give-up of a known defense is an express waiver.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires the word waiver before a give-up can be express. The letter clearly states that the company knows of the late notice and intentionally relinquishes that defense.
